abstract: Following Shrager and Johnson (1995) we study growth of logi(cid:173) cal function complexity in a network swept by two overlapping waves: one of pruning, and the other of Hebbian reinforcement of connections. Results indicate a significant spatial gradient in the appearance of both linearly separable and non linearly separable functions of the two inputs of the network; the n.l.s. cells are much sparser and their slope of appearance is sensitive to parameters in a highly non-linear way.
originalAbstract: Following Shrager and Johnson (1995) we study growth of logi(cid:173) cal function complexity in a network swept by two overlapping waves: one of pruning, and the other of Hebbian reinforcement of connections. Results indicate a significant spatial gradient in the appearance of both linearly separable and non linearly separable functions of the two inputs of the network; the n.l.s. cells are much sparser and their slope of appearance is sensitive to parameters in a highly non-linear way.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the complexity of logical functions develops across a network. Two overlapping waves move through the network: one prunes connections, and the other reinforces them through Hebbian learning. The question is how this combination of connection removal and strengthening relates to the kinds of functions that appear.

The analysis distinguishes linearly separable functions from functions that are not linearly separable, using the network's two inputs. This distinction separates functions whose outputs can be divided by a linear boundary from those requiring a more complex division. The reported results show a significant spatial gradient in the appearance of both types.

Cells representing nonlinearly separable functions are much sparser. Moreover, the slope describing their appearance changes with model parameters in a strongly nonlinear way. Thus, the richer logical functions do not simply emerge uniformly throughout the network or vary proportionally with parameter changes. The findings connect the spatial organization of pruning and reinforcement with the distribution and sensitivity of computational complexity.
summary.tldr: Overlapping pruning and reinforcement waves produce spatial gradients in logical complexity, with sparse nonlinear functions showing strong parameter sensitivity.

title: Explorations with the Dynamic Wave Model

abstract: Applications of Gaussian mixture models occur frequently in the fields of statistics and artificial neural networks. One of the key issues arising from any mixture model application is how to es(cid:173) timate the optimum number of mixture components. This paper extends the Reversible-Jump Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to the case of multivariate spherical Gaussian mixtures using a hierarchical prior model. Using this method the number of mixture components is no longer fixed but becomes a param(cid:173) eter of the model which we shall estimate. The Reversible-Jump MCMC algorithm is capable of moving between parameter sub(cid:173) spaces which correspond to models with different numbers of mix(cid:173) ture components. As a result a sample from the full joint distribu(cid:173) tion of all unknown model parameters is generated. The technique is then demonstrated on a simulated example and a well known vowel dataset.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture represents data using several Gaussian components, but deciding how many components to include is itself a modeling problem. This paper treats that number as an unknown to estimate alongside the other parameters. It focuses on multivariate spherical Gaussian mixtures, whose individual components have the same spread in every direction.

The authors extend reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo to this setting using a hierarchical prior model. The key capability is movement between parameter spaces belonging to mixtures with different numbers of components. Because adding or removing a component changes how many parameters a model has, the sampling procedure must handle changes in dimension as part of its operation.

The result is a sample from the joint distribution of the unknown model parameters, including the component count. This connects model-size selection with parameter estimation in one probabilistic procedure. The paper demonstrates the technique on simulated data and a vowel dataset, illustrating its application to both a constructed example and observed multivariate data.
summary.tldr: Reversible-jump sampling estimates both the parameters and the number of components in multivariate spherical Gaussian mixtures.

title: An Application of Reversible-Jump MCMC to Multivariate Spherical Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: We derive and analyse robust optimization schemes for noisy vector quantization on the basis of deterministic annealing. Starting from a cost function for central clustering that incorporates distortions from channel noise we develop a soft topographic vector quantization al(cid:173) gorithm (STVQ) which is based on the maximum entropy principle and which performs a maximum-likelihood estimate in an expectation(cid:173) maximization (EM) fashion. Annealing in the temperature parameter f3 leads to phase transitions in the existing code vector representation dur(cid:173) ing the cooling process for which we calculate critical temperatures and modes as a function of eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the data and the transition matrix of the channel noise. A whole family of vector quantization algorithms is derived from STVQ, among them a deterministic annealing scheme for Kohonen's self-organizing map (SOM). This algorithm, which we call SSOM, is then applied to vector quantization of image data to be sent via a noisy binary symmetric channel. The algorithm's performance is compared to those of LBG and STVQ. While it is naturally superior to LBG, which does not take into account channel noise, its results compare very well to those of STVQ, which is computationally much more demanding.

paragraphs: Compressing data for transmission involves two sources of distortion: replacing the original data with a compact representation and corruption during transmission. This paper develops vector quantization methods that account for both. Its starting cost function includes channel noise, so the representation is optimized for what a receiver may recover.

The authors derive soft topographic vector quantization using maximum entropy and an expectation-maximization style procedure. Deterministic annealing gradually changes a temperature parameter, producing transitions in the code-vector representation. The paper analytically relates the critical temperatures and transition modes to the data covariance and the channel's noise-transition matrix.

This framework yields several algorithms, including an annealed version of the self-organizing map called SSOM. On image data transmitted through a noisy binary symmetric channel, SSOM outperforms LBG, which ignores channel noise, and compares favorably with the more computationally demanding STVQ. The findings connect a principled treatment of transmission errors with a less expensive learning procedure that retains strong reported performance.
summary.tldr: An annealed self-organizing map learns image compression codes that account for channel noise while comparing favorably with a more demanding method.

title: An Annealed Self-Organizing Map for Source Channel Coding

abstract: The complexity of cortical circuits may be characterized by the number of synapses per neuron. We study the dependence of complexity on the fraction of the cortical volume that is made up of "wire" (that is, ofaxons and dendrites), and find that complexity is maximized when wire takes up about 60% of the cortical volume. This prediction is in good agree(cid:173) ment with experimental observations. A consequence of our arguments is that any rearrangement of neurons that takes more wire would sacrifice computational power. Wiring a brain presents formidable problems because of the extremely large number of con(cid:173) nections: a microliter of cortex contains approximately 105 neurons, 109 synapses, and 4 km ofaxons, with 60% of the cortical volume being taken up with "wire", half of this by axons and the other half by dendrites. [ 1] Each cortical neighborhood must have exactly the right balance of components; if too many cell bodies were present in a particular mm cube, for example, insufficient space would remain for the axons, dendrites and synapses. Here we ask "What fraction of the cortical volume should be wires (axons + dendrites)?" We ar(cid:173) gue that physiological properties ofaxons and dendrites dictate an optimal wire fraction of 0.6, just what is actually observed. To calculate the optimal wire fraction, we start with a real cortical region containing a fixed number of neurons, a mm cube, for example, and imagine perturbing it by adding or sub(cid:173) tracting synapses and the axons and dendrites needed to support them. The rules for per(cid:173) turbing the cortical cube require that the existing circuit connections and function remain intact (except for what may have been removed in the perturbation), that no holes are cre(cid:173) ated, and that all added (or subtracted) synapses are typical of those present; as wire volume is added, the volume of the cube of course increases. The ratio of the number of synapses per neuron in the perturbed cortex to that in the real cortex is denoted by 8, a parameter we call the relative complexity. We require that the volume of non-wire components (cell bodies, blood vessels, glia, etc) is unchanged by our perturbation and use 4> to denote the volume fraction of the perturbed cortical region that is made up of wires (axons + dendrites; 4> can vary between zero and one), with the fraction for the real brain being 4>0. paragraphs: The paper examines how cortical space should be divided between wiring and other components. Wiring means axons and dendrites, and circuit complexity is measured by synapses per neuron. The question is which wiring fraction supports the greatest complexity under the authors' model of cortical organization.

Their argument considers a region with a fixed number of neurons and changes its synapses together with the wiring needed to support them. The volume of non-wiring components remains unchanged, added or removed synapses are typical, and existing connections and function are preserved except where removed by the perturbation. These assumptions define the comparison underlying the optimization.

The analysis places maximum complexity at a wiring fraction of about 60%, in good agreement with experimental observations. Within the authors' argument, rearrangements requiring more wire would sacrifice computational power. The result offers a spatial explanation for the observed balance of cortical components: allocating space to connections has an optimum under the stated constraints, rather than complexity simply increasing with the proportion devoted to wiring.
summary.tldr: Under the paper's cortical model, synapses per neuron are maximized when axons and dendrites occupy about 60% of cortical volume.

title: Wiring Optimization in the Brain

abstract: High dimensional data modeling is difficult mainly because the so-called "curse of dimensionality". We propose a technique called "Gaussianiza(cid:173) tion" for high dimensional density estimation, which alleviates the curse of dimensionality by exploiting the independence structures in the data. Gaussianization is motivated from recent developments in the statistics literature: projection pursuit, independent component analysis and Gaus(cid:173) sian mixture models with semi-tied covariances. We propose an iter(cid:173) ative Gaussianization procedure which converges weakly: at each it(cid:173) eration, the data is first transformed to the least dependent coordinates and then each coordinate is marginally Gaussianized by univariate tech(cid:173) niques. Gaussianization offers density estimation sharper than traditional kernel methods and radial basis function methods. Gaussianization can be viewed as efficient solution of nonlinear independent component anal(cid:173) ysis and high dimensional projection pursuit.

Gaussianization is motivated from recent developments in the statistics literature: projection pursuit, independent component analysis and Gaus(cid:173) sian mixture models with semi-tied covariances. We propose an iter(cid:173) ative Gaussianization procedure which converges weakly: at each it(cid:173) eration, the data is first transformed to the least dependent coordinates and then each coordinate is marginally Gaussianized by univariate tech(cid:173) niques. Gaussianization offers density estimation sharper than traditional kernel methods and radial basis function methods. Gaussianization can be viewed as efficient solution of nonlinear independent component anal(cid:173) ysis and high dimensional projection pursuit.

paragraphs: Gaussianization tackles high-dimensional density estimation: learning how probability is distributed across observations with many coordinates. The paper attributes much of the difficulty to the curse of dimensionality and proposes exploiting independence structure in the data. Its aim is to make the modeling problem more manageable by progressively changing the representation of the observations.

Each iteration has two stages. First, the data is transformed into coordinates that are as weakly dependent as possible. Then each coordinate is individually transformed toward a Gaussian distribution using a one-dimensional technique. Repeating these operations combines a treatment of relationships between coordinates with simpler transformations of their individual distributions. The authors establish weak convergence for this iterative procedure.

The paper reports sharper density estimation than traditional kernel and radial basis function methods. It also interprets Gaussianization as an efficient approach to nonlinear independent component analysis and high-dimensional projection pursuit. These connections explain why the procedure is useful beyond making individual variables Gaussian: it aims to organize the joint distribution so that its dependence structure becomes easier to handle.
summary.tldr: Gaussianization alternates dependence-reducing coordinate transformations with one-dimensional Gaussianization to estimate high-dimensional densities.

title: Gaussianization

This allocation scheme distributes funds across various securities or ﬁ- nancial markets while simultaneously complying with speciﬁc allocation constraints which meet the requirements of an investor. The portfolio optimization algorithm is modeled by a feedforward neural network. The underlying expected return forecasts are based on error correction neural networks (ECNN), which utilize the last model error as an auxiliary input to evaluate their own misspeciﬁcation. The portfolio optimization is implemented such that (i.) the allocations comply with investor’s constraints and that (ii.) the risk of the portfo- lio can be controlled. abstract: Greedy approximation algorithms have been frequently used to obtain sparse solutions to learning problems. In this paper, we present a general greedy algorithm for solving a class of convex optimization problems. We derive a bound on the rate of approximation for this algorithm, and show that our algorithm includes a number of earlier studies as special cases.
originalAbstract: Greedy approximation algorithms have been frequently used to obtain sparse solutions to learning problems. In this paper, we present a general greedy algorithm for solving a class of convex optimization problems. We derive a bound on the rate of approximation for this algorithm, and show that our algorithm includes a number of earlier studies as special cases.

paragraphs: The paper develops a general greedy algorithm for a class of convex optimization problems. Its motivation comes from learning problems where greedy approximation has been used to obtain sparse solutions. Sparsity means representing a solution with relatively few contributing components, making the choice of what to add at each stage central to the approach.

The theoretical contribution is a bound on the algorithm’s approximation rate. Such a bound describes how approximation quality progresses as the algorithm proceeds, giving a mathematical account of its behavior beyond simply specifying a sequence of greedy choices. The stated result concerns the class of convex problems covered by the analysis.

The authors also show that several earlier approaches fit inside their algorithm as special cases. This makes the work a unifying framework: methods previously studied separately can be understood through a shared procedure and analysis. Its significance is therefore both algorithmic and explanatory, connecting the practical motivation for sparse approximation with a general result about the rate of improvement.
summary.tldr: A general greedy algorithm unifies earlier convex approximation methods and comes with an approximation-rate bound.

title: A General Greedy Approximation Algorithm with Applications

abstract: We study an explicit parametric model of documents, queries, and rel- evancy assessment for Information Retrieval (IR). Mean-ﬁeld methods are applied to analyze the model and derive efﬁcient practical algorithms to estimate the parameters in the problem. The hyperparameters are es- timated by a fast approximate leave-one-out cross-validation procedure based on the cavity method. The algorithm is further evaluated on several benchmark databases by comparing with standard algorithms in IR.
originalAbstract: We study an explicit parametric model of documents, queries, and rel- evancy assessment for Information Retrieval (IR). Mean-ﬁeld methods are applied to analyze the model and derive efﬁcient practical algorithms to estimate the parameters in the problem. The hyperparameters are es- timated by a fast approximate leave-one-out cross-validation procedure based on the cavity method. The algorithm is further evaluated on several benchmark databases by comparing with standard algorithms in IR.

paragraphs: Information retrieval connects a user's query with documents judged relevant to it. This paper studies an explicit parametric probabilistic model of documents, queries, and relevance assessments. Placing these elements within one model makes parameter estimation a central part of learning how the retrieval system should relate queries to documents.

The authors apply mean-field methods to analyze the model and derive efficient practical algorithms for estimating its parameters. They also address hyperparameters, which govern the model or estimation procedure. These are selected using a fast approximation to leave-one-out cross-validation based on the cavity method, connecting model fitting with a separate mechanism for choosing its higher-level settings.

The resulting algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark databases against standard information retrieval algorithms. The abstract reports the evaluation but does not specify a comparative performance outcome. The methodological contribution is the combination of an explicit retrieval model, efficient approximate parameter estimation, and a fast approximate validation procedure for selecting hyperparameters.
summary.tldr: Mean-field inference and approximate cross-validation provide practical parameter and hyperparameter estimation for a probabilistic information retrieval model.

title: Mean Field Approach to a Probabilistic Model in Information Retrieval

abstract: Various problems in machine learning, databases, and statistics involve pairwise distances among a set of objects. It is often desirable for these distances to satisfy the properties of a metric, especially the triangle inequality. Applications where metric data is useful include clustering, classification, metric-based indexing, and approximation algorithms for various graph problems. This paper presents the Metric Nearness Problem: Given a dissimilarity matrix, find the “nearest” matrix of distances that satisfy the triangle inequalities. For `p nearness measures, this paper develops efficient triangle fixing algorithms that compute globally optimal solutions by exploiting the inherent structure of the problem. Empirically, the algorithms have time and storage costs that are linear in the number of triangle constraints. The methods can also be easily parallelized for additional speed.

It is often desirable for these distances to satisfy the properties of a metric, especially the triangle inequality. Applications where metric data is useful include clustering, classification, metric-based indexing, and approximation algorithms for various graph problems. This paper presents the Metric Nearness Problem: Given a dissimilarity matrix, find the “nearest” matrix of distances that satisfy the triangle inequalities. For `p nearness measures, this paper develops efficient triangle fixing algorithms that compute globally optimal solutions by exploiting the inherent structure of the problem. Empirically, the algorithms have time and storage costs that are linear in the number of triangle constraints. The methods can also be easily parallelized for additional speed.

paragraphs: The paper addresses pairwise dissimilarities that do not satisfy the triangle inequality. This inequality requires a direct distance to be no greater than the distance obtained by going through a third object. Such metric structure is useful in clustering, classification, indexing, and approximation algorithms for graph problems.

The authors formulate the Metric Nearness Problem: adjust a dissimilarity matrix into the nearest distance matrix satisfying the triangle inequalities. For the specified p-based nearness measures, they develop triangle-fixing algorithms that exploit the problem's structure and compute globally optimal solutions. The objective therefore includes both satisfying the constraints and minimizing the prescribed change to the original matrix.

Empirically, the algorithms' time and storage costs grow linearly with the number of triangle constraints. This scaling statement is about constraints, rather than the number of objects. The methods can also be parallelized for additional speed. Together, the optimization guarantee and observed computational behavior make the formulation a practical approach to repairing nonmetric dissimilarity data.
summary.tldr: Triangle-fixing algorithms find globally optimal nearby metric distances, with empirically linear costs in the number of triangle constraints.

title: Triangle Fixing Algorithms for the Metric Nearness Problem

abstract: We propose a highly efficient framework for kernel multi-class models with a large and structured set of classes. Kernel parameters are learned automatically by maximizing the cross-validation log likelihood, and predictive probabilities are estimated. We demonstrate our approach on large scale text classification tasks with hierarchical class structure, achieving state-of-the-art results in an order of magnitude less time than previous work.
originalAbstract: We propose a highly efficient framework for kernel multi-class models with a large and structured set of classes. Kernel parameters are learned automatically by maximizing the cross-validation log likelihood, and predictive probabilities are estimated. We demonstrate our approach on large scale text classification tasks with hierarchical class structure, achieving state-of-the-art results in an order of magnitude less time than previous work.

paragraphs: Classification becomes demanding when a model must distinguish among a large collection of related categories. This paper proposes an efficient framework for kernel multiclass models designed for that setting. Its target is a structured set of classes, with hierarchical text classification providing the demonstrated application.

The framework learns kernel parameters automatically by maximizing cross-validation log likelihood. This makes performance on held-out portions of the training data part of the parameter-selection objective. Because the criterion concerns likelihood, it evaluates the probabilities assigned to outcomes rather than only whether the selected class is correct. The framework also estimates predictive probabilities for its classifications.

On large text classification tasks with hierarchical classes, the authors report state-of-the-art results in roughly one tenth of the time taken by previous work. The stated contribution thus combines predictive performance with reduced computation in the evaluated setting. It also brings automatic kernel tuning and probability estimation into one framework, making model selection a central part of the proposed approach to large structured classification problems.
summary.tldr: Automatic cross-validation tuning enables efficient kernel classification across large hierarchies, with strong reported text-classification results.

title: Cross-Validation Optimization for Large Scale Hierarchical Classification Kernel Methods

abstract: We consider a generalization of stochastic bandit problems where the set of arms, X, is allowed to be a generic topological space. We constraint the mean-payoff function with a dissimilarity function over X in a way that is more general than Lipschitz. We construct an arm selection policy whose regret improves upon previous result for a large class of problems. In particular, our results imply that if X is the unit hypercube in a Euclidean space and the mean-payoff function has a finite number of global maxima around which the behavior of the function is locally Hölder with a known exponent, then the expected regret is bounded up to a logarithmic factor by $n$, i.e., the rate of the growth of the regret is independent of the dimension of the space. Moreover, we prove the minimax optimality of our algorithm for the class of mean-payoff functions we consider.
originalAbstract: We consider a generalization of stochastic bandit problems where the set of arms, X, is allowed to be a generic topological space. We constraint the mean-payoff function with a dissimilarity function over X in a way that is more general than Lipschitz. We construct an arm selection policy whose regret improves upon previous result for a large class of problems. In particular, our results imply that if X is the unit hypercube in a Euclidean space and the mean-payoff function has a finite number of global maxima around which the behavior of the function is locally Hölder with a known exponent, then the expected regret is bounded up to a logarithmic factor by $n$, i.e., the rate of the growth of the regret is independent of the dimension of the space. Moreover, we prove the minimax optimality of our algorithm for the class of mean-payoff functions we consider.

paragraphs: Stochastic bandit problems involve choosing actions with uncertain rewards while learning which choices are best. This paper allows the action set to be a generic topological space, rather than requiring a finite list. It constrains expected rewards through a dissimilarity function using a condition more general than a Lipschitz restriction.

The authors construct an action-selection policy with improved regret guarantees for a broad class of problems. Regret measures the reward lost through the sequence of choices relative to optimal behavior. The analysis connects the policy's performance to the structure of the reward function over the action space.

One stated consequence concerns a Euclidean unit hypercube with finitely many global maxima and locally Hölder behavior around them with a known exponent. Under these conditions, the reported regret growth rate is independent of the space's dimension. The authors also prove minimax optimality for their considered function class. These are conditional theoretical guarantees: the geometric and local regularity assumptions are part of what makes the dimension-independent statement possible.
summary.tldr: An action-selection policy achieves improved, minimax-optimal regret guarantees for a structured class of bandits over general action spaces.

title: Online Optimization in X-Armed Bandits

abstract: We present a probabilistic latent factor model which can be used for studying spatio-temporal datasets. The spatial and temporal structure is modeled by using Gaussian process priors both for the loading matrix and the factors. The posterior distributions are approximated using the variational Bayesian framework. High computational cost of Gaussian process modeling is reduced by using sparse approximations. The model is used to compute the reconstructions of the global sea surface temperatures from a historical dataset. The results suggest that the proposed model can outperform the state-of-the-art reconstruction systems.

The spatial and temporal structure is modeled by using Gaussian process priors both for the loading matrix and the factors. The posterior distributions are approximated using the variational Bayesian framework. High computational cost of Gaussian process modeling is reduced by using sparse approximations. It represents the observations through hidden factors and a loading matrix, so the model can describe variation using underlying components and the ways those components contribute to the observed data.

Gaussian process priors are placed on both the loadings and the factors to model spatial and temporal relationships. The authors approximate the posterior distributions with variational Bayesian inference. They also use sparse approximations to reduce the high computational cost associated with Gaussian process modeling, making computational efficiency part of the proposed inference approach.

This is evidence for the potential value of modeling spatial and temporal structure together through probabilistic factors, with approximate inference and sparse computation supporting the reconstruction task.
summary.tldr: A sparse variational Gaussian-process factor model jointly captures spatial and temporal structure, with promising historical sea-surface-temperature reconstructions.

title: Variational Gaussian-process factor analysis for modeling spatio-temporal data

abstract: Regularized risk minimization often involves non-smooth optimization, either because of the loss function (e.g., hinge loss) or the regularizer (e.g., $\ell_1$-regularizer). Gradient descent methods, though highly scalable and easy to implement, are known to converge slowly on these problems. In this paper, we develop novel accelerated gradient methods for stochastic optimization while still preserving their computational simplicity and scalability. The proposed algorithm, called SAGE (Stochastic Accelerated GradiEnt), exhibits fast convergence rates on stochastic optimization with both convex and strongly convex objectives. Experimental results show that SAGE is faster than recent (sub)gradient methods including FOLOS, SMIDAS and SCD. Moreover, SAGE can also be extended for online learning, resulting in a simple but powerful algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization problems that arise when fitting a model involves a nonsmooth loss or regularizer. Examples include hinge loss and l1 regularization. Ordinary gradient-based methods are attractive because they are simple and scalable, but their convergence can be slow in these settings. The authors seek faster progress while retaining those practical advantages.

Their algorithm, SAGE, introduces acceleration into stochastic gradient optimization. The paper establishes fast convergence rates for both convex and strongly convex objectives. These are two explicitly identified classes of optimization problems for which the method’s convergence behavior is studied. The approach is designed to preserve the computational simplicity and scalability that make gradient methods useful.

Experimental comparisons find SAGE faster than FOLOS, SMIDAS, and SCD, the recent gradient or subgradient methods examined in the paper. The authors also extend the approach to online learning. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support acceleration as a way to improve optimization speed without abandoning a relatively simple learning procedure.
summary.tldr: SAGE accelerates stochastic gradient optimization while preserving simplicity and scalability, with an extension to online learning.

title: Accelerated Gradient Methods for Stochastic Optimization and Online Learning

abstract: Boosting combines weak classifiers to form highly accurate predictors. Although the case of binary classification is well understood, in the multiclass setting, the "correct" requirements on the weak classifier, or the notion of the most efficient boosting algorithms are missing. In this paper, we create a broad and general framework, within which we make precise and identify the optimal requirements on the weak-classifier, as well as design the most effective, in a certain sense, boosting algorithms that assume such requirements.
originalAbstract: Boosting combines weak classifiers to form highly accurate predictors. Although the case of binary classification is well understood, in the multiclass setting, the "correct" requirements on the weak classifier, or the notion of the most efficient boosting algorithms are missing. In this paper, we create a broad and general framework, within which we make precise and identify the optimal requirements on the weak-classifier, as well as design the most effective, in a certain sense, boosting algorithms that assume such requirements.

paragraphs: Boosting builds an accurate predictor by combining classifiers that are individually weak. For two-class problems, the theoretical relationship between weak learners and boosting is well understood. This paper addresses the corresponding multiclass problem, where predictions must distinguish among more than two categories and the appropriate requirements on a weak learner had been less clearly established.

The authors introduce a broad framework that makes those requirements precise. Within it, they identify optimal conditions on the weak classifier and construct boosting algorithms that operate under those conditions. The contribution therefore links two questions: what the component learner must provide, and how a boosting procedure should use that capability.

This matters because claims about the effectiveness of a boosting algorithm depend on the assumptions made about its weak learner. The framework supplies a common basis for expressing both. Its optimality claims are made within that framework and in the particular sense studied by the paper; the abstract does not claim that one algorithm is universally best for every multiclass application.
summary.tldr: A general multiclass boosting framework identifies optimal weak-learner requirements and designs algorithms that are most effective in the framework’s stated sense.

title: A Theory of Multiclass Boosting

abstract: Spectral clustering is based on the spectral relaxation of the normalized/ratio graph cut criterion. While the spectral relaxation is known to be loose, it has been shown recently that a non-linear eigenproblem yields a tight relaxation of the Cheeger cut. In this paper, we extend this result considerably by providing a characterization of all balanced graph cuts which allow for a tight relaxation. Although the resulting optimization problems are non-convex and non-smooth, we provide an efficient first-order scheme which scales to large graphs. Moreover, our approach comes with the quality guarantee that given any partition as initialization the algorithm either outputs a better partition or it stops immediately.

paragraphs: Graph clustering can be expressed as cutting a graph into groups while balancing the resulting partition. Spectral clustering approaches this through a relaxed version of the graph-cut objective. The paper starts from a known weakness of that approach: the spectral relaxation can be loose, leaving a gap between the relaxed problem and the desired partitioning criterion.

Earlier work had established a tight relaxation for the Cheeger cut through a nonlinear eigenproblem. This paper broadens that result by characterizing all balanced graph cuts that admit a tight relaxation. The contribution therefore concerns which partitioning objectives can receive this stronger mathematical treatment, rather than only one particular cut criterion.

The resulting optimization problems are nonconvex and nonsmooth, but the authors provide an efficient first-order method that scales to large graphs. It also has a concrete initialization guarantee: from any supplied partition, it either returns a better partition or stops immediately. That guarantee concerns improvement over the starting partition, rather than a claim of globally optimal clustering.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes balanced graph cuts with tight relaxations and provides a scalable algorithm that improves its initial partition or stops.

title: Beyond Spectral Clustering - Tight Relaxations of Balanced Graph Cuts

abstract: We present an approach to detecting and analyzing the 3D configuration of objects in real-world images with heavy occlusion and clutter. We focus on the application of finding and analyzing cars. We do so with a two-stage model; the first stage reasons about 2D shape and appearance variation due to within-class variation(station wagons look different than sedans) and changes in viewpoint. Rather than using a view-based model, we describe a compositional representation that models a large number of effective views and shapes using a small number of local view-based templates. We use this model to propose candidate detections and 2D estimates of shape. These estimates are then refined by our second stage, using an explicit 3D model of shape and viewpoint. We use a morphable model to capture 3D within-class variation, and use a weak-perspective camera model to capture viewpoint. We learn all model parameters from 2D annotations. We demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy for detection, viewpoint estimation, and 3D shape reconstruction on challenging images from the PASCAL VOC 2011 dataset.

We demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy for detection, viewpoint estimation, and 3D shape reconstruction on challenging images from the PASCAL VOC 2011 dataset.

paragraphs: Detecting a car in a cluttered image is only part of understanding it: the system must also estimate its viewpoint and three-dimensional shape despite occlusion. The paper handles these linked tasks with two stages, first reasoning about visible two-dimensional structure and then refining the result with an explicit three-dimensional model.

The first stage combines a small collection of local view-based templates into a representation covering many effective shapes and viewpoints. This accommodates differences between car types as well as changes in viewing angle. It produces candidate detections and two-dimensional shape estimates that provide the starting point for the second stage.

The refinement stage uses a morphable model for variation in three-dimensional car shape and a weak-perspective camera model for viewpoint. All model parameters are learned from two-dimensional annotations. On challenging PASCAL VOC 2011 images, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy for detection, viewpoint estimation, and three-dimensional reconstruction. The findings support combining flexible local image evidence with explicit geometric refinement.
summary.tldr: A two-stage car model combines local image templates with explicit 3D refinement to detect and reconstruct cars in cluttered, occluded images.

title: Analyzing 3D Objects in Cluttered Images

abstract: Factor analysis models effectively summarise the covariance structure of high dimensional data, but the solutions are typically hard to interpret. This motivates attempting to find a disjoint partition, i.e. a clustering, of observed variables so that variables in a cluster are highly correlated. We introduce a Bayesian non-parametric approach to this problem, and demonstrate advantages over heuristic methods proposed to date.
originalAbstract: Factor analysis models effectively summarise the covariance structure of high dimensional data, but the solutions are typically hard to interpret. This motivates attempting to find a disjoint partition, i.e. a clustering, of observed variables so that variables in a cluster are highly correlated. We introduce a Bayesian non-parametric approach to this problem, and demonstrate advantages over heuristic methods proposed to date.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to make the relationships among many measured variables easier to interpret. Factor analysis can summarize their covariance structure, describing how variables vary together, but its resulting representation can be difficult to understand. The authors pursue a more explicit summary: divide the observed variables into separate groups whose members are highly correlated.

The objects being clustered are the variables themselves. The desired result is a disjoint partition, so each variable belongs to one group. This gives the representation a direct interpretation: a group collects measurements that tend to vary together. The proposed approach frames this grouping problem using Bayesian nonparametric modeling, providing a probabilistic alternative to the heuristic methods discussed in the paper.

The authors report advantages over those heuristic approaches. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling choice and an interpretability goal: use a Bayesian framework to seek clearly separated groups of related variables. It offers another way to summarize high-dimensional covariance when an explicit grouping is the desired output.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric model groups correlated variables into disjoint clusters to make high-dimensional covariance structure easier to interpret.

title: A nonparametric variable clustering model

abstract: We study the problem of estimating, in the sense of optimal transport metrics, a measure which is assumed supported on a manifold embedded in a Hilbert space. By establishing a precise connection between optimal transport metrics, optimal quantization, and learning theory, we derive new probabilistic bounds for the performance of a classic algorithm in unsupervised learning (k-means), when used to produce a probability measure derived from the data. In the course of the analysis, we arrive at new lower bounds, as well as probabilistic bounds on the convergence rate of the empirical law of large numbers, which, unlike existing bounds, are applicable to a wide class of measures.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately data can be used to estimate a probability measure when error is assessed using optimal transport metrics. The measure is assumed to be supported on a manifold embedded in a Hilbert space. This places the estimation problem in a geometric setting, where the structure of the space supporting the data is part of the analysis.

The authors establish a connection between optimal transport, optimal quantization, and learning theory. They use this connection to obtain probabilistic performance bounds for k-means when its output is used to construct a probability measure from observations. This gives the familiar clustering algorithm an additional interpretation as a tool for approximating an underlying distribution.

The analysis also produces new lower bounds and probabilistic convergence-rate bounds for the empirical law of large numbers. The authors state that the latter apply to a broad class of measures beyond the reach of existing bounds. The findings connect practical distribution approximation with theoretical limits and guarantees on how empirical distributions approach their underlying measures.
summary.tldr: Connections between optimal transport, quantization, and learning theory yield new guarantees for k-means as a probability-measure estimator.

title: Learning Probability Measures with respect to Optimal Transport Metrics

abstract: Psychologists are interested in developing instructional policies that boost student learning. An instructional policy specifies the manner and content of instruction. For example, in the domain of concept learning, a policy might specify the nature of exemplars chosen over a training sequence. Traditional psychological studies compare several hand-selected policies, e.g., contrasting a policy that selects only difficult-to-classify exemplars with a policy that gradually progresses over the training sequence from easy exemplars to more difficult (known as {\em fading}). We propose an alternative to the traditional methodology in which we define a parameterized space of policies and search this space to identify the optimum policy. For example, in concept learning, policies might be described by a fading function that specifies exemplar difficulty over time. We propose an experimental technique for searching policy spaces using Gaussian process surrogate-based optimization and a generative model of student performance. Instead of evaluating a few experimental conditions each with many human subjects, as the traditional methodology does, our technique evaluates many experimental conditions each with a few subjects. Even though individual subjects provide only a noisy estimate of the population mean, the optimization method allows us to determine the shape of the policy space and identify the global optimum, and is as efficient in its subject budget as a traditional A-B comparison. We evaluate the method via two behavioral studies, and suggest that the method has broad applicability to optimization problems involving humans in domains beyond the educational arena.

paragraphs: An instructional policy specifies what learners encounter and how instruction unfolds. For concept learning, it might determine how example difficulty changes over a training sequence. Traditional experiments compare a few policies selected by researchers. This paper instead defines a parameterized policy space and searches it for the policy that produces the best learning outcomes.

The proposed experimental method combines Gaussian-process surrogate optimization with a generative model of student performance. The optimization procedure uses noisy individual outcomes to infer the shape of the policy space and identify its global optimum.

This matters because the same experimental budget can support a broader search over instructional choices. They also suggest applicability to human-centered optimization beyond education, extending the methodological idea of searching policies through noisy behavioral measurements.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process optimization searches instructional policy spaces using noisy student outcomes with participant-budget efficiency comparable to an A-B comparison.

title: Optimizing Instructional Policies

abstract: Bipartite ranking aims to learn a real-valued ranking function that orders positive instances before negative instances. Recent efforts of bipartite ranking are focused on optimizing ranking accuracy at the top of the ranked list. Most existing approaches are either to optimize task specific metrics or to extend the rank loss by emphasizing more on the error associated with the top ranked instances, leading to a high computational cost that is super-linear in the number of training instances. We propose a highly efficient approach, titled TopPush, for optimizing accuracy at the top that has computational complexity linear in the number of training instances. We present a novel analysis that bounds the generalization error for the top ranked instances for the proposed approach. Empirical study shows that the proposed approach is highly competitive to the state-of-the-art approaches and is 10-100 times faster.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking learns scores that place positive examples ahead of negative ones. In many ranking tasks, accuracy near the top of the list is especially important. This paper addresses the computational expense of optimizing that region, where existing approaches often require more than linear growth in work as training data increase.

The authors propose TopPush, an approach aimed directly at accuracy among the highest-ranked instances. Its computational complexity is linear in the number of training instances. This scaling matters because it makes the size of the training set a more manageable contributor to computational cost while retaining the focus on the top of the ranking.

The paper also derives a generalization error bound specifically for top-ranked instances, connecting its training approach to performance beyond the training examples. Empirically, TopPush is highly competitive with state-of-the-art approaches and runs 10–100 times faster in the reported study. The contribution combines an efficient ranking objective and algorithm with theoretical analysis targeted to the same part of the list that motivates the method.
summary.tldr: TopPush optimizes top-of-list ranking accuracy with linear training-set complexity and reported speed gains of 10–100 times.

title: Top Rank Optimization in Linear Time

abstract: Performance metrics for binary classification are designed to capture tradeoffs between four fundamental population quantities: true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Despite significant interest from theoretical and applied communities, little is known about either optimal classifiers or consistent algorithms for optimizing binary classification performance metrics beyond a few special cases. We consider a fairly large family of performance metrics given by ratios of linear combinations of the four fundamental population quantities. This family includes many well known binary classification metrics such as classification accuracy, AM measure, F-measure and the Jaccard similarity coefficient as special cases. Our analysis identifies the optimal classifiers as the sign of the thresholded conditional probability of the positive class, with a performance metric-dependent threshold. The optimal threshold can be constructed using simple plug-in estimators when the performance metric is a linear combination of the population quantities, but alternative techniques are required for the general case. We propose two algorithms for estimating the optimal classifiers, and prove their statistical consistency. Both algorithms are straightforward modifications of standard approaches to address the key challenge of optimal threshold selection, thus are simple to implement in practice. The first algorithm combines a plug-in estimate of the conditional probability of the positive class with optimal threshold selection. The second algorithm leverages recent work on calibrated asymmetric surrogate losses to construct candidate classifiers. We present empirical comparisons between these algorithms on benchmark datasets.

This paper studies a broad family of metrics expressed as ratios of linear combinations of those four population quantities. The family includes accuracy, AM measure, F-measure, and Jaccard similarity, bringing several familiar evaluation goals into one analysis.

Both modify standard approaches and are described as straightforward to implement. Benchmark comparisons examine their empirical behavior. The theoretical result explains how probability estimation or surrogate-based learning can be connected to the particular metric a practitioner wants to optimize.
summary.tldr: For a broad family of binary classification metrics, optimal prediction uses metric-specific probability thresholds that two proposed consistent algorithms estimate.

title: Consistent Binary Classification with Generalized Performance Metrics

abstract: Tree structured group Lasso (TGL) is a powerful technique in uncovering the tree structured sparsity over the features, where each node encodes a group of features. It has been applied successfully in many real-world applications. However, with extremely large feature dimensions, solving TGL remains a significant challenge due to its highly complicated regularizer. In this paper, we propose a novel Multi-Layer Feature reduction method (MLFre) to quickly identify the inactive nodes (the groups of features with zero coefficients in the solution) hierarchically in a top-down fashion, which are guaranteed to be irrelevant to the response. Thus, we can remove the detected nodes from the optimization without sacrificing accuracy. The major challenge in developing such testing rules is due to the overlaps between the parents and their children nodes. By a novel hierarchical projection algorithm, MLFre is able to test the nodes independently from any of their ancestor nodes. Moreover, we can integrate MLFre---that has a low computational cost---with any existing solvers. Experiments on both synthetic and real data sets demonstrate that the speedup gained by MLFre can be orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Tree structured group Lasso organizes features into a hierarchy of groups and encourages sparsity consistent with that structure. Its regularizer can make optimization difficult when the feature space is extremely large. This paper proposes Multi-Layer Feature reduction, or MLFre, to remove groups that are guaranteed to have zero coefficients in the solution.

MLFre examines the hierarchy from the top down. The central complication is that parent groups overlap with their children, making it difficult to test groups separately. A hierarchical projection algorithm allows a node to be tested independently of its ancestors. Once a group is certified inactive, it can be excluded from optimization without sacrificing solution accuracy.

The authors describe the screening procedure as inexpensive and compatible with existing solvers. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that its speedups can reach orders of magnitude. The result demonstrates how exploiting the feature hierarchy before or during optimization can substantially reduce the work required to solve the same structured sparsity problem.
summary.tldr: MLFre safely removes inactive feature groups from tree structured group Lasso, with reported speedups reaching orders of magnitude.

title: Multi-Layer Feature Reduction for Tree Structured Group Lasso via Hierarchical Projection

abstract: Given a directed acyclic graph $G,$ and a set of values $y$ on the vertices, the Isotonic Regression of $y$ is a vector $x$ that respects the partial order described by $G,$ and minimizes $\|x-y\|,$ for a specified norm. This paper gives improved algorithms for computing the Isotonic Regression for all weighted $\ell_{p}$-norms with rigorous performance guarantees. Our algorithms are quite practical, and their variants can be implemented to run fast in practice.
originalAbstract: Given a directed acyclic graph $G,$ and a set of values $y$ on the vertices, the Isotonic Regression of $y$ is a vector $x$ that respects the partial order described by $G,$ and minimizes $\|x-y\|,$ for a specified norm. This paper gives improved algorithms for computing the Isotonic Regression for all weighted $\ell_{p}$-norms with rigorous performance guarantees. Our algorithms are quite practical, and their variants can be implemented to run fast in practice.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression adjusts a collection of values so that they obey specified ordering relationships while staying as close as possible to the originals. Here, a directed acyclic graph describes those relationships, and each vertex has an observed value. The desired output satisfies the graph’s partial order and minimizes a chosen measure of discrepancy.

The choice of discrepancy matters because it defines which adjustments count as costly. This paper provides improved algorithms across all weighted Lp norms, covering a family of objectives rather than a single error measure. The ordering constraints remain the organizing structure of the problem, while the norm determines how deviation from the observed values is evaluated.

The algorithms come with rigorous performance guarantees. The authors also describe them as practical and state that variants can be implemented to run quickly in practice. The contribution is therefore computational: it improves methods for solving order-constrained fitting problems while supporting a broad range of weighted distance objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper improves algorithms for fitting values to graph-defined ordering constraints across all weighted Lp norms.

title: Fast, Provable Algorithms for Isotonic Regression in all L_p-norms

abstract: The F-measure is an important and commonly used performance metric for binary prediction tasks. By combining precision and recall into a single score, it avoids disadvantages of simple metrics like the error rate, especially in cases of imbalanced class distributions. The problem of optimizing the F-measure, that is, of developing learning algorithms that perform optimally in the sense of this measure, has recently been tackled by several authors. In this paper, we study the problem of F-measure maximization in the setting of online learning. We propose an efficient online algorithm and provide a formal analysis of its convergence properties. Moreover, first experimental results are presented, showing that our method performs well in practice.

Moreover, first experimental results are presented, showing that our method performs well in practice.

paragraphs: Binary prediction is often evaluated using the F-measure, which combines precision and recall. This is especially useful when class frequencies are imbalanced, a setting where simple error rate can be an inadequate guide. The paper takes that evaluation choice seriously by making F-measure maximization the learning objective.

Its focus is online learning, where learning proceeds as examples arrive. The authors propose an efficient online algorithm for optimizing the F-measure and formally analyze its convergence. This extends the question of learning for this metric into a sequential setting, connecting the algorithm's objective to the score used to judge its predictions.

Initial experiments show that the method performs well in practice. These empirical findings complement the convergence analysis: one addresses mathematical behavior, while the other provides early evidence of practical usefulness. The contribution is a metric-focused online learning method, motivated by the mismatch that can arise when a binary predictor is evaluated through precision and recall but trained with a simpler performance objective.
summary.tldr: An efficient online algorithm directly targets F-measure, with convergence analysis and encouraging initial experiments.

title: Online F-Measure Optimization

abstract: We study fast learning rates when the losses are not necessarily bounded and may have a distribution with heavy tails. To enable such analyses, we introduce two new conditions: (i) the envelope function $\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}|\ell \circ f|$, where $\ell$ is the loss function and $\mathcal{F}$ is the hypothesis class, exists and is $L^r$-integrable, and (ii) $\ell$ satisfies the multi-scale Bernstein's condition on $\mathcal{F}$. Under these assumptions, we prove that learning rate faster than $O(n^{-1/2})$ can be obtained and, depending on $r$ and the multi-scale Bernstein's powers, can be arbitrarily close to $O(n^{-1})$. We then verify these assumptions and derive fast learning rates for the problem of vector quantization by $k$-means clustering with heavy-tailed distributions. The analyses enable us to obtain novel learning rates that extend and complement existing results in the literature from both theoretical and practical viewpoints.
originalAbstract: We study fast learning rates when the losses are not necessarily bounded and may have a distribution with heavy tails. To enable such analyses, we introduce two new conditions: (i) the envelope function $\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}|\ell \circ f|$, where $\ell$ is the loss function and $\mathcal{F}$ is the hypothesis class, exists and is $L^r$-integrable, and (ii) $\ell$ satisfies the multi-scale Bernstein's condition on $\mathcal{F}$. Under these assumptions, we prove that learning rate faster than $O(n^{-1/2})$ can be obtained and, depending on $r$ and the multi-scale Bernstein's powers, can be arbitrarily close to $O(n^{-1})$. We then verify these assumptions and derive fast learning rates for the problem of vector quantization by $k$-means clustering with heavy-tailed distributions. The analyses enable us to obtain novel learning rates that extend and complement existing results in the literature from both theoretical and practical viewpoints.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed losses allow unusually large errors, making learning-rate analysis harder than when losses are bounded. This paper studies conditions under which learning can still improve faster than the familiar rate proportional to one over the square root of the sample size. Its results accommodate losses that need not be bounded.

The analysis introduces two requirements. First, an envelope covering the absolute losses across the hypothesis class must exist and have a finite r-th moment. Second, the loss must satisfy a multi-scale Bernstein condition on that class. Together, these assumptions provide the control needed to establish faster rates despite the possibility of large loss values.

Under these conditions, the authors prove rates faster than O(n⁻¹ᐟ²). Depending on the moment parameter and the powers in the Bernstein condition, the rates can approach O(n⁻¹) arbitrarily closely. They also verify the assumptions for vector quantization using k-means with heavy-tailed distributions. This application shows how the general conditions yield concrete guarantees beyond bounded-loss settings.
summary.tldr: Fast learning rates remain possible with heavy-tailed losses under moment and multi-scale Bernstein conditions, including for k-means vector quantization.

title: Fast learning rates with heavy-tailed losses

abstract: Dynamic time warping (DTW) is a fundamental technique in time series analysis for comparing one curve to another using a flexible time-warping function. However, it was designed to compare a single pair of curves. In many applications, such as in metabolomics and image series analysis, alignment is simultaneously needed for multiple pairs. Because the underlying warping functions are often related, independent application of DTW to each pair is a sub-optimal solution. Yet, it is largely unknown how to efficiently conduct a joint alignment with all warping functions simultaneously considered, since any given warping function is constrained by the others and dynamic programming cannot be applied. In this paper, we show that the joint alignment problem can be transformed into a network flow problem and thus can be exactly and efficiently solved by the max flow algorithm, with a guarantee of global optimality. We name the proposed approach graphical time warping (GTW), emphasizing the graphical nature of the solution and that the dependency structure of the warping functions can be represented by a graph. Modifications of DTW, such as windowing and weighting, are readily derivable within GTW. We also discuss optimal tuning of parameters and hyperparameters in GTW. We illustrate the power of GTW using both synthetic data and a real case study of an astrocyte calcium movie.

The contribution is a computational formulation that treats related alignments together, making their dependency structure part of the optimization rather than leaving each curve pair to be aligned independently.
summary.tldr: Graphical time warping converts coupled curve alignment into a network flow problem that can be solved efficiently with global optimality.

title: Graphical Time Warping for Joint Alignment of Multiple Curves

abstract: Fluorescent calcium indicators are a popular means for observing the spiking activity of large neuronal populations. Unfortunately, extracting the spike train of each neuron from raw fluorescence calcium imaging data is a nontrivial problem. We present a fast online active set method to solve this sparse nonnegative deconvolution problem. Importantly, the algorithm progresses through each time series sequentially from beginning to end, thus enabling real-time online spike inference during the imaging session. Our algorithm is a generalization of the pool adjacent violators algorithm (PAVA) for isotonic regression and inherits its linear-time computational complexity. We gain remarkable increases in processing speed: more than one order of magnitude compared to currently employed state of the art convex solvers relying on interior point methods. Our method can exploit warm starts; therefore optimizing model hyperparameters only requires a handful of passes through the data. The algorithm enables real-time simultaneous deconvolution of $O(10^5)$ traces of whole-brain zebrafish imaging data on a laptop.

This paper treats recovery as sparse nonnegative deconvolution: inferring a sparse sequence of nonnegative events from the measured fluorescence time series.

The authors introduce an active-set algorithm that processes each series sequentially from beginning to end. This organization enables inference during the imaging session. The method generalizes the pool adjacent violators algorithm used in isotonic regression and retains linear-time computational complexity. It can also reuse an existing solution through warm starts, so adjusting model hyperparameters requires only a handful of passes over the data.

The reported processing speed exceeds that of commonly used interior-point convex solvers by more than an order of magnitude. The algorithm also enables real-time simultaneous deconvolution of roughly one hundred thousand whole-brain zebrafish imaging traces on a laptop. These findings connect an efficient optimization method to a concrete experimental capability: estimating neuronal activity while a large-scale recording is still underway.
summary.tldr: A linear-time sequential deconvolution algorithm enables real-time spike inference from large calcium-imaging recordings.

title: Fast Active Set Methods for Online Spike Inference from Calcium Imaging

abstract: Learning directed acyclic graphs using both observational and interventional data is now a fundamentally important problem due to recent technological developments in genomics that generate such single-cell gene expression data at a very large scale. In order to utilize this data for learning gene regulatory networks, efficient and reliable causal inference algorithms are needed that can make use of both observational and interventional data. In this paper, we present two algorithms of this type and prove that both are consistent under the faithfulness assumption. These algorithms are interventional adaptations of the Greedy SP algorithm and are the first algorithms using both observational and interventional data with consistency guarantees. Moreover, these algorithms have the advantage that they are nonparametric, which makes them useful also for analyzing non-Gaussian data. In this paper, we present these two algorithms and their consistency guarantees, and we analyze their performance on simulated data, protein signaling data, and single-cell gene expression data.

paragraphs: Causal discovery can draw on both observations of a system and data collected after interventions. The paper develops algorithms that use these two sources together to learn directed acyclic graphs. Its motivating setting is biological network discovery, where large-scale single-cell measurements create a need for efficient and reliable causal analysis.

The authors introduce two interventional adaptations of the Greedy SP algorithm. Both receive consistency guarantees under the faithfulness assumption, making that assumption central to the theoretical claim. Consistency concerns recovery with increasing data; it should not be read as a promise of exact recovery from every finite dataset. The algorithms are also nonparametric and can therefore be used with non-Gaussian data.

Performance is analyzed on simulated data, protein signaling measurements, and single-cell gene expression data. These evaluations connect the algorithmic proposal to the biological settings that motivate it. The main stated contribution is the combination of observational and interventional evidence with conditional consistency guarantees, extending permutation-based causal inference to settings where actively changing a system supplies additional information.
summary.tldr: Two nonparametric causal-discovery algorithms combine observational and interventional data, with consistency guarantees under faithfulness.

title: Permutation-based Causal Inference Algorithms with Interventions

abstract: The Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU) method is a ubiquitous meta-algorithm that works as follows: A distribution is maintained on a certain set, and at each step the probability assigned to action $\gamma$ is multiplied by $(1 -\epsilon C(\gamma))>0$ where $C(\gamma)$ is the ``cost" of action $\gamma$ and then rescaled to ensure that the new values form a distribution. We analyze MWU in congestion games where agents use \textit{arbitrary admissible constants} as learning rates $\epsilon$ and prove convergence to \textit{exact Nash equilibria}. Interestingly, this convergence result does not carry over to the nearly homologous MWU variant where at each step the probability assigned to action $\gamma$ is multiplied by $(1 -\epsilon)^{C(\gamma)}$ even for the simplest case of two-agent, two-strategy load balancing games, where such dynamics can provably lead to limit cycles or even chaotic behavior.

paragraphs: Multiplicative weights update maintains a probability distribution over actions and adjusts each action's weight according to its cost. This paper studies its behavior in congestion games when agents use constant learning rates. The central question is whether repeated updates settle at an exact Nash equilibrium or continue moving indefinitely.

For the update that multiplies an action's probability by 1−εC and then normalizes, the authors prove convergence to exact Nash equilibria for arbitrary admissible constant learning rates. Here, C is the action's cost and ε is the learning rate; admissibility includes keeping the multiplicative factor positive. The result therefore permits constant rates without asserting that every numerical choice is valid.

A closely related rule replaces that factor with (1−ε)^C, yet its behavior can be radically different. Even a load balancing game with two agents and two strategies can exhibit limit cycles or chaos under this variant. The comparison shows that seemingly similar cost-based updates can have fundamentally different long-term dynamics.
summary.tldr: One constant-rate multiplicative weights rule converges in congestion games, while a closely related rule can produce cycles or chaos.

title: Multiplicative Weights Update with Constant Step-Size in Congestion Games: Convergence, Limit Cycles and Chaos

abstract: Distributed training of deep nets is an important technique to address some of the present day computing challenges like memory consumption and computational demands. Classical distributed approaches, synchronous or asynchronous, are based on the parameter server architecture, i.e., worker nodes compute gradients which are communicated to the parameter server while updated parameters are returned. Recently, distributed training with AllReduce operations gained popularity as well. While many of those operations seem appealing, little is reported about wall-clock training time improvements. In this paper, we carefully analyze the AllReduce based setup, propose timing models which include network latency, bandwidth, cluster size and compute time, and demonstrate that a pipelined training with a width of two combines the best of both synchronous and asynchronous training. Specifically, for a setup consisting of a four-node GPU cluster we show wall-clock time training improvements of up to 5.4x compared to conventional approaches.

paragraphs: Distributed training spreads a neural network's computational work across machines, but communication can affect how quickly training actually finishes. This paper focuses on elapsed training time in systems based on AllReduce operations. It examines the practical timing of distributed work rather than relying only on the appeal of a communication mechanism.

The authors develop timing models that include network latency, bandwidth, the number of machines, and computation time. These factors jointly determine the cost of coordinating training. Based on this analysis, they propose Pipe-SGD, a decentralized framework using pipelined training with a width of two, which they describe as combining benefits of synchronous and asynchronous approaches.

On a four-node GPU cluster, the reported wall-clock training improvement reaches up to 5.4 times compared with conventional approaches. That figure belongs to the evaluated setup and is an upper reported improvement. The broader contribution is to connect a particular pipeline design with an explicit account of the communication and computation costs that determine real training speed.
summary.tldr: Pipe-SGD uses a width-two training pipeline and reports up to 5.4-fold wall-clock speedups on a four-node GPU cluster.

title: Pipe-SGD: A Decentralized Pipelined SGD Framework for Distributed Deep Net Training

abstract: Estimating how uncertain an AI system is in its predictions is important to improve the safety of such systems. Uncertainty in predictive can result from uncertainty in model parameters, irreducible \emph{data uncertainty} and uncertainty due to distributional mismatch between the test and training data distributions. Different actions might be taken depending on the source of the uncertainty so it is important to be able to distinguish between them. Recently, baseline tasks and metrics have been defined and several practical methods to estimate uncertainty developed. These methods, however, attempt to model uncertainty due to distributional mismatch either implicitly through \emph{model uncertainty} or as \emph{data uncertainty}. This work proposes a new framework for modeling predictive uncertainty called Prior Networks (PNs) which explicitly models \emph{distributional uncertainty}. PNs do this by parameterizing a prior distribution over predictive distributions. This work focuses on uncertainty for classification and evaluates PNs on the tasks of identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) samples and detecting misclassification on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, where they are found to outperform previous methods. Experiments on synthetic and MNIST and CIFAR-10 data show that unlike previous non-Bayesian methods PNs are able to distinguish between data and distributional uncertainty.

paragraphs: A prediction can be uncertain because the data are inherently ambiguous, the model parameters are uncertain, or the input differs from the training distribution. These sources can call for different responses. This paper introduces Prior Networks to explicitly represent the distributional-mismatch component instead of absorbing it into other uncertainty measures.

A Prior Network parameterizes a prior distribution over predictive distributions. The paper focuses on classification and evaluates whether this representation can identify out-of-distribution inputs and detect classification mistakes. The experiments include synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.

On MNIST and CIFAR-10, Prior Networks outperform previous methods on the reported detection tasks. The experiments also show a distinction between data uncertainty and distributional uncertainty that earlier non-Bayesian methods did not achieve. The abstract gives no detection rates, so the result establishes comparative evidence in these settings rather than a quantified guarantee of reliable uncertainty estimates everywhere.
summary.tldr: Prior Networks distinguish uncertainty in the data from uncertainty caused by distributional mismatch.

title: Predictive Uncertainty Estimation via Prior Networks

abstract: As an incremental-gradient algorithm, the hybrid stochastic gradient descent (HSGD) enjoys merits of both stochastic and full gradient methods for finite-sum minimization problem. However, the existing rate-of-convergence analysis for HSGD is made under with-replacement sampling (WRS) and is restricted to convex problems. It is not clear whether HSGD still carries these advantages under the common practice of without-replacement sampling (WoRS) for non-convex problems. In this paper, we affirmatively answer this open question by showing that under WoRS and for both convex and non-convex problems, it is still possible for HSGD (with constant step-size) to match full gradient descent in rate of convergence, while maintaining comparable sample-size-independent incremental first-order oracle complexity to stochastic gradient descent. For a special class of finite-sum problems with linear prediction models, our convergence results can be further improved in some cases. Extensive numerical results confirm our theoretical affirmation and demonstrate the favorable efficiency of WoRS-based HSGD.
