paragraphs: Hybrid stochastic gradient descent combines features of stochastic and full-gradient methods for objectives expressed as finite sums. Earlier convergence analysis covered convex problems with sampling that allows replacement. This paper asks whether the method's advantages can extend to sampling without replacement and to nonconvex objectives.

The authors show that, in both convex and nonconvex settings under without-replacement sampling, constant-step-size HSGD can match full gradient descent's convergence rate while retaining incremental first-order oracle complexity comparable to stochastic gradient descent and independent of sample size. These are two distinct advantages: how quickly convergence progresses and how much incremental gradient information is required.

For a special class of finite-sum objectives using linear prediction models, some convergence results can be improved further. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate favorable efficiency for the without-replacement version. The contribution broadens the settings in which HSGD's combined advantages can be established, while retaining the qualified claim that the stronger linear-model results apply only in some cases.
summary.tldr: Hybrid SGD can retain favorable convergence and oracle complexity under without-replacement sampling, including for nonconvex problems.

title: New Insight into Hybrid Stochastic Gradient Descent: Beyond With-Replacement Sampling and Convexity

abstract: Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (WGANs) can be used to generate realistic samples from complicated image distributions. The Wasserstein metric used in WGANs is based on a notion of distance between individual images, which induces a notion of distance between probability distributions of images. So far the community has considered $\ell^2$ as the underlying distance. We generalize the theory of WGAN with gradient penalty to Banach spaces, allowing practitioners to select the features to emphasize in the generator. We further discuss the effect of some particular choices of underlying norms, focusing on Sobolev norms. Finally, we demonstrate a boost in performance for an appropriate choice of norm on CIFAR-10 and CelebA.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein generative adversarial network compares distributions of images using a distance that ultimately depends on how individual images are compared. That underlying choice matters: it determines which image differences contribute to the training objective. The paper starts from the observation that prior WGAN work had used the ordinary ℓ² distance for this purpose.

The authors extend the theory of WGANs with gradient penalties to Banach spaces. This broader mathematical setting allows different norms to define image distance, giving practitioners a way to choose which features the generator should emphasize. The paper examines several such choices, with particular attention to Sobolev norms and their effect on the model.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CelebA show improved performance for an appropriate choice of norm. The finding supports treating the underlying image distance as a meaningful modeling decision. It does not establish that every alternative norm improves generation; the reported benefit depends on choosing one that works well for the task. The contribution combines that empirical result with a theoretical framework for making such choices.
summary.tldr: Extending gradient-penalty WGANs to Banach spaces lets image-distance choices emphasize different features and can improve generation.

title: Banach Wasserstein GAN

abstract: Goal-oriented reinforcement learning has recently been a practical framework for robotic manipulation tasks, in which an agent is required to reach a certain goal defined by a function on the state space. However, the sparsity of such reward definition makes traditional reinforcement learning algorithms very inefficient. Hindsight Experience Replay (HER), a recent advance, has greatly improved sample efficiency and practical applicability for such problems. It exploits previous replays by constructing imaginary goals in a simple heuristic way, acting like an implicit curriculum to alleviate the challenge of sparse reward signal. In this paper, we introduce Hindsight Goal Generation (HGG), a novel algorithmic framework that generates valuable hindsight goals which are easy for an agent to achieve in the short term and are also potential for guiding the agent to reach the actual goal in the long term. We have extensively evaluated our goal generation algorithm on a number of robotic manipulation tasks and demonstrated substantially improvement over the original HER in terms of sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Goal-oriented reinforcement learning can provide very little feedback when rewards depend on reaching a specified target. An agent may gather many experiences without receiving a useful success signal. Hindsight Experience Replay helps by reinterpreting past experience using imagined goals, creating an implicit progression of learning opportunities from what the agent has already done.

This paper introduces Hindsight Goal Generation to improve the choice of those goals. Its framework generates goals that are achievable in the near term while also having potential to guide the agent toward the actual target over the longer term. The key consideration is therefore both immediate feasibility and relevance to the eventual objective.

The authors evaluate the approach on several robotic manipulation tasks and report substantial gains in sample efficiency over the original hindsight replay method. This means the reported improvement concerns how effectively the agent learns from its experience. The findings support goal generation as an important part of addressing sparse rewards, with intermediate goals serving as useful learning opportunities on the way toward the desired task.
summary.tldr: Hindsight Goal Generation improves sample efficiency in tested robotic tasks by choosing attainable intermediate goals with potential to support the final objective.

title: Exploration via Hindsight Goal Generation

abstract: The likelihood function is a fundamental component in Bayesian statistics. However, evaluating the likelihood of an observation is computationally intractable in many applications. In this paper, we propose a non-parametric approximation of the likelihood that identifies a probability measure which lies in the neighborhood of the nominal measure and that maximizes the probability of observing the given sample point. We show that when the neighborhood is constructed by the Kullback-Leibler divergence, by moment conditions or by the Wasserstein distance, then our optimistic likelihood can be determined through the solution of a convex optimization problem, and it admits an analytical expression in particular cases. We also show that the posterior inference problem with our optimistic likelihood approximation enjoys strong theoretical performance guarantees, and it performs competitively in a probabilistic classification task.

In this paper, we propose a non-parametric approximation of the likelihood that identifies a probability measure which lies in the neighborhood of the nominal measure and that maximizes the probability of observing the given sample point. We show that when the neighborhood is constructed by the Kullback-Leibler divergence, by moment conditions or by the Wasserstein distance, then our optimistic likelihood can be determined through the solution of a convex optimization problem, and it admits an analytical expression in particular cases. We also show that the posterior inference problem with our optimistic likelihood approximation enjoys strong theoretical performance guarantees, and it performs competitively in a probabilistic classification task.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference uses a likelihood to express how compatible an observation is with a model, but calculating that likelihood can be computationally intractable. This paper proposes a nonparametric approximation built around a neighborhood of a nominal probability measure. The method searches within that neighborhood for a measure that gives the observed sample point the largest probability.

The resulting likelihood is called optimistic because it selects the most favorable nearby measure for the observation. The neighborhood controls which alternatives are available. The authors show that neighborhoods defined through Kullback–Leibler divergence, moment conditions, or Wasserstein distance lead to convex optimization problems. In particular cases, the approximate likelihood also has an analytical expression.

These computational results make the proposed approximation accessible through structured optimization rather than an intractable likelihood calculation. The paper also establishes strong theoretical performance guarantees for posterior inference using the approximation and reports competitive performance on a probabilistic classification task. The contribution connects a specific likelihood construction with both computational tractability and support for its use in inference.
summary.tldr: An optimistic likelihood approximation selects the most favorable nearby probability measure and is computable by convex optimization for several neighborhood definitions.

title: Optimistic Distributionally Robust Optimization for Nonparametric Likelihood Approximation

abstract: We study the problem of emergent communication, in which language arises because speakers and listeners must communicate information in order to solve tasks. In temporally extended reinforcement learning domains, it has proved hard to learn such communication without centralized training of agents, due in part to a difficult joint exploration problem. We introduce inductive biases for positive signalling and positive listening, which ease this problem. In a simple one-step environment, we demonstrate how these biases ease the learning problem. We also apply our methods to a more extended environment, showing that agents with these inductive biases achieve better performance, and analyse the resulting communications protocols.

We introduce inductive biases for positive signalling and positive listening, which ease this problem. In a simple one-step environment, we demonstrate how these biases ease the learning problem. We also apply our methods to a more extended environment, showing that agents with these inductive biases achieve better performance, and analyse the resulting communications protocols.

paragraphs: Emergent communication studies how agents develop a communication system because exchanging information helps them solve a task. In reinforcement learning tasks that unfold over time, learning this behavior without centralized training has been difficult. Part of the difficulty is joint exploration: speakers and listeners must discover useful communication behavior together.

The paper introduces inductive biases for positive signalling and positive listening. These are learning preferences intended to encourage the two sides of communication: producing informative signals and responding to messages. Addressing both sides matters because communication depends on a relationship between what one agent sends and how another agent uses it.

The authors first use a simple environment with a single step to demonstrate how these biases make learning easier. They then apply the approach to a longer environment, where agents equipped with the biases achieve better performance, and analyze the communication protocols that emerge. The findings provide evidence that encouraging signalling and listening can help agents overcome the coordination difficulties involved in learning to communicate.
summary.tldr: Learning biases that encourage signalling and listening help reinforcement learning agents develop useful communication in the tested environments.

title: Biases for Emergent Communication in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study Contextual Unsupervised Sequential Selection (USS), a new variant of the stochastic contextual bandits problem where the loss of an arm cannot be inferred from the observed feedback. In our setup, arms are associated with fixed costs and are ordered, forming a cascade. In each round, a context is presented, and the learner selects the arms sequentially till some depth. The total cost incurred by stopping at an arm is the sum of fixed costs of arms selected and the stochastic loss associated with the arm. The learner's goal is to learn a decision rule that maps contexts to arms with the goal of minimizing the total expected loss. The problem is challenging as we are faced with an unsupervised setting as the total loss cannot be estimated. Clearly, learning is feasible only if the optimal arm can be inferred (explicitly or implicitly) from the problem structure. We observe that learning is still possible when the problem instance satisfies the so-called 'Contextual Weak Dominance' (CWD) property. Under CWD, we propose an algorithm for the contextual USS problem and demonstrate that it has sub-linear regret. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate our algorithm.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study Contextual Unsupervised Sequential Selection (USS), a new variant of the stochastic contextual bandits problem where the loss of an arm cannot be inferred from the observed feedback. In our setup, arms are associated with fixed costs and are ordered, forming a cascade. In each round, a context is presented, and the learner selects the arms sequentially till some depth. The total cost incurred by stopping at an arm is the sum of fixed costs of arms selected and the stochastic loss associated with the arm. The learner's goal is to learn a decision rule that maps contexts to arms with the goal of minimizing the total expected loss. The problem is challenging as we are faced with an unsupervised setting as the total loss cannot be estimated. Clearly, learning is feasible only if the optimal arm can be inferred (explicitly or implicitly) from the problem structure. We observe that learning is still possible when the problem instance satisfies the so-called 'Contextual Weak Dominance' (CWD) property. Under CWD, we propose an algorithm for the contextual USS problem and demonstrate that it has sub-linear regret. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential selection when the learner receives contextual information but cannot infer an option's loss from the observed feedback. Options are arranged in an ordered cascade, each with a fixed cost. On each round, the learner chooses how far to proceed, paying the accumulated costs plus the uncertain loss of the option where it stops.

The goal is to learn a context-dependent stopping rule that minimizes expected total loss. Ordinary feedback-based comparison is unavailable because the total loss cannot be estimated. The authors identify Contextual Weak Dominance as a structural property under which learning remains possible. This provides a sufficient condition for recovering useful decisions despite the absence of directly observable losses.

Under that property, the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear regret: its accumulated disadvantage relative to the comparison decision rule grows more slowly than the number of rounds. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the algorithm. The central result is conditional on the problem's structure; Contextual Weak Dominance enables the guarantee, rather than being claimed as necessary for every learnable instance.
summary.tldr: A contextual sequential-selection algorithm achieves sublinear regret under Contextual Weak Dominance even when observed feedback cannot reveal losses.

title: Online Algorithm for Unsupervised Sequential Selection with Contextual Information

abstract: Wasserstein \textbf{D}istributionally \textbf{R}obust \textbf{O}ptimization (DRO) is concerned with finding decisions that perform well on data that are drawn from the worst probability distribution within a Wasserstein ball centered at a certain nominal distribution. In recent years, it has been shown that various DRO formulations of learning models admit tractable convex reformulations. However, most existing works propose to solve these convex reformulations by general-purpose solvers, which are not well-suited for tackling large-scale problems. In this paper, we focus on a family of Wasserstein distributionally robust support vector machine (DRSVM) problems and propose two novel epigraphical projection-based incremental algorithms to solve them. The updates in each iteration of these algorithms can be computed in a highly efficient manner. Moreover, we show that the DRSVM problems considered in this paper satisfy a Hölderian growth condition with explicitly determined growth exponents. Consequently, we are able to establish the convergence rates of the proposed incremental algorithms. Our numerical results indicate that the proposed methods are orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art, and the performance gap grows considerably as the problem size increases.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization seeks decisions that perform well against the worst distribution within a specified neighborhood of a nominal distribution. For learning models, some such problems can be rewritten as tractable convex optimization tasks. Yet a tractable formulation can still be costly at scale, especially when solved using general-purpose software.

This paper focuses on a family of distributionally robust support vector machine problems. It introduces two incremental algorithms based on epigraphical projections, with iteration updates that can be computed efficiently. The authors also prove that the considered problems satisfy a Hölderian growth condition and determine its growth exponents explicitly. That mathematical structure enables convergence-rate guarantees for the algorithms.

Numerical results show speedups of orders of magnitude over the state of the art, with the gap growing considerably as problem size increases. These findings support specialized optimization as a way to make this family of robust learning problems more practical. The theoretical rates apply to the problems analyzed, while the reported speed advantages come from the numerical evaluations.
summary.tldr: Two specialized incremental algorithms solve Wasserstein-robust SVM problems with convergence guarantees and large reported computational speedups.

title: Fast Epigraphical Projection-based Incremental Algorithms for Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Support Vector Machine

abstract: We propose a simple extension of {\sl top-down decision tree learning heuristics} such as ID3, C4.5, and CART. Our algorithm achieves provable guarantees for all target functions $f: \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ with respect to the uniform distribution, circumventing impossibility results showing that existing heuristics fare poorly even for simple target functions. The crux of our extension is a new splitting criterion that takes into account the correlations between $f$ and {\sl small subsets} of its attributes. The splitting criteria of existing heuristics (e.g. Gini impurity and information gain), in contrast, are based solely on the correlations between $f$ and its {\sl individual} attributes. Our algorithm satisfies the following guarantee: for all target functions $f : \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$, sizes $s\in \N$, and error parameters $\eps$, it constructs a decision tree of size $s^{\tilde{O}((\log s)^2/\eps^2)}$ that achieves error $\le O(\opt_s) + \eps$, where $\opt_s$ denotes the error of the optimal size-$s$ decision tree for $f$. A key technical notion that drives our analysis is the {\sl noise stability} of $f$, a well-studied smoothness measure of $f$.

paragraphs: Top-down decision-tree methods choose successive splits using criteria such as information gain or Gini impurity. This paper identifies a restriction of these criteria: they consider correlations between the target and individual attributes. The proposed extension also examines correlations involving small groups of attributes, allowing interactions to influence split selection.

For Boolean inputs and Boolean targets under the uniform distribution, the authors prove a guarantee that applies to every target function. Given a reference tree size s and an error tolerance, the algorithm constructs a potentially much larger tree whose error is bounded by a constant multiple of the best size-s tree's error plus that tolerance. The construction has an explicit size bound that grows with s and tighter tolerance.

The analysis uses noise stability, a measure of a function's smoothness. The result circumvents impossibility findings for existing splitting heuristics, which can fail even on simple targets. Its strength is broad coverage of target functions within the stated distributional setting; the comparison does not promise to match the reference tree's size.
summary.tldr: A decision-tree splitting criterion using small attribute groups provides approximation guarantees for all Boolean targets under the uniform distribution.

title: Universal guarantees for decision tree induction via a higher-order splitting criterion

abstract: Deep neural nets typically perform end-to-end backpropagation to learn the weights, a procedure that creates synchronization constraints in the weight update step across layers and is not biologically plausible. Recent advances in unsupervised contrastive representation learning invite the question of whether a learning algorithm can also be made local, that is, the updates of lower layers do not directly depend on the computation of upper layers. While Greedy InfoMax separately learns each block with a local objective, we found that it consistently hurts readout accuracy in state-of-the-art unsupervised contrastive learning algorithms, possibly due to the greedy objective as well as gradient isolation. In this work, we discover that by overlapping local blocks stacking on top of each other, we effectively increase the decoder depth and allow upper blocks to implicitly send feedbacks to lower blocks. This simple design closes the performance gap between local learning and end-to-end contrastive learning algorithms for the first time. Aside from standard ImageNet experiments, we also show results on complex downstream tasks such as object detection and instance segmentation directly using readout features.

paragraphs: End-to-end backpropagation ties updates in lower network layers to computations in upper layers, creating synchronization requirements. LoCo investigates whether contrastive representations can instead be learned through local updates. The challenge is to preserve useful features while reducing this direct dependence across the full network.

The authors find that separately training blocks with Greedy InfoMax hurts readout accuracy in the contrastive learning methods they examine. They suggest that greedy objectives and isolated gradients may explain the loss. LoCo changes the arrangement by overlapping successive local blocks. This effectively deepens the decoder and gives upper blocks a way to provide implicit feedback to lower ones.

The paper reports that this simple arrangement closes the performance gap between local and end-to-end contrastive learning in its evaluations. Beyond ImageNet experiments, it tests readout features directly on object detection and instance segmentation. The findings indicate that local learning need not impose the same representation-quality penalty observed with separately trained blocks, and that coordination through overlap can matter for demanding downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: LoCo overlaps locally trained blocks to provide implicit feedback and close the reported gap with end-to-end contrastive representation learning.

title: LoCo: Local Contrastive Representation Learning

abstract: Approximate inference techniques are the cornerstone of probabilistic methods based on Gaussian process priors. Despite this, most work approximately optimizes standard divergence measures such as the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which lack the basic desiderata for the task at hand, while chiefly offering merely technical convenience. We develop a new approximate inference method for Gaussian process models which overcomes the technical challenges arising from abandoning these convenient divergences. Our method---dubbed Quantile Propagation (QP)---is similar to expectation propagation (EP) but minimizes the $L_2$ Wasserstein distance (WD) instead of the KL divergence. The WD exhibits all the required properties of a distance metric, while respecting the geometry of the underlying sample space. We show that QP matches quantile functions rather than moments as in EP and has the same mean update but a smaller variance update than EP, thereby alleviating EP's tendency to over-estimate posterior variances. Crucially, despite the significant complexity of dealing with the WD, QP has the same favorable locality property as EP, and thereby admits an efficient algorithm. Experiments on classification and Poisson regression show that QP outperforms both EP and variational Bayes.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models often require approximate probabilistic inference. Common methods optimize divergences such as Kullback–Leibler divergence, partly because they are technically convenient. This paper develops Quantile Propagation, which instead uses the L2 Wasserstein distance, a metric that incorporates the geometry of the underlying sample space.

The method resembles expectation propagation but changes what is matched during approximation. Expectation propagation matches moments, whereas Quantile Propagation matches quantile functions, which describe values at different probability levels. The authors show that its mean update is the same as expectation propagation’s, while its variance update is smaller. This helps alleviate expectation propagation’s tendency to overestimate posterior variances.

Using Wasserstein distance introduces technical complexity, but the method retains expectation propagation’s favorable locality property. That allows efficient updates without abandoning the new distance measure. Experiments on classification and Poisson regression report better performance than both expectation propagation and variational Bayes. The findings show that changing the geometry of approximation can improve inference while preserving a computational structure that makes the method practical.
summary.tldr: Quantile Propagation uses Wasserstein distance for efficient Gaussian process inference and reduces expectation propagation’s tendency to overestimate uncertainty.

title: Quantile Propagation for Wasserstein-Approximate Gaussian Processes

abstract: Features extracted from deep layers of classification networks are widely used as image descriptors. Here, we exploit an unexplored property of these features: their internal dissimilarity. While small image patches are known to have similar statistics across image scales, it turns out that the internal distribution of deep features varies distinctively between scales. We show how this deep self dissimilarity (DSD) property can be used as a powerful visual fingerprint. Particularly, we illustrate that full-reference and no-reference image quality measures derived from DSD are highly correlated with human preference. In addition, incorporating DSD as a loss function in training of image restoration networks, leads to results that are at least as photo-realistic as those obtained by GAN based methods, while not requiring adversarial training.

paragraphs: This paper examines an image property hidden in the features produced by deep classification networks. Small image patches are known to have similar statistical characteristics across scales. The authors find that distributions of deeper features instead change distinctively across scales, and they use these internal differences as an image fingerprint called deep self-dissimilarity.

The fingerprint supports image quality assessment in two settings: with a reference image and without one. Measures derived from deep self-dissimilarity correlate strongly with human preferences in the reported evaluation. This suggests that comparing how deep feature distributions vary across scales captures information relevant to perceived image quality.

The authors also use deep self-dissimilarity as a training loss for image restoration networks. The resulting restored images are reported to be at least as photorealistic as those produced by GAN-based methods, without requiring adversarial training. The same underlying property therefore serves both as an assessment tool and as a training signal. Its value lies in making internal differences across image scales useful for evaluating and improving visual results.
summary.tldr: Differences in deep image features across scales provide quality measures aligned with human preferences and a useful loss for photorealistic restoration.

title: Deep Self-Dissimilarities as Powerful Visual Fingerprints

abstract: Graphs have been widely used in data mining and machine learning due to their unique representation of real-world objects and their interactions. As graphs are getting bigger and bigger nowadays, it is common to see their subgraphs separately collected and stored in multiple local systems. Therefore, it is natural to consider the subgraph federated learning setting, where each local system holds a small subgraph that may be biased from the distribution of the whole graph. Hence, the subgraph federated learning aims to collaboratively train a powerful and generalizable graph mining model without directly sharing their graph data. In this work, towards the novel yet realistic setting of subgraph federated learning, we propose two major techniques: (1) FedSage, which trains a GraphSage model based on FedAvg to integrate node features, link structures, and task labels on multiple local subgraphs; (2) FedSage+, which trains a missing neighbor generator along FedSage to deal with missing links across local subgraphs. Empirical results on four real-world graph datasets with synthesized subgraph federated learning settings demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed techniques. At the same time, consistent theoretical implications are made towards their generalization ability on the global graphs.

paragraphs: Large graphs may be split across local systems, each holding only a small and potentially biased subgraph. Subgraph federated learning aims to train a shared graph model without directly exchanging those graph data. This setting has an additional structural difficulty: connections between separately stored subgraphs may be missing from each system’s local view.

The paper proposes FedSage, which combines GraphSage with federated averaging to learn from node features, links, and task labels distributed across local subgraphs. FedSage+ extends it with a missing-neighbor generator trained alongside the graph model. The generator addresses absent cross-subgraph connections, so the method considers both distributed model training and incomplete neighborhood information.

Experiments use four real-world graph datasets with synthesized federated subgraph partitions. They show effectiveness and efficiency for the proposed methods, while the theoretical analysis provides consistent implications for generalization to the global graph. The evidence supports reconstructing missing neighborhood information as a useful addition to federated graph learning under the studied partitioned-data settings.
summary.tldr: FedSage+ combines federated graph learning with missing-neighbor generation to address incomplete connections across locally stored subgraphs.

title: Subgraph Federated Learning with Missing Neighbor Generation

abstract: Absence of large-scale labeled data in the practitioner's target domain can be a bottleneck to applying machine learning algorithms in practice. Transfer learning is a popular strategy for leveraging additional data to improve the downstream performance, but finding the most relevant data to transfer from can be challenging. Neural Data Server (NDS), a search engine that recommends relevant data for a given downstream task, has been previously proposed to address this problem (Yan et al., 2020). NDS uses a mixture of experts trained on data sources to estimate similarity between each source and the downstream task. Thus, the computational cost to each user grows with the number of sources and requires an expensive training step for each data provider.To address these issues, we propose Scalable Neural Data Server (SNDS), a large-scale search engine that can theoretically index thousands of datasets to serve relevant ML data to end users. SNDS trains the mixture of experts on intermediary datasets during initialization, and represents both data sources and downstream tasks by their proximity to the intermediary datasets. As such, computational cost incurred by users of SNDS remains fixed as new datasets are added to the server, without pre-training for the data providers.We validate SNDS on a plethora of real world tasks and find that data recommended by SNDS improves downstream task performance over baselines. We also demonstrate the scalability of our system by demonstrating its ability to select relevant data for transfer outside of the natural image setting.

paragraphs: Transfer learning can help when a target task has limited labeled data, but choosing relevant source data is itself difficult. Earlier Neural Data Server systems estimate relevance using experts trained on source datasets. This makes user computation grow with the number of sources and imposes an expensive training step on each data provider.

Scalable Neural Data Server changes the reference point for comparison. It trains experts on intermediary datasets during initialization, then represents both source datasets and target tasks by their proximity to those intermediaries. Because comparisons use this shared reference structure, user computation stays fixed as sources are added, and providers do not need to pretrain models.

The system can theoretically index thousands of datasets. Across real-world tasks, its recommended data improves downstream performance over baselines. The authors also demonstrate relevant source selection beyond natural images. These results support a data-recommendation approach that separates growth in the source collection from growth in the user's computation while retaining useful transfer recommendations.
summary.tldr: SNDS recommends transfer-learning data through shared intermediary datasets, keeping user computation fixed as the source collection grows.

title: Scalable Neural Data Server: A Data Recommender for Transfer Learning

abstract: A common challenge across all areas of machine learning is that training data is not distributed like test data, due to natural shifts or adversarial examples; such examples are referred to as out-of-distribution (OOD) test examples. We consider a model where one may abstain from predicting, at a fixed cost. In particular, our transductive abstention algorithm takes labeled training examples and unlabeled test examples as input, and provides predictions with optimal prediction loss guarantees. The loss bounds match standard generalization bounds when test examples are i.i.d. from the training distribution, but add an additional term that is the cost of abstaining times the statistical distance between the train and test distribution (or the fraction of adversarial examples). For linear regression, we give a polynomial-time algorithm based on Celis-Dennis-Tapia optimization algorithms. For binary classification, we show how to efficiently implement it using a proper agnostic learner (i.e., an Empirical Risk Minimizer) for the class of interest. Our work builds on recent work of Goldwasser, Kalais, and Montasser (2020) who gave error and abstention guarantees for transductive binary classification.

Our work builds on recent work of Goldwasser, Kalais, and Montasser (2020) who gave error and abstention guarantees for transductive binary classification.

paragraphs: When test data differs from training data, a model may benefit from declining to predict on some examples. This paper studies abstention with a fixed cost. Its algorithm is transductive: it receives labeled training examples and the unlabeled test examples together before deciding which predictions to make.

The resulting prediction-loss guarantees match standard generalization bounds when test examples are independently drawn from the training distribution. Under shift, the bounds add a term equal to the abstention cost multiplied by a statistical measure of distribution mismatch, or by the fraction of adversarial examples. This explicitly relates the cost of handling unfamiliar data to the extent of the shift.

The paper also gives computational implementations for two learning settings. Linear regression admits a polynomial-time algorithm based on Celis-Dennis-Tapia optimization methods. Binary classification can be implemented efficiently using a proper agnostic learner, described as an empirical risk minimizer for the relevant class. The contribution ties optimal loss guarantees to concrete procedures for balancing prediction against paid abstention.
summary.tldr: A transductive abstention method provides optimal loss guarantees that account explicitly for distribution shift and the cost of declining predictions.

title: Towards optimally abstaining from prediction with OOD test examples

abstract: We train hierarchical Transformers on the task of synthesizing hardware circuits directly out of high-level logical speciﬁcations in linear-time temporal logic (LTL). The LTL synthesis problem is a well-known algorithmic challenge with a long history and an annual competition is organized to track the improvement of algorithms and tooling over time. New approaches using machine learning might open a lot of possibilities in this area, but suffer from the lack of sufﬁcient amounts of training data. In this paper, we consider a method to generate large amounts of additional training data, i.e., pairs of speciﬁcations and circuits implementing them. We ensure that this synthetic data is sufﬁciently close to human-written speciﬁcations by mining common patterns from the speciﬁcations used in the synthesis competitions. We show that hierarchical Transformers trained on this synthetic data solve a signiﬁcant portion of problems from the synthesis competitions, and even out-of-distribution examples from a recent case study.

paragraphs: This paper trains hierarchical Transformers to generate hardware circuits from high-level logical requirements expressed in linear-time temporal logic. The task is circuit synthesis: producing a circuit that implements a specification. It is an established algorithmic challenge, and a major obstacle for learning-based approaches is the limited supply of suitable specification–circuit training pairs.

The authors address that obstacle by generating additional paired training data. To make the synthetic specifications resemble human-written ones, they mine recurring patterns from specifications used in synthesis competitions. Those patterns guide data generation, tying the expanded training collection to the kinds of logical requirements that appear in established synthesis problems.

Hierarchical Transformers trained on this data solve a significant portion of the competition problems. They also solve out-of-distribution examples from a recent case study. The findings support pattern-based synthetic data as a useful way to train neural synthesis systems when direct training examples are scarce. The reported successes span both competition-derived tasks and examples beyond the training distribution.
summary.tldr: Synthetic training pairs built from specification patterns help hierarchical Transformers synthesize circuits for competition and out-of-distribution problems.

title: Neural Circuit Synthesis from Specification Patterns

abstract: Adversarial examples are often cited by neuroscientists and machine learning researchers as an example of how computational models diverge from biological sensory systems. Recent work has proposed adding biologically-inspired components to visual neural networks as a way to improve their adversarial robustness. One surprisingly effective component for reducing adversarial vulnerability is response stochasticity, like that exhibited by biological neurons. Here, using recently developed geometrical techniques from computational neuroscience, we investigate how adversarial perturbations influence the internal representations of standard, adversarially trained, and biologically-inspired stochastic networks. We find distinct geometric signatures for each type of network, revealing different mechanisms for achieving robust representations. Next, we generalize these results to the auditory domain, showing that neural stochasticity also makes auditory models more robust to adversarial perturbations. Geometric analysis of the stochastic networks reveals overlap between representations of clean and adversarially perturbed stimuli, and quantitatively demonstrate that competing geometric effects of stochasticity mediate a tradeoff between adversarial and clean performance. Our results shed light on the strategies of robust perception utilized by adversarially trained and stochastic networks, and help explain how stochasticity may be beneficial to machine and biological computation.

We find distinct geometric signatures for each type of network, revealing different mechanisms for achieving robust representations. Next, we generalize these results to the auditory domain, showing that neural stochasticity also makes auditory models more robust to adversarial perturbations. Geometric analysis of the stochastic networks reveals overlap between representations of clean and adversarially perturbed stimuli, and quantitatively demonstrate that competing geometric effects of stochasticity mediate a tradeoff between adversarial and clean performance. Our results shed light on the strategies of robust perception utilized by adversarially trained and stochastic networks, and help explain how stochasticity may be beneficial to machine and biological computation.

paragraphs: Randomness in neural responses can reduce a network’s vulnerability to adversarial inputs. This paper investigates why, using geometric tools from computational neuroscience to examine internal representations. It compares standard networks, adversarially trained networks, and biologically inspired stochastic networks to understand how their responses to perturbations differ.

The analysis finds distinct geometric patterns across the three network types, indicating different mechanisms for robust representations. In stochastic networks, representations of clean and adversarially altered stimuli overlap. The authors also extend the investigation beyond vision and show that neural stochasticity improves adversarial robustness in the evaluated auditory models.

The results do not portray stochasticity as an unqualified benefit. Competing geometric effects mediate a tradeoff between performance on clean inputs and performance under adversarial perturbations. By quantifying that relationship, the work helps explain both the usefulness and the costs of response randomness. It also provides a way to compare robust perception strategies in trained and stochastic networks, informing how stochasticity may benefit machine and biological computation.
summary.tldr: Geometric analysis explains how neural stochasticity can improve visual and auditory adversarial robustness while creating a tradeoff with clean-input performance.

title: Neural Population Geometry Reveals the Role of Stochasticity in Robust Perception

abstract: Predicting molecular properties with data-driven methods has drawn much attention in recent years. Particularly, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various molecular generation and prediction tasks. In cases where labeled data is scarce, GNNs can be pre-trained on unlabeled molecular data to first learn the general semantic and structural information before being finetuned for specific tasks. However, most existing self-supervised pretraining frameworks for GNNs only focus on node-level or graph-level tasks. These approaches cannot capture the rich information in subgraphs or graph motifs. For example, functional groups (frequently-occurred subgraphs in molecular graphs) often carry indicative information about the molecular properties. To bridge this gap, we propose Motif-based Graph Self-supervised Learning (MGSSL) by introducing a novel self-supervised motif generation framework for GNNs. First, for motif extraction from molecular graphs, we design a molecule fragmentation method that leverages a retrosynthesis-based algorithm BRICS and additional rules for controlling the size of motif vocabulary. Second, we design a general motif-based generative pretraining framework in which GNNs are asked to make topological and label predictions. This generative framework can be implemented in two different ways, i.e., breadth-first or depth-first. Finally, to take the multi-scale information in molecular graphs into consideration, we introduce a multi-level self-supervised pre-training. Extensive experiments on various downstream benchmark tasks show that our methods outperform all state-of-the-art baselines.

Motif-based Graph Self-supervised Learning, or MGSSL, makes those substructures explicit. The authors also introduce multilevel pretraining to account for information at several scales within molecular graphs. Experiments on a variety of downstream benchmarks report improvements over all compared state-of-the-art baselines. The results support incorporating chemically meaningful subgraph structure into pretraining, so the learned representation includes relationships that node-level or whole-graph objectives alone may fail to capture.
summary.tldr: MGSSL pretrains molecular graph networks through motif generation and multilevel learning, improving downstream molecular property prediction.

title: Motif-based Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: Learning to execute algorithms is a fundamental problem that has been widely studied. Prior work (Veličković et al., 2019) has shown that to enable systematic generalisation on graph algorithms it is critical to have access to the intermediate steps of the program/algorithm. In many reasoning tasks, where algorithmic-style reasoning is important, we only have access to the input and output examples. Thus, inspired by the success of pre-training on similar tasks or data in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer vision, we set out to study how we can transfer algorithmic reasoning knowledge. Specifically, we investigate how we can use algorithms for which we have access to the execution trace to learn to solve similar tasks for which we do not. We investigate two major classes of graph algorithms, parallel algorithms such as breadth-first search and Bellman-Ford and sequential greedy algorithms such as Prims and Dijkstra. Due to the fundamental differences between algorithmic reasoning knowledge and feature extractors such as used in Computer vision or NLP, we hypothesis that standard transfer techniques will not be sufficient to achieve systematic generalisation. To investigate this empirically we create a dataset including 9 algorithms and 3 different graph types. We validate this empirically and show how instead multi-task learning can be used to achieve the transfer of algorithmic reasoning knowledge.

paragraphs: Learning an algorithm from examples is easier to supervise when the model can see intermediate execution steps. Many reasoning tasks provide only inputs and final outputs. This paper asks whether knowledge learned from algorithms with available execution traces can help models solve similar tasks whose intermediate steps are unavailable.

The authors create a dataset containing nine algorithms and three graph types. They use it to test whether familiar transfer techniques can produce systematic generalization in algorithmic reasoning.

The empirical results support the concern that standard transfer techniques are insufficient in the studied setting. The paper instead demonstrates transfer through multi-task learning, showing how learning related algorithmic tasks together can convey useful reasoning knowledge when target-task traces are missing.
summary.tldr: Experiments on graph algorithms show that multi-task learning can transfer algorithmic reasoning knowledge to tasks lacking execution traces.

title: How to transfer algorithmic reasoning knowledge to learn new algorithms?

abstract: Variational methods are extremely popular in the analysis of network data. Statistical guarantees obtained for these methods typically provide asymptotic normality for the problem of estimation of global model parameters under the stochastic block model. In the present work, we consider the case of networks with missing links that is important in application and show that the variational approximation to the maximum likelihood estimator converges at the minimax rate. This provides the first minimax optimal and tractable estimator for the problem of parameter estimation for the stochastic block model with missing links. We complement our results with numerical studies of simulated and real networks, which confirm the advantages of this estimator over current methods.

paragraphs: Variational methods are widely used to analyze network data because they offer tractable approximations to difficult estimation problems. This paper studies their statistical quality for stochastic block models when some network links are missing, a setting relevant to incomplete observations.

Earlier guarantees typically described asymptotic normality when estimating global model parameters. The authors instead establish that a variational approximation to the maximum likelihood estimator converges at the minimax rate in the missing-link setting.

A minimax rate describes the best achievable scaling of estimation error over the model class under study. Matching that rate means the approximation attains the optimal statistical order while remaining computationally tractable. The paper presents this as the first estimator combining those properties for this parameter-estimation problem.

Numerical studies on simulated and real networks complement the theoretical result and confirm advantages over existing methods. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: a practical approximate inference procedure receives a strong rate guarantee for network parameter estimation with missing links.
summary.tldr: Variational estimation achieves the minimax convergence rate for stochastic block models with missing links while remaining tractable.

title: Optimality of variational inference for stochasticblock model with missing links

abstract: Constructing Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies that adhere to safety requirements is an emerging field of study. RL agents learn via trial and error with an objective to optimize a reward signal. Often policies that are designed to accumulate rewards do not satisfy safety specifications. We present a methodology for counterexample guided refinement of a trained RL policy against a given safety specification. Our approach has two main components. The first component is an approach to discover failure trajectories using Bayesian optimization over multiple parameters of uncertainty from a policy learnt in a model-free setting. The second component selectively modifies the failure points of the policy using gradient-based updates. The approach has been tested on several RL environments, and we demonstrate that the policy can be made to respect the safety specifications through such targeted changes.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy trained to accumulate reward may still violate a safety specification. This paper starts with an already trained policy and asks how to refine its behavior against an explicit safety requirement. The approach uses counterexamples: trajectories showing where the policy fails to satisfy that requirement.

The first component searches for these failure trajectories using Bayesian optimization over multiple uncertainty parameters. The policy being examined was learned in a model-free setting. The second component uses gradient-based updates to selectively change the policy at the identified failure points. Searching for failures and making targeted corrections thus play distinct roles in the refinement process.

Experiments in several reinforcement learning environments demonstrate that these targeted changes can make the policy respect the tested safety specifications. The stated result is a demonstration of successful refinement, rather than an unrestricted guarantee covering every possible trajectory. The approach matters because it ties policy modification to concrete evidence of failure instead of relying on reward optimization alone to produce the desired safety behavior.
summary.tldr: Bayesian optimization finds safety-violating trajectories, which guide targeted gradient updates to refine trained reinforcement learning policies.

title: Counterexample Guided RL Policy Refinement Using Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Sampling-based inference and learning techniques, especially Bayesian inference, provide an essential approach to handling uncertainty in machine learning (ML). As these techniques are increasingly used in daily life, it becomes essential to safeguard the ML systems with various trustworthy-related constraints, such as fairness, safety, interpretability. Mathematically, enforcing these constraints in probabilistic inference can be cast into sampling from intractable distributions subject to general nonlinear constraints, for which practical efficient algorithms are still largely missing. In this work, we propose a family of constrained sampling algorithms which generalize Langevin Dynamics (LD) and Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) to incorporate a moment constraint specified by a general nonlinear function. By exploiting the gradient flow structure of LD and SVGD, we derive two types of algorithms for handling constraints, including a primal-dual gradient approach and the constraint controlled gradient descent approach. We investigate the continuous-time mean-field limit of these algorithms and show that they have O(1/t) convergence under mild conditions. Moreover, the LD variant converges linearly assuming that a log Sobolev like inequality holds. Various numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms in trustworthy settings.

paragraphs: Sampling methods help machine learning systems represent uncertainty, but applications may also require constraints associated with fairness, safety, or interpretability. This paper studies how to incorporate such requirements into sampling from difficult probability distributions. Its mathematical setting uses a moment constraint defined by a general nonlinear function, expressing a requirement on a distributional average.

The authors extend Langevin dynamics and Stein variational gradient descent using their gradient-flow structure. They derive two approaches: a primal-dual gradient method and a constraint-controlled gradient descent method. Both incorporate the constraint into the evolution used to perform sampling, creating a family of constrained algorithms from these established unconstrained methods.

The Langevin variant has linear convergence under the additional assumption of a log-Sobolev-like inequality. Numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency in trustworthy settings. The contribution pairs practical algorithm designs with convergence results whose scope is explicitly tied to the analyzed limits and assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Langevin and Stein sampling methods to nonlinear moment constraints, with conditional convergence guarantees and numerical demonstrations.

title: Sampling with Trusthworthy Constraints: A Variational Gradient Framework

abstract: We study the power of learning via mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the loss of a differentiable model or neural network, and ask what learning problems can be learnt using this paradigm. We show that SGD can always simulate learning with statistical queries (SQ), but its ability to go beyond that depends on the precision $\rho$ of the gradients and the minibatch size $b$. With fine enough precision relative to minibatch size, namely when $b \rho$ is small enough, SGD can go beyond SQ learning and simulate any sample-based learning algorithm and thus its learning power is equivalent to that of PAC learning; this extends prior work that achieved this result for $b=1$. Moreover, with polynomially many bits of precision (i.e. when $\rho$ is exponentially small), SGD can simulate PAC learning regardless of the batch size. On the other hand, when $b \rho^2$ is large enough, the power of SGD is equivalent to that of SQ learning.

paragraphs: This paper asks which learning problems can, in principle, be solved by minibatch SGD applied to differentiable models or neural networks. It compares that paradigm with statistical-query learning and with general sample-based learning in the PAC framework. The analysis identifies gradient precision and minibatch size as decisive factors.

SGD can always simulate statistical-query learning. When the product of batch size b and the gradient precision parameter rho is sufficiently small, it can also simulate any sample-based learning algorithm, matching PAC learning power. This extends an earlier result for single-example batches. If rho is exponentially small, corresponding to polynomially many precision bits, the simulation works regardless of batch size.

In another regime, where b times rho squared is sufficiently large, SGD has exactly statistical-query learning power. Thus, the abstract gives different equivalence results under different precision and batch-size conditions. These are statements about what the learning paradigm can represent through simulation, rather than a claim that an ordinary training setup automatically finds every learnable solution.
summary.tldr: SGD's theoretical learning power ranges from statistical-query learning to full PAC learning depending on gradient precision and minibatch size.

title: On the Power of Differentiable Learning versus PAC and SQ Learning

abstract: Generative probabilistic modeling of biological sequences has widespread existing and potential use across biology and biomedicine, particularly given advances in high-throughput sequencing, synthesis and editing. However, we still lack methods with nucleotide resolution that are tractable at the scale of whole genomes and that can achieve high predictive accuracy in theory and practice. In this article we propose a new generative sequence model, the Bayesian embedded autoregressive (BEAR) model, which uses a parametric autoregressive model to specify a conjugate prior over a nonparametric Bayesian Markov model. We explore, theoretically and empirically, applications of BEAR models to a variety of statistical problems including density estimation, robust parameter estimation, goodness-of-fit tests, and two-sample tests. We prove rigorous asymptotic consistency results including nonparametric posterior concentration rates. We scale inference in BEAR models to datasets containing tens of billions of nucleotides. On genomic, transcriptomic, and metagenomic sequence data we show that BEAR models provide large increases in predictive performance as compared to parametric autoregressive models, among other results. BEAR models offer a flexible and scalable framework, with theoretical guarantees, for building and critiquing generative models at the whole genome scale.

Its Bayesian embedded autoregressive model, or BEAR, combines a parametric autoregressive model with a nonparametric Bayesian Markov model. The autoregressive component specifies a conjugate prior, providing a structured starting point for the more flexible Bayesian component.

The authors investigate this construction for several statistical tasks, including estimating sequence probabilities, estimating parameters robustly, checking whether a model fits observations, and testing whether two samples differ. summary.tldr: BEAR combines autoregressive modeling with nonparametric Bayesian inference to improve biological sequence prediction at whole-genome scale.

title: A generative nonparametric Bayesian model for whole genomes

abstract: We present temporally abstract actor-critic (TAAC), a simple but effective off-policy RL algorithm that incorporates closed-loop temporal abstraction into the actor-critic framework. TAAC adds a second-stage binary policy to choose between the previous action and a new action output by an actor. Crucially, its "act-or-repeat" decision hinges on the actually sampled action instead of the expected behavior of the actor. This post-acting switching scheme let the overall policy make more informed decisions. TAAC has two important features: a) persistent exploration, and b) a new compare-through Q operator for multi-step TD backup, specially tailored to the action repetition scenario. We demonstrate TAAC's advantages over several strong baselines across 14 continuous control tasks. Our surprising finding reveals that while achieving top performance, TAAC is able to "mine" a significant number of repeated actions with the trained policy even on continuous tasks whose problem structures on the surface seem to repel action repetition. This suggests that aside from encouraging persistent exploration, action repetition can find its place in a good policy behavior. Code is available at https://github.com/hnyu/taac.

paragraphs: In continuous control, an agent can sometimes benefit from continuing its previous action instead of choosing a different one at every step. TAAC incorporates this decision into an off-policy actor-critic algorithm. A second binary policy chooses between repeating the previous action and using a new action proposed by the actor.

The timing of this choice is central: the switching policy sees the action actually sampled by the actor before deciding whether to use it. This gives it more specific information than a decision based on the actor’s expected behavior. The method also provides persistent exploration and introduces a compare-through Q operator for multi-step value updates tailored to action repetition.

Across 14 continuous control tasks, TAAC demonstrates advantages over several strong baselines. The trained policies retain substantial action repetition while achieving top performance, even in tasks whose apparent structure seems unfavorable to repetition. This suggests that repeating actions can contribute to effective final behavior as well as helping an agent explore during learning.
summary.tldr: TAAC improves continuous control by learning when to repeat the previous action after inspecting a newly sampled alternative.

title: TAAC: Temporally Abstract Actor-Critic for Continuous Control

abstract: From CNNs to attention mechanisms, encoding inductive biases into neural networks has been a fruitful source of improvement in machine learning. Adding auxiliary losses to the main objective function is a general way of encoding biases that can help networks learn better representations. However, since auxiliary losses are minimized only on training data, they suffer from the same generalization gap as regular task losses. Moreover, by adding a term to the loss function, the model optimizes a different objective than the one we care about. In this work we address both problems: first, we take inspiration from transductive learning and note that after receiving an input but before making a prediction, we can fine-tune our networks on any unsupervised loss. We call this process tailoring, because we customize the model to each input to ensure our prediction satisfies the inductive bias. Second, we formulate meta-tailoring, a nested optimization similar to that in meta-learning, and train our models to perform well on the task objective after adapting them using an unsupervised loss. The advantages of tailoring and meta-tailoring are discussed theoretically and demonstrated empirically on a diverse set of examples.

paragraphs: Auxiliary losses can encourage a neural network to follow useful assumptions about its inputs, but optimizing them only during training does not ensure the same behavior on new inputs. Adding them to the main training loss also changes the objective being optimized. The paper proposes a different way to incorporate these inductive biases.

Tailoring adapts a network after it receives an input and before it makes a prediction, using an unsupervised objective. This customizes the model to the current input without requiring its label. The authors then introduce meta-tailoring: a nested training procedure that judges task performance after the model has undergone this unsupervised adaptation.

This arrangement connects the adaptation step to the task objective the model ultimately needs to satisfy. Instead of merely asking a network to minimize an auxiliary loss during training, it trains for useful predictions following adaptation. The paper discusses theoretical advantages and demonstrates empirical benefits across diverse examples, supporting prediction-time optimization as a way to encode inductive biases.
summary.tldr: Tailoring adapts networks to each input using an unsupervised loss, while meta-tailoring trains them to perform well after that adaptation.

title: Tailoring: encoding inductive biases by optimizing unsupervised objectives at prediction time

abstract: In lifelong learning, a model learns different tasks sequentially throughout its lifetime. State-of-the-art deep learning models, however, struggle to generalize in this setting and suffer from catastrophic forgetting of old tasks when learning new ones. While a number of approaches have been developed in an attempt to ameliorate this problem, there are no established, unified or generalized frameworks for rigorous evaluations of proposed solutions; a problem which is particularly pronounced in the domain of NLP. The few existing benchmarks are typically limited to a specific flavor of lifelong learning -- continual open-set classification -- where new classes, as opposed to tasks, are learned incrementally. Moreover, the only general lifelong learning benchmark combines a multi-label classification setup with a multi-class classification setup resulting in misleading gradients during training. We empirically demonstrate that the catastrophic forgetting observed here can be attributed to the experimental design rather than to any inherent modeling limitations. To address these issues, we propose an experimental framework for true, general lifelong learning in NLP. Using this framework, we develop a comprehensive suite of benchmarks that target different properties of lifelong learning (e.g., forgetting or intransigence); experiment with diverse facets of language learning: multi-domain, multilingual and different levels of linguistic hierarchy; and present a continuous evaluation scheme under a new metric: Area Under the Lifelong Test Curve. Our framework reveals shortcomings of prevalent memory-based solutions, demonstrating they are unable to outperform a simple experience replay baseline under the realistic lifelong learning setup.

paragraphs: Lifelong language learning asks a model to learn tasks sequentially while retaining earlier abilities. Evaluating this is difficult when benchmarks cover only newly added classes or mix incompatible task setups. The paper identifies a benchmark that combines multi-label and multi-class classification, producing misleading training gradients.

The authors empirically attribute the forgetting observed in that benchmark to its experimental design rather than inherent modeling limitations. This is a finding about the investigated setup, not an explanation for all catastrophic forgetting. They propose a more general NLP evaluation framework and build benchmarks spanning multiple domains, languages, and levels of linguistic hierarchy.

The framework separately targets properties such as forgetting and difficulty learning new tasks, and introduces Area Under the Lifelong Test Curve for continuous evaluation. Under the authors' realistic lifelong-learning setup, prevalent memory-based methods fail to outperform a simple experience replay baseline. The findings show how benchmark design can change conclusions about method effectiveness and provide a more structured basis for evaluating both retention and continued learning.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes a lifelong-learning benchmark artifact and introduces broader evaluations where prevalent memory-based methods do not beat simple experience replay.

title: Towards a robust experimental framework and benchmark for lifelong language learning

abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has yielded remarkable improvements in many different domains including computer vision, natural language processing and speech processing by leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data. In the specific context of speech, however, and despite promising results, there exists a clear lack of standardization in the evaluation process for comprehensive comparisons of these models. This issue gets even worse with the investigation of SSL approaches for other languages than English. We present LeBenchmark, an open-source and reproducible framework for assessing SSL from French speech data. It includes documented, large-scale and heterogeneous corpora, seven pretrained SSL wav2vec 2.0 models shared with the community, and a clear evaluation protocol made of four downstream tasks along with their scoring scripts: automatic speech recognition, spoken language understanding, automatic speech translation and automatic emotion recognition. For the first time, SSL models are analyzed and compared on the latter domains both from a task-agnostic (i.e. frozen) and task-specific (i.e. fine-tuned w.r.t the downstream task) perspectives. We report state-of-the-art performance on most considered French tasks and provide a readable evaluation set-up for the development of future SSL models for speech processing.

Alongside those results, the released models, data resources, and evaluation setup provide a reproducible basis for developing and comparing further speech-learning methods.
summary.tldr: LeBenchmark standardizes French speech evaluation across four tasks and compares frozen versus fine-tuned self-supervised models.

title: Task Agnostic and Task Specific Self-Supervised Learning from Speech with LeBenchmark

abstract: Importance Sampling (IS) is a method for approximating expectations with respect to a target distribution using independent samples from a proposal distribution and the associated to importance weights. In many cases, the target distribution is known up to a normalization constant and self-normalized IS (SNIS) is then used. While the use of self-normalization can have a positive effect on the dispersion of the estimator, it introduces bias. In this work, we propose a new method BR-SNIS whose complexity is essentially the same as SNIS and which significantly reduces bias. This method is a wrapper, in the sense that it uses the same proposal samples and importance weights but makes a clever use of iterated sampling-importance-resampling (i-SIR) to form a bias-reduced version of the estimator. We derive the proposed algorithm with rigorous theoretical results, including novel bias, variance, and high-probability bounds. We illustrate our findings with numerical examples.

paragraphs: Importance sampling estimates an average under a target distribution using samples drawn from a different, accessible proposal distribution. Each sample receives a weight that accounts for this mismatch. When the target is available only up to an unknown normalization constant, self-normalized importance sampling combines the weighted samples through an estimated normalization.

That normalization can reduce the estimator's dispersion, but it also introduces bias: its average answer need not equal the quantity being estimated. The paper proposes BR-SNIS to reduce this bias while keeping computational complexity essentially comparable to ordinary self-normalized importance sampling. It operates as a wrapper around the same proposal samples and importance weights.

The wrapper uses iterated sampling-importance-resampling to construct a different estimator from those ingredients. The authors support the construction with bounds on bias, variance, and the probability of large errors, alongside numerical illustrations. The stated result is substantial bias reduction, rather than elimination of bias. Its practical significance is improving the estimator without requiring a different source of samples or a new set of importance weights.
summary.tldr: BR-SNIS reuses importance samples and weights to substantially reduce self-normalization bias at essentially the same computational complexity.

title: BR-SNIS: Bias Reduced Self-Normalized Importance Sampling

abstract: The quantum many-body problem lies at the center of the most important open challenges in condensed matter, quantum chemistry, atomic, nuclear, and high-energy physics. While quantum Monte Carlo, when applicable, remains the most powerful numerical technique capable of treating dozens or hundreds of degrees of freedom with high accuracy, it is restricted to models that are not afflicted by the infamous sign problem. A powerful alternative that has emerged in recent years is the use of neural networks as variational estimators for quantum states. In this work, we propose a symmetry-projected variational solution in the form of linear combinations of simple restricted Boltzmann machines. This construction allows one to explore states outside of the original variational manifold and increase the representation power with moderate computational effort. Besides allowing one to restore spatial symmetries, an expansion in terms of Krylov states using a Lanczos recursion offers a solution that can further improve the quantum state accuracy. We illustrate these ideas with an application to the Heisenberg $J_1-J_2$ model on the square lattice, a paradigmatic problem under debate in condensed matter physics, and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in the representation of the ground state.

paragraphs: Neural networks can serve as variational approximations to quantum states, offering an alternative for many-body problems where other numerical methods face difficulties. This paper studies how to systematically improve such representations. Its starting point is a construction that combines simple restricted Boltzmann machines rather than relying on one original variational family.

The proposed state is a symmetry-projected linear combination of these networks. Combining them allows the representation to reach states outside the original variational manifold, increasing expressive power with moderate computational effort. Symmetry projection also restores spatial symmetries. These components provide a structured way to enlarge the space of candidate quantum states.

The authors then use Lanczos recursion to build an expansion in Krylov states, which can further improve the approximation's accuracy. They demonstrate the approach on the square-lattice Heisenberg J1-J2 model and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for its ground-state representation. The result supports combining neural representations with symmetry and Lanczos-based refinement for this many-body problem; it does not establish a general resolution of the sign problem.
summary.tldr: Symmetry-projected combinations of neural quantum states and Lanczos refinement achieve state-of-the-art ground-state accuracy on the studied J1-J2 model.

title: Systematic improvement of neural network quantum states using Lanczos

abstract: Dense video understanding requires answering several questions such as who is doing what to whom, with what, how, why, and where. Recently, Video Situation Recognition (VidSitu) is framed as a task for structured prediction of multiple events, their relationships, and actions and various verb-role pairs attached to descriptive entities. This task poses several challenges in identifying, disambiguating, and co-referencing entities across multiple verb-role pairs, but also faces some challenges of evaluation. In this work, we propose the addition of spatio-temporal grounding as an essential component of the structured prediction task in a weakly supervised setting, and present a novel three stage Transformer model, VideoWhisperer, that is empowered to make joint predictions. In stage one, we learn contextualised embeddings for video features in parallel with key objects that appear in the video clips to enable fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning. The second stage sees verb-role queries attend and pool information from object embeddings, localising answers to questions posed about the action. The final stage generates these answers as captions to describe each verb-role pair present in the video. Our model operates on a group of events (clips) simultaneously and predicts verbs, verb-role pairs, their nouns, and their grounding on-the-fly. When evaluated on a grounding-augmented version of the VidSitu dataset, we observe a large improvement in entity captioning accuracy, as well as the ability to localize verb-roles without grounding annotations at training time.

paragraphs: Describing a video in detail requires connecting actions to their participants and tracking which entities different descriptions refer to. This paper extends video situation recognition by adding spatial and temporal grounding: associating descriptions with locations and times in the video. The proposed VideoWhisperer model uses three Transformer stages. First, it learns contextual representations of video features and important objects.
