paragraphs: Convolutional layers are intuitive, but their detailed mathematical structure can make them harder to analyze than dense layers. This complicates adapting theoretical results and optimization methods to convolutions. The paper introduces a tensor-network view that expresses the underlying tensor multiplications through diagrams and evaluates them efficiently with einsum operations.

These diagrams can be manipulated to perform transformations such as differentiation. The authors derive representations for automatic-differentiation operations and commonly used curvature approximations, supporting convolution hyperparameters, batches, channel groups, and arbitrary convolution dimensions. They also introduce simplifications based on the connectivity pattern of convolutions, allowing a computation's diagram to be reduced before it is evaluated.

The paper tests whether this representation brings practical computational benefits. Its implementation speeds up a recently proposed KFAC variant by as much as 4.5 times while removing the standard implementation's memory overhead. It also enables hardware-efficient tensor dropout for approximate backpropagation. The contribution therefore combines a framework for reasoning about convolutions with demonstrated improvements for particular derivative and curvature computations.
summary.tldr: A tensor-network formulation makes convolutional computations easier to manipulate and accelerates an evaluated KFAC variant by up to 4.5 times.

title: Convolutions and More as Einsum: A Tensor Network Perspective with Advances for Second-Order Methods

abstract: Over the several recent years, there has been a boom in development of Flow Matching (FM) methods for generative modeling. One intriguing property pursued by the community is the ability to learn flows with straight trajectories which realize the Optimal Transport (OT) displacements. Straightness is crucial for the fast integration (inference) of the learned flow's paths. Unfortunately, most existing flow straightening methods are based on non-trivial iterative FM procedures which accumulate the error during training or exploit heuristics based on minibatch OT. To address these issues, we develop and theoretically justify the novel Optimal Flow Matching approach which allows recovering the straight OT displacement for the quadratic transport in just one FM step. The main idea of our approach is the employment of vector field for FM which are parameterized by convex functions. The code of our OFM implementation and the conducted experiments is available at https://github.com/Jhomanik/Optimal-Flow-Matching

paragraphs: Flow-matching generative models learn paths that transport one distribution into another. Straight trajectories are desirable because they support fast numerical integration during inference. Existing approaches to straightening these paths often require iterative flow-matching procedures, which can accumulate training error, or rely on heuristics that solve transport problems within minibatches.

Optimal Flow Matching introduces a theoretically justified route to recovering straight optimal-transport displacements for quadratic transport. Its key design choice is to parameterize the flow-matching vector field using convex functions. This places the desired transport structure within the model's construction and enables recovery through a single flow-matching step in the proposed approach.

The one-step statement concerns the flow-matching procedure used to recover the transport displacement; the abstract does not identify it with a single gradient update or a measured inference speedup. The stated contribution is a direct, theoretically supported approach to straight transport trajectories. The authors also provide an implementation and experiments, connecting the mathematical proposal with an executable method.
summary.tldr: Optimal Flow Matching uses convex-function parameterizations to recover straight quadratic optimal-transport displacements in one flow-matching step.

title: Optimal Flow Matching: Learning Straight Trajectories in Just One Step

abstract: This work studies the problem of out-of-distribution fluid dynamics modeling. Previous works usually design effective neural operators to learn from mesh-based data structures. However, in real-world applications, they would suffer from distribution shifts from the variance of system parameters and temporal evolution of the dynamical system. In this paper, we propose a novel approach named \underline{P}rompt Evol\underline{u}tion with G\underline{r}aph OD\underline{E} (\method{}) for out-of-distribution fluid dynamics modeling. The core of our \method{} is to learn time-evolving prompts using a graph ODE to adapt spatio-temporal forecasting models to different scenarios. In particular, our \method{} first learns from historical observations and system parameters in the frequency domain to explore multi-view context information, which could effectively initialize prompt embeddings. More importantly, we incorporate the interpolation of observation sequences into a graph ODE, which can capture the temporal evolution of prompt embeddings for model adaptation. These time-evolving prompt embeddings are then incorporated into basic forecasting models to overcome temporal distribution shifts. We also minimize the mutual information between prompt embeddings and observation embeddings to enhance the robustness of our model to different distributions. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets validate the superiority of the proposed \method{} in comparison to various baselines.

paragraphs: Fluid forecasting models can encounter distribution shifts when system parameters change or the dynamics evolve over time. PURE addresses this by learning prompts that themselves change over time and adapt an underlying forecasting model. Here, prompts are learned embeddings that carry contextual information into the model's predictions.

The method first processes historical observations and system parameters in the frequency domain to initialize those embeddings from multiple views of the context. It then uses a graph ordinary differential equation, incorporating interpolated observation sequences, to model how the prompts evolve. The changing embeddings are supplied to the forecasting model to address temporal distribution shifts.

PURE also minimizes mutual information between prompt embeddings and observation embeddings as a mechanism for improving robustness across distributions. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show better performance than the evaluated baselines. The contribution is an adaptation mechanism that follows the evolving system, combining contextual initialization with continuous prompt dynamics instead of relying on a single fixed description of the forecasting scenario.
summary.tldr: PURE uses graph-ODE-driven prompts that evolve over time to adapt fluid forecasting models to distribution shifts.

title: PURE: Prompt Evolution with Graph ODE for Out-of-distribution Fluid Dynamics Modeling

abstract: Recent work demonstrates that, post-training large language models with open-domain instruction following data have achieved colossal success. Simultaneously, human Chatbot Arena has emerged as one of the most reasonable benchmarks for model evaluation and developmental guidance. However, the processes of manually curating high-quality training data and utilizing online human evaluation platforms are both expensive and limited. To mitigate the manual and temporal costs associated with post-training, this paper introduces a Simulated Chatbot Arena named WizardArena, which is fully based on and powered by open-source LLMs. For evaluation scenario, WizardArena can efficiently predict accurate performance rankings among different models based on offline test set. For training scenario, we simulate arena battles among various state-of-the-art models on a large scale of instruction data, subsequently leveraging the battle results to constantly enhance target model in both the supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning . Experimental results demonstrate that our WizardArena aligns closely with the online human arena rankings, and our models trained on offline extensive battle data exhibit significant performance improvements during SFT, DPO, and PPO stages.

paragraphs: WizardArena aims to reduce the manual effort and waiting involved in evaluating and improving instruction-following language models. It simulates chatbot competitions offline using open-source language models. The same arena setup serves two purposes: estimating comparative model rankings and generating battle results that guide further model training.

For evaluation, WizardArena predicts rankings from an offline test set. For training, it runs large-scale simulated battles among strong models on instruction data and uses the results to improve a target model. This process supports supervised fine-tuning as well as subsequent preference-based and reinforcement-learning stages, connecting comparison outcomes directly to post-training.

The experiments show that WizardArena’s rankings closely align with those from an online human arena. Models trained using extensive offline battle data also achieve significant improvements during SFT, DPO, and PPO stages. These findings support the simulated arena as both an evaluation tool and a source of training guidance, with empirical agreement to human rankings in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: WizardArena simulates offline model competitions to predict human-arena rankings and generate feedback that improves language-model post-training.

title: WizardArena: Post-training Large Language Models via Simulated Offline Chatbot Arena

abstract: We develop a method to generate prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage rate that is robust to corruptions in the training data, such as missing or noisy variables. Our approach builds on conformal prediction, a powerful framework to construct prediction sets that are valid under the i.i.d assumption. Importantly, naively applying conformal prediction does not provide reliable predictions in this setting, due to the distribution shift induced by the corruptions. To account for the distribution shift, we assume access to privileged information (PI). The PI is formulated as additional features that explain the distribution shift, however, they are only available during training and absent at test time.We approach this problem by introducing a novel generalization of weighted conformal prediction and support our method with theoretical coverage guarantees. Empirical experiments on both real and synthetic datasets indicate that our approach achieves a valid coverage rate and constructs more informative predictions compared to existing methods, which are not supported by theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs sets of possible answers with a guaranteed coverage rate under its assumptions. Missing or noisy training variables can create a distribution shift that makes a naive application unreliable. This paper develops a way to retain coverage guarantees when training-data corruption causes that mismatch.

The method assumes access to privileged information: additional features that explain the shift but are available only during training. It introduces a generalization of weighted conformal prediction that uses this information to account for the distribution change. The key challenge is obtaining reliable prediction sets at test time even though those explanatory features are no longer available.

The authors provide theoretical coverage guarantees for their approach. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets indicate that it achieves valid coverage and produces more informative predictions than the compared existing methods, which lack the stated theoretical support. The contribution therefore connects training-only knowledge about corruption to test-time uncertainty estimates, with the availability of suitable privileged information forming an explicit assumption of the approach.
summary.tldr: A generalized weighted conformal method uses training-only privileged information to provide coverage guarantees despite corruption-induced distribution shifts.

title: Robust Conformal Prediction Using Privileged Information

abstract: Modern datasets in neuroscience enable unprecedented inquiries into the relationship between complex behaviors and the activity of many simultaneously recorded neurons. While latent variable models can successfully extract low-dimensional embeddings from such recordings, using them to generate realistic spiking data, especially in a behavior-dependent manner, still poses a challenge. Here, we present Latent Diffusion for Neural Spiking data (LDNS), a diffusion-based generative model with a low-dimensional latent space: LDNS employs an autoencoder with structured state-space (S4) layers to project discrete high-dimensional spiking data into continuous time-aligned latents. On these inferred latents, we train expressive (conditional) diffusion models, enabling us to sample neural activity with realistic single-neuron and population spiking statistics. We validate LDNS on synthetic data, accurately recovering latent structure, firing rates, and spiking statistics. Next, we demonstrate its flexibility by generating variable-length data that mimics human cortical activity during attempted speech. We show how to equip LDNS with an expressive observation model that accounts for single-neuron dynamics not mediated by the latent state, further increasing the realism of generated samples. Finally, conditional LDNS trained on motor cortical activity during diverse reaching behaviors can generate realistic spiking data given reach direction or unseen reach trajectories. In summary, LDNS simultaneously enables inference of low-dimensional latents and realistic conditional generation of neural spiking datasets, opening up further possibilities for simulating experimentally testable hypotheses.

paragraphs: Neural recordings capture discrete spikes from many neurons, but generating realistic recordings linked to behavior remains difficult. Latent Diffusion for Neural Spiking data, or LDNS, combines low-dimensional representation learning with generative modeling. It aims to extract compact descriptions of neural activity and use them to produce realistic new activity.

An autoencoder with structured state-space layers converts high-dimensional spike recordings into continuous, time-aligned latent representations. Diffusion models are then trained in that latent space, including models conditioned on behavior. An additional observation model can represent individual-neuron dynamics that are not mediated by the shared latent state, further improving the realism of generated recordings.

On synthetic data, LDNS recovers latent structure, firing rates, and spiking statistics. The authors also generate variable-length recordings resembling human cortical activity during attempted speech. For motor-cortex recordings, conditional generation produces realistic spikes from reach directions or previously unseen reach trajectories. Together, these results support both representation inference and behavior-dependent generation, with potential for simulating hypotheses that could subsequently be tested experimentally.
summary.tldr: LDNS combines an autoencoder and latent diffusion to infer compact neural representations and generate realistic, behavior-conditioned spike recordings.

title: Latent Diffusion for Neural Spiking Data

abstract: Priority queues are one of the most fundamental and widely used data structures in computer science. Their primary objective is to efficiently support the insertion of new elements with assigned priorities and the extraction of the highest priority element. In this study, we investigate the design of priority queues within the learning-augmented framework, where algorithms use potentially inaccurate predictions to enhance their worst-case performance.We examine three prediction models spanning different use cases, and we show how the predictions can be leveraged to enhance the performance of priority queue operations. Moreover, we demonstrate the optimality of our solution and discuss some possible applications.

In this study, we investigate the design of priority queues within the learning-augmented framework, where algorithms use potentially inaccurate predictions to enhance their worst-case performance.We examine three prediction models spanning different use cases, and we show how the predictions can be leveraged to enhance the performance of priority queue operations. Moreover, we demonstrate the optimality of our solution and discuss some possible applications.

paragraphs: A priority queue maintains elements with assigned priorities and supports two central operations: inserting a new element and extracting the element with the highest priority. This paper studies how predictions can help perform those operations more efficiently. It places this familiar data structure within the learning-augmented framework, where predictive information may be useful even though it can be inaccurate.

The authors examine three prediction models covering different use cases. For each, the question is how the queue's algorithm can use the available predictions to improve operational performance. Treating predictions as potentially imperfect is part of the formulation, so the problem concerns algorithm design with uncertain guidance rather than assuming that future behavior is known exactly.

The paper shows how these prediction models can enhance priority-queue operations and establishes optimality of its solution within the studied framework. It also discusses possible applications. Its contribution is therefore both a set of methods for incorporating predictions into a fundamental data structure and a theoretical account of the performance those methods can achieve.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes priority queues that use potentially inaccurate predictions to improve operation performance.

title: Learning-Augmented Priority Queues

abstract: Algorithms with predictions are gaining traction across various domains, as a way to surpass traditional worst-case bounds through (machine-learned) advice. We study the canonical problem of $k$-facility location mechanism design,where the $n$ agents are strategic and might misreport their locations. We receive a prediction for each agent's location, and these predictions are crucially allowed to be only "mostly" and "approximately" correct (MAC for short): a $\delta$-fraction of the predicted locations are allowed to be arbitrarily incorrect, and the remainder of the predictions are required to be correct up to an $\varepsilon$-error. Moreover, we make no assumption on the independence of the errors.Can such "flawed" predictions allow us to beat the current best bounds for strategyprooffacility location?We show how natural robustness of the $1$-median (also known as the geometric median) of a set of points leads to an algorithm for single-facility location with MAC predictions. We extend our results to a natural "balanced" variant of the $k$-facility case, and show that without balancedness, robustness completely breaks down even for $k=2$ facilities on a line. As our main result, for this "unbalanced" setting we devise a truthful random mechanism, which outperforms the best known mechanism (with no predictions) by Lu et al.~[2010]. En route, we introduce the problem of "second" facility location, in which the first facility location is already fixed. Our robustness findings may be of independent interest, as quantitative versions of classic breakdown-point results in robust statistics.

paragraphs: Facility-location mechanisms choose where to place facilities for agents who may strategically misreport their locations. This paper asks whether imperfect predictions of those locations can improve strategyproof mechanisms. Its MAC setting permits a fraction delta of predictions to be arbitrarily wrong, with the remaining predictions accurate within epsilon, without assuming independent errors.

For one facility, the authors use the robustness of the geometric median to construct an algorithm with MAC predictions. They extend the results to a balanced version of the multiple-facility problem. Balance matters: without it, the robustness breaks down even for two facilities on a line, so the same reasoning cannot simply be carried over.

For the unbalanced setting, the main result is a truthful randomized mechanism that improves on the best known mechanism without predictions. The work also introduces a second-facility problem in which the first facility is already fixed. Together, the results identify both the usefulness of flawed advice and a structural obstacle that requires a different mechanism.
summary.tldr: Mostly approximately correct location predictions improve truthful facility placement, with balance determining when geometric-median robustness applies.

title: MAC Advice for facility location mechanism design

abstract: Randomness is an unavoidable part of training deep learning models, yet something that traditional training data attribution algorithms fail to rigorously account for. They ignore the fact that, due to stochasticity in the initialisation and batching, training on the same dataset can yield different models. In this paper, we address this shortcoming through introducing _distributional_ training data attribution (d-TDA), the goal of which is to predict how the distribution of model outputs (over training runs) depends upon the dataset. Intriguingly, we find that _influence functions_ (IFs), a popular data attribution tool, are 'secretly distributional': they emerge from our framework as the limit to unrolled differentiation, without requiring restrictive convexity assumptions. This provides a new perspective on the effectiveness of IFs in deep learning. We demonstrate the practical utility of d-TDA in experiments, including improving data pruning for vision transformers and identifying influential examples with diffusion models.

paragraphs: Training the same neural network on the same dataset can produce different models because initialization and batching are random. Traditional training data attribution does not rigorously account for this variation. The paper asks how a dataset affects the distribution of model outputs across training runs, expanding attribution beyond a single trained outcome.

The authors formalize this goal as distributional training data attribution. Within that framework, influence functions emerge as a limit of unrolled differentiation, which follows the effects of changes through training steps. This connection does not require restrictive convexity assumptions. It offers a distributional interpretation of an established attribution tool and a new perspective on why it can work in deep learning.

Experiments demonstrate uses of the framework in improving data pruning for vision transformers and identifying influential examples with diffusion models. These applications connect the theoretical reframing to practical dataset decisions. The central contribution is to make training randomness part of the attribution target, so influence concerns how outputs vary across possible training runs.
summary.tldr: Distributional training data attribution accounts for training randomness and gives influence functions a new interpretation without restrictive convexity assumptions.

title: Distributional Training Data Attribution: What do Influence Functions Sample?

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning optimization have unveiled two intriguing phenomena under large learning rates: Edge of Stability (EoS) and Progressive Sharpening (PS), challenging classical Gradient Descent (GD) analyses. Current research approaches, using either generalist frameworks or minimalist examples, face significant limitations in explaining these phenomena. This paper advances the minimalist approach by introducing a two-layer network with a two-dimensional input, where one dimension is relevant to the response and the other is irrelevant. Through this model, we rigorously prove the existence of progressive sharpening and self-stabilization under large learning rates, and establish non-asymptotic analysis of the training dynamics and sharpness along the entire GD trajectory. Besides, we connect our minimalist example to existing works by reconciling the existence of a well-behaved "stable set" between minimalist and generalist analyses, and extending the analysis of Gradient Flow Solution sharpness to our two-dimensional input scenario. These findings provide new insights into the EoS phenomenon from both parameter and input data distribution perspectives, potentially informing more effective optimization strategies in deep learning practice.

paragraphs: Large learning rates can produce training behavior that classical gradient descent analyses struggle to explain. This paper studies two related phenomena: progressive sharpening and the edge of stability. Rather than analyzing a large network directly, it constructs a two-layer network with a two-dimensional input. One input dimension matters for predicting the response, while the other is irrelevant.

Within this small model, the authors rigorously establish progressive sharpening and self-stabilization under large learning rates. Their analysis tracks both training dynamics and sharpness throughout the gradient descent trajectory. Because the results are non-asymptotic, they address behavior during training rather than describing only what happens in a limiting regime.

The paper also connects this example to broader theoretical approaches by reconciling their accounts of a well-behaved stable set and extending an existing gradient-flow sharpness analysis. The contribution is an analytically tractable setting that connects parameter behavior with input structure. Its findings could inform optimization strategies, although that practical implication is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: A small two-layer network enables rigorous analysis of progressive sharpening and self-stabilization during gradient descent with large learning rates.

title: A Minimalist Example of Edge-of-Stability and Progressive Sharpening

abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) is crucial for both assessing their capabilities and identifying safety or robustness issues prior to deployment. Reliably measuring abstract and complex phenomena such as `safety' and `robustness' requires strong construct validity, that is, having measures that represent what matters to the phenomenon. With a team of 29 expert reviewers, we conduct a systematic review of 445 LLM benchmarks from leading conferences in natural language processing and machine learning. Across the reviewed articles, we find patterns related to the measured phenomena, tasks, and scoring metrics which undermine the validity of the resulting claims. To address these shortcomings, we provide eight key recommendations and detailed actionable guidance to researchers and practitioners in developing LLM benchmarks.

paragraphs: A benchmark score is useful only insofar as it measures the capability or property it is meant to represent. This paper examines that connection through construct validity: whether an evaluation captures what matters to a complex concept such as safety or robustness. The concern is especially relevant when benchmark results inform judgments before deployment.

A team of 29 expert reviewers systematically reviews 445 language-model benchmarks from leading natural language processing and machine learning conferences. They identify recurring patterns involving the phenomena being measured, the tasks chosen to represent them, and the metrics used to score performance. These patterns undermine the validity of claims made from the resulting evaluations.

The paper responds with eight recommendations and detailed practical guidance for benchmark developers and users. Its contribution is to connect evaluation design with the strength of the conclusions an evaluation can support. A task and a scoring rule do more than produce a number: their relationship to the intended concept determines how that number should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: A review of 445 language-model benchmarks finds validity problems in how concepts, tasks, and scores support evaluation claims.

title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks

abstract: Diffusion models have become prevalent in generative modeling due to their ability to sample from complex distributions. To improve the quality of generated samples and their compliance with user requirements, two commonly used methods are: (i) Alignment, which involves finetuning a diffusion model to align it with a reward; and (ii) Composition, which combines several pretrained diffusion models together, each emphasizing a desirable attribute in the generated outputs. However, trade-offs often arise when optimizing for multiple rewards or combining multiple models, as they can often represent competing properties. Existing methods cannot guarantee that the resulting model faithfully generates samples with all the desired properties. To address this gap, we propose a constrained optimization framework that unifies alignment and composition of diffusion models by enforcing that the aligned model satisfies reward constraints and/or remains close to each pretrained model. We provide a theoretical characterization of the solutions to the constrained alignment and composition problems and develop a Lagrangian-based primal-dual training algorithm to approximate these solutions. Empirically, we demonstrate our proposed approach in image generation, applying it to alignment and composition, and show that our aligned or composed model satisfies constraints effectively. Our implementation can be found at: https://github.com/shervinkhalafi/constrained_comp_align.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can be adapted by rewarding desirable outputs or by combining pretrained models that emphasize different properties. Both approaches become difficult when those properties compete. Improving one objective can undermine another, and existing methods do not guarantee that the resulting model faithfully captures every desired property.

This paper places alignment and composition within one constrained optimization framework. For alignment, the model must satisfy reward constraints. For composition, it can be required to remain close to each contributing pretrained model. The framework can also combine these requirements. This formulation makes competing demands explicit instead of leaving their balance entirely implicit in an optimization objective.

The authors theoretically characterize solutions to these constrained problems and develop a Lagrangian primal-dual training algorithm that approximates them. Image-generation experiments demonstrate both alignment and composition, with the resulting models effectively satisfying the imposed constraints. The findings support constrained learning as a practical way to manage competing requirements, while the algorithm's approximate nature remains distinct from the theoretical characterization of the solutions.
summary.tldr: A constrained learning framework unifies diffusion-model alignment and composition, with an approximate training algorithm that effectively satisfies constraints in image-generation experiments.

title: Composition and Alignment of Diffusion Models using Constrained Learning

abstract: The rise of parallel computing hardware has made it increasingly important to understand which nonlinear state space models can be efficiently parallelized. Recent advances have shown that evaluating a state space model can be recast as solving a parallelizable optimization problem, and sometimes this approach yields dramatic speed-ups in evaluation time. However, the factors that govern the difficulty of these optimization problems remain unclear, limiting the larger adoption of the technique. In this work, we establish a precise relationship between the dynamics of a nonlinear system and the conditioning of its corresponding optimization formulation. We show that the predictability of a system, defined as the degree to which small perturbations in state influence future behavior, directly governs the number of optimization steps required for evaluation. In predictable systems, the state trajectory can be computed in $\mathcal{O}((\log T)^2)$ time, where $T$ is the sequence length, a major improvement over the conventional sequential approach. In contrast, chaotic or unpredictable systems exhibit poor conditioning, with the consequence that parallel evaluation converges too slowly to be useful. Importantly, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that for predictable systems, the optimization problem is always well-conditioned, whereas for unpredictable systems, the conditioning degrades exponentially as a function of the sequence length. We validate our claims through extensive experiments, providing practical guidance on when nonlinear dynamical systems can be efficiently parallelized, and highlighting predictability as a key design principle for parallelizable models.

paragraphs: Evaluating a nonlinear state-space model normally involves advancing through a sequence of dependent states. An alternative reformulates the trajectory as an optimization problem that can be solved using parallel computation. This paper explains why that approach can be dramatically faster for some systems yet too slow to be useful for others.

The key quantity is predictability, defined through how small changes in a state affect future behavior. The authors connect this property to the conditioning of the trajectory optimization problem, which governs how many optimization steps are needed. Under their analysis, predictable systems yield well-conditioned problems and allow trajectories of length T to be computed in time proportional to the square of log T.

For unpredictable or chaotic systems, conditioning deteriorates exponentially with sequence length, making the parallel optimization approach converge too slowly to be useful. Experiments validate the theoretical relationship. The result offers a criterion for choosing when to use parallel evaluation and a model-design principle: dynamics that preserve predictability can also support efficient trajectory computation.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear system’s predictability determines whether optimization-based parallel trajectory evaluation is efficient or poorly conditioned.

title: Predictability Enables Parallelization of Nonlinear State Space Models

abstract: Modeling hierarchical latent dynamics behind time series data is critical for capturing temporal dependencies across multiple levels of abstraction in real-world tasks. However, existing temporal causal representation learning methods fail to capture such dynamics, as they fail to recover the joint distribution of hierarchical latent variables from \textit{single-timestep observed variables}. Interestingly, we find that the joint distribution of hierarchical latent variables can be uniquely determined using three conditionally independent observations. Building on this insight, we propose a Causally Hierarchical Latent Dynamic (CHiLD) identification framework. Our approach first employs temporal contextual observed variables to identify the joint distribution of multi-layer latent variables. Sequentially, we exploit the natural sparsity of the hierarchical structure among latent variables to identify latent variables within each layer. Guided by the theoretical results, we develop a time series generative model grounded in variational inference. This model incorporates a contextual encoder to reconstruct multi-layer latent variables and normalize flow-based hierarchical prior networks to impose the independent noise condition of hierarchical latent dynamics. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of CHiLD in modeling hierarchical latent dynamics.

paragraphs: Time series can reflect hidden processes organized into several levels, with each level contributing to the observed dynamics. Recovering that hierarchy is difficult when only one timestep's observations are used. This paper finds that three conditionally independent observations can uniquely determine the joint distribution of hierarchical latent variables, providing a foundation for its identification framework.

CHiLD first uses observed temporal context to identify the joint distribution across latent layers. It then exploits sparsity in the hierarchical structure to identify variables within each layer. These are distinct parts of the task: recovering how hidden variables behave jointly and distinguishing the variables that make up each level.

Guided by the theory, the authors construct a generative time-series model using variational inference. A contextual encoder reconstructs the multilayer latent variables, while normalizing-flow hierarchical prior networks impose the independent-noise condition. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical claims and demonstrate effective modeling of hierarchical dynamics. The conditional independence and structural properties are central to the identification argument, rather than incidental implementation details.
summary.tldr: CHiLD uses temporal context, conditional independence, and hierarchical sparsity to identify and model multiple layers of hidden time-series dynamics.

title: Towards Identifiability of Hierarchical Temporal Causal Representation Learning

abstract: Thompson Sampling (TS) has emerged as a powerful algorithm for sequential decision-making, with strong empirical success and theoretical guarantees. However, it has been shown that its behavior under stringent safety and robustness criteria --- such as safety of cumulative regret distribution and robustness to model mis-specification --- can sometimes perform poorly. In this work, we try to address these aspects through the lens of adaptive variance inflation for Gaussian Thompson Sampling. Our one-line change introduces a time- and arm-dependent inflation factor into the sampling variance, and yields several compelling benefits. The resulting policy achieves provably worst-case optimal expected regret and worst-case optimal fast-decaying regret tail bounds, even in the presence of heavy-tailed (sub-exponential) noise or mis-specified environments. The policy is also robust to mis-specified noise variances. Beyond cumulative regret, we further demonstrate that our method ensures strong post-experiment guarantees: simple regret and estimation error per arm exhibit fast-decaying tail probabilities, contributing to more reliable and robust downstream decisions. Finally, we extend our policy to incorporate settings with unknown arm-specific variances and empirically validate the consistent performance of our approach across a range of environments.

paragraphs: Thompson Sampling makes sequential decisions by sampling from estimates of how rewarding each available option might be. Strong average performance can still coexist with unfavorable outcomes in some runs or sensitivity to incorrect modeling assumptions. This paper studies how changing the sampling variance can improve those aspects of Gaussian Thompson Sampling.

The proposed modification introduces a variance inflation factor that depends on both time and the particular option being considered. The authors establish worst-case optimal expected regret and worst-case optimal bounds on how quickly the probability of large regret decreases. Their results also cover sub-exponential noise and misspecified environments, and the policy tolerates incorrectly specified noise variances.

The analysis extends beyond rewards accumulated during the experiment. It also gives rapidly decreasing tail probabilities for simple regret and estimation error for each option, supporting more reliable decisions afterward. An extension handles unknown variances that differ across options. Experiments report consistent performance across multiple environments, complementing the theoretical account of how this small policy change improves reliability.
summary.tldr: A time- and option-dependent increase in Thompson Sampling variance improves regret guarantees, robustness, and the reliability of decisions made after experimentation.

title: Adaptive Variance Inflation in Thompson Sampling: Efficiency, Safety, Robustness, and Beyond

abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) methods have shown strong potential in aligning text-to-image diffusion models with human preferences by training on paired comparisons. These methods improve training stability by avoiding the REINFORCE algorithm but still struggle with challenges such as accurately estimating image probabilities due to the non-linear nature of the sigmoid function and the limited diversity of offline datasets. In this paper, we introduce Diffusion Denoising Ranking Optimization (Diffusion-DRO), a new preference learning framework grounded in inverse reinforcement learning. Diffusion-DRO removes the dependency on a reward model by casting preference learning as a ranking problem, thereby simplifying the training objective into a denoising formulation and overcoming the non-linear estimation issues found in prior methods. Moreover, Diffusion-DRO uniquely integrates offline expert demonstrations with online policy-generated negative samples, enabling it to effectively capture human preferences while addressing the limitations of offline data. Comprehensive experiments show that Diffusion-DRO delivers improved generation quality across a range of challenging and unseen prompts, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both both quantitative metrics and user studies. Our source code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/basiclab/DiffusionDRO.

paragraphs: Diffusion-DRO aims to align text-to-image diffusion models with human preferences. The paper identifies two difficulties in existing preference methods: probability-estimation issues associated with a nonlinear sigmoid objective and the restricted diversity of offline training data. Its approach reformulates preference learning as ranking, drawing on inverse reinforcement learning.

This ranking formulation removes the need for a reward model and produces a denoising-based training objective. It is designed to overcome the nonlinear estimation problem encountered by earlier methods. Training also combines offline expert demonstrations with negative samples generated by the current policy online, bringing newly generated examples into the preference-learning process instead of relying entirely on a fixed dataset.

Experiments report better generation quality on challenging prompts and prompts unseen during training. Diffusion-DRO outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both quantitative evaluations and user studies. The significance is the combination of a simpler denoising formulation with an evolving source of comparison samples, addressing both the mathematical structure of preference training and the coverage of examples available to it.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-DRO learns image preferences through denoising-based ranking and online negative samples, improving reported generation quality and user-study results.

title: Ranking-based Preference Optimization for Diffusion Models from Implicit User Feedback

abstract: We consider the basic problem of learning Single-Index Models with respect to the square loss under the Gaussian distribution in the presence of adversarial label noise. Our main contribution is the first computationally efficient algorithm for this learning task, achieving a constant factor approximation, that succeeds for the class of {\em all} monotone activations with bounded moment of order $2 + \zeta,$ for $\zeta > 0.$ This class in particular includes all monotone Lipschitz functions and even discontinuous functions like (possibly biased) halfspaces. Prior work for the case of unknown activation either does not attain constant factor approximation or succeeds for a substantially smaller family of activations. The main conceptual novelty of our approach lies in developing an optimization framework that steps outside the boundaries of usual gradient methods and instead identifies a useful vector field to guide the algorithm updates by directly leveraging the problem structure, properties of Gaussian spaces, and regularity of monotone functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning single-index models with squared error when labels may contain adversarial noise. The input distribution is assumed to be Gaussian. Its main result is a computationally efficient algorithm achieving a constant-factor approximation across all monotone activation functions satisfying a bounded-moment condition of order 2 + ζ, where ζ is positive.

That function class includes monotone Lipschitz activations as well as discontinuous functions such as possibly biased halfspaces. The breadth matters because earlier results for unknown activations either lacked constant-factor approximation or covered substantially smaller families. The result therefore expands the activation types supported by an efficient robust-learning guarantee under the stated distributional and moment assumptions.

The algorithm’s conceptual contribution is an optimization framework guided by a useful vector field rather than ordinary gradient methods. Its update directions exploit the learning problem’s structure, properties of Gaussian spaces, and regularity associated with monotonicity. This shows how problem-specific update rules can establish guarantees for a broader function class, including cases with discontinuities and corrupted labels.
summary.tldr: A vector-field-guided algorithm efficiently learns broad classes of monotone single-index models under Gaussian inputs and adversarial label noise.

title: Robustly Learning Monotone Single-Index Models

abstract: The role of hidden units in recurrent neural networks is typically seen as modeling memory, with research focusing on enhancing information retention through gating mechanisms. A less explored perspective views hidden units as active participants in the computation performed by the network, rather than passive memory stores. In this work, we revisit bilinear operations, which involve multiplicative interactions between hidden units and input embeddings. We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that they constitute a natural inductive bias for representing the evolution of hidden states in state tracking tasks. These are the simplest type of tasks that require hidden units to actively contribute to the behavior of the network. We also show that bilinear state updates form a natural hierarchy corresponding to state tracking tasks of increasing complexity, with popular linear recurrent networks such as Mamba residing at the lowest-complexity center of that hierarchy.

paragraphs: Research on recurrent neural networks often treats hidden units primarily as memory, emphasizing mechanisms that retain information over time. This paper examines their role in computation itself. It focuses on state-tracking tasks, where the hidden state must actively help determine the network's behavior as inputs arrive, making storage alone an incomplete description of its function.

The authors revisit bilinear state updates, which create multiplicative interactions between hidden units and input embeddings. They show theoretically and empirically that these interactions provide a natural inductive bias for modeling how hidden states evolve in state-tracking problems. The architecture thereby gives the current state an active role in processing the incoming input.

The paper also organizes bilinear updates into a hierarchy associated with state-tracking tasks of increasing complexity. Popular linear recurrent networks, including Mamba, occupy the lowest-complexity center of this hierarchy. This perspective connects architectural choices to computational demands and provides a way to understand recurrent models beyond how successfully they preserve past information.
summary.tldr: Bilinear recurrent updates let hidden states actively shape computation and form a hierarchy suited to increasingly complex state-tracking tasks.

title: Revisiting Bi-Linear State Transitions in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained models with custom data leads to numerous expert models on specific tasks. Merging models into one universal model to empower multi-task ability refraining from data leakage has gained popularity. With the expansion in data and model size, parameter-efficient tuning becomes the common practice for obtaining task-specific models efficiently. However, few methods are dedicated to efficient merging, and existing methods designed for full fine-tuning merging fail under efficient merging. To address the issue, we analyze from low-rank decomposition and reveal that direction robustness during merging is crucial for merging efficient modules. We furthermore uncover that compensating for the gap between stark singular values contributes to direction robustness. Therefore, we propose RobustMerge, a training-free parameter-efficient merging method with complementary parameter adaptation to maintain direction robustness. Specifically, we (1) prune parameters and scale coefficients from inter-parameter relations for singular values to maintain direction stability away from task interference, and (2) perform cross-task normalization to enhance unseen task generalization. We establish a benchmark consisting of diverse multimodal tasks, on which we conduct experiments to certify the outstanding performance and generalizability of our method. Additional studies and extensive analyses further showcase the effectiveness.

paragraphs: Combining task-specific models can produce a single model with multiple capabilities. However, methods designed to merge fully fine-tuned models can fail when the task-specific changes are parameter-efficient modules. This paper analyzes that problem through low-rank decomposition and identifies robustness of parameter directions as a crucial factor.

The authors find that compensating for large gaps between singular values helps preserve direction robustness during merging. RobustMerge implements this idea without additional training. It prunes parameters and scales coefficients using inter-parameter relationships to stabilize directions against task interference. Cross-task normalization provides another component aimed at improving generalization to unseen tasks.

The paper introduces a benchmark spanning diverse multimodal tasks and evaluates the method's performance and generalizability on it. Additional studies support the effectiveness of the approach. The central contribution is a merging procedure tailored to the structure of parameter-efficient updates, using relationships within and across task modules to protect useful directions as their capabilities are combined.
summary.tldr: RobustMerge combines parameter-efficient multimodal experts without training by stabilizing parameter directions and normalizing across tasks.

title: RobustMerge: Parameter-Efficient Model Merging for MLLMs with Direction Robustness

abstract: In this work, we aim to incentivize the reasoning ability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via reinforcement learning (RL) and develop an effective approach that mitigates the sparse reward and advantage vanishing issues during RL. To this end, we propose Share-GRPO, a novel RL approach that tackle these issues by exploring and sharing diverse reasoning trajectories over expanded question space. Specifically, Share-GRPO first expands the question space for a given question via data transformation techniques, and then encourages MLLM to effectively explore diverse reasoning trajectories over the expanded question space and shares the discovered reasoning trajectories across the expanded questions during RL. In addition, Share-GRPO also shares reward information during advantage computation, which estimates solution advantages hierarchically across and within question variants, allowing more accurate estimation of relative advantages and improving the stability of policy training. Extensive evaluations over 6 widely-used reasoning benchmarks showcase the superior performance of our method. Code is available at https://github.com/HJYao00/R1-ShareVL.

paragraphs: Share-GRPO aims to strengthen reasoning in multimodal language models through reinforcement learning. It addresses sparse rewards and vanishing advantages, two problems that can leave training with little useful signal about which generated solutions should be encouraged. Its strategy is to connect exploration and reward information across related versions of a question.

For each original question, data transformations create an expanded set of question variants. The model explores reasoning trajectories across this expanded space and shares discovered trajectories among the variants during training. This gives the reinforcement-learning procedure access to diverse reasoning attempts connected to the same starting question.

The method also shares reward information when estimating advantages, the relative scores used to guide policy updates. It computes these estimates hierarchically, considering comparisons both across question variants and within each variant. The authors describe this as improving estimation accuracy and training stability. Evaluations on six widely used reasoning benchmarks report superior performance, supporting the use of coordinated exploration and shared reward comparisons to improve multimodal reasoning training.
summary.tldr: Share-GRPO improves multimodal reasoning training by sharing reasoning trajectories and reward information across transformed question variants.

title: R1-ShareVL: Incentivizing Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models via Share-GRPO

abstract: Outdoor 3D semantic scene generation produces realistic and semantically rich environments for applications such as urban simulation and autonomous driving. However, advances in this direction are constrained by the absence of publicly available, well-annotated datasets. We introduce SketchSem3D, the first large‑scale benchmark for generating 3D outdoor semantic scenes from abstract freehand sketches and pseudo‑labeled annotations of satellite images. SketchSem3D includes two subsets, Sketch-based SemanticKITTI and Sketch-based KITTI-360 (containing LiDAR voxels along with their corresponding sketches and annotated satellite images), to enable standardized, rigorous, and diverse evaluations. We also propose Cylinder Mamba Diffusion (CymbaDiff) that significantly enhances spatial coherence in outdoor 3D scene generation. CymbaDiff imposes structured spatial ordering, explicitly captures cylindrical continuity and vertical hierarchy, and preserves both physical neighborhood relationships and global context within the generated scenes. Extensive experiments on SketchSem3D demonstrate that CymbaDiff achieves superior semantic consistency, spatial realism, and cross-dataset generalization. The code and dataset will be available at here.

paragraphs: Generating outdoor 3D scenes requires both plausible geometry and meaningful semantic organization. This paper addresses the task of generating such scenes from abstract freehand sketches, together with the shortage of suitable annotated data. It introduces SketchSem3D, described as the first large-scale benchmark for this setting using sketches and satellite-image annotations produced through pseudo-labeling.

The benchmark contains sketch-based versions of SemanticKITTI and KITTI-360. Each brings together LiDAR voxels, corresponding sketches, and annotated satellite images, supporting standardized evaluation across different data sources. Alongside the benchmark, the authors introduce Cylinder Mamba Diffusion, or CymbaDiff, to improve the spatial coherence of generated outdoor environments.

CymbaDiff organizes spatial processing to capture continuity around cylindrical structure and relationships across vertical levels. Its design aims to retain both nearby physical relationships and context spanning the scene. Experiments on SketchSem3D report better semantic consistency, spatial realism, and generalization across datasets. The combined contribution is an evaluation resource and a generation method whose structure explicitly reflects the spatial relationships that coherent outdoor scenes need.
summary.tldr: CymbaDiff uses structured spatial diffusion for coherent sketch-guided 3D outdoor scenes, alongside the new SketchSem3D benchmark.

title: CymbaDiff: Structured Spatial Diffusion for Sketch-based 3D Semantic Urban Scene Generation

abstract: We consider a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with i.i.d. rewards where the expected reward function is multimodal with at most $m$ modes. We propose the first known computationally tractable algorithm for computing the solution to the Graves-Lai optimization problem, which in turn enables the implementation of asymptotically optimal algorithms for this bandit problem.
originalAbstract: We consider a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with i.i.d. rewards where the expected reward function is multimodal with at most $m$ modes. We propose the first known computationally tractable algorithm for computing the solution to the Graves-Lai optimization problem, which in turn enables the implementation of asymptotically optimal algorithms for this bandit problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies a stochastic bandit problem in which a learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. Here, multimodal describes the shape of the expected reward function: it has at most m modes, or peaks. The setting assumes independent and identically distributed rewards, and the upper bound on the number of modes is part of the problem's structure.

The main contribution is a computationally tractable algorithm for solving the Graves-Lai optimization problem in this setting. That optimization is a key step in making asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms implementable. The distinction matters because a theoretical prescription for optimal behavior is more useful when the computation it requires can actually be performed.

The authors describe their solver as the first known tractable method for this problem. Its stated consequence is to enable asymptotically optimal algorithms for the specified multimodal bandit setting. This is a long-run optimality result, rather than a statement that every early decision is optimal. The contribution connects a structured reward assumption with a computational route to implementing the corresponding optimal learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A tractable Graves-Lai solver enables asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms when expected rewards have at most m modes.

title: Multimodal Bandits: Regret Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms

abstract: We investigate scaling laws for stochastic momentum algorithms on the power law random features model, parameterized by data complexity, target complexity, and model size. When trained with a stochastic momentum algorithm, our analysis reveals four distinct loss curve shapes determined by varying data-target complexities. While traditional stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGD-M) yields identical scaling law exponents to SGD, dimension-adapted Nesterov acceleration (DANA) improves these exponents by scaling momentum hyperparameters based on model size and data complexity. This outscaling phenomenon, which also improves compute-optimal scaling behavior, is achieved by DANA across a broad range of data and target complexities, while traditional methods fall short. Extensive experiments on high-dimensional synthetic quadratics validate our theoretical predictions and large-scale text experiments with LSTMs show DANA's improved loss exponents over SGD hold in a practical setting.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can differ in how quickly their losses improve as model size and computational resources increase. This paper studies those scaling relationships for stochastic momentum algorithms in a power law random features model. The analysis varies data complexity, target complexity, and model size, revealing four distinct shapes of training loss curves.

Within this setting, conventional stochastic gradient descent with momentum has the same scaling exponents as stochastic gradient descent. The proposed dimension-adapted Nesterov acceleration, or DANA, changes momentum hyperparameters according to model size and data complexity. This adaptation improves the scaling exponents across a broad range of the studied data and target complexities, including compute-optimal scaling behavior.

The authors validate their theoretical predictions with experiments on high-dimensional synthetic quadratic problems. They also report improved loss exponents over SGD in large-scale text experiments using LSTMs. These results connect a theoretical scaling advantage with an observed advantage in a practical sequence-modeling setting. The central finding is that adapting momentum to problem structure can change scaling behavior, beyond the effect of conventional momentum.
summary.tldr: DANA adapts momentum to model size and data complexity, improving scaling exponents theoretically and in synthetic and LSTM experiments.

title: Dimension-adapted Momentum Outscales SGD

abstract: Tabular data have been playing a vital role in diverse real-world fields, including healthcare, finance, etc. With the recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs), early explorations of extending LLMs to the domain of tabular data have been developed. Most of these LLM-based methods typically first serialize tabular data into natural language descriptions, and then tune LLMs or directly infer on these serialized data. However, these methods suffer from two key inherent issues: (i) data perspective: existing data serialization methods lack universal applicability for structured tabular data, and may pose privacy risks through direct textual exposure, and (ii) model perspective: LLM fine-tuning methods struggle with tabular data, and in-context learning scalability is bottle-necked by input length constraints (suitable for few-shot learning). This work explores a novel direction of integrating LLMs into tabular data through logical decision tree rules as intermediaries, proposing a decision tree enhancer with LLM-derived rule for tabular prediction, DeLTa. The proposed DeLTa avoids tabular data serialization, and can be applied to full data learning setting without LLM fine-tuning. Specifically, we leverage the reasoning ability of LLMs to redesign an improved rule given a set of decision tree rules. Furthermore, we provide a calibration method for original decision trees via new generated rule by LLM, which approximates the error correction vector to steer the original decision tree predictions in the direction of ``errors'' reducing. Finally, extensive experiments on diverse tabular benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Applying language models to tables often starts by turning rows into text. The paper identifies problems with this approach: serialization may not suit all table structures, direct textual exposure can create privacy risks, and input-length limits restrict in-context learning. Fine-tuning language models on tabular data also presents difficulties.

DeLTa connects language models to tabular prediction through decision-tree rules. Given a collection of existing rules, the language model uses its reasoning ability to construct an improved rule. The system therefore works with the tree's logical representation and avoids serializing the underlying table into natural-language descriptions.

A calibration method then uses the generated rule to adjust the original tree's predictions. It approximates an error-correction vector intended to move predictions toward lower error. The framework supports learning from the full dataset without fine-tuning the language model. Experiments across diverse tabular benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, supporting decision rules as a useful interface between language-model reasoning and established predictors for structured data.
summary.tldr: DeLTa uses language-model-generated decision rules to calibrate tree predictions without serializing tables or fine-tuning the language model.

title: LLM Meeting Decision Trees on Tabular Data

abstract: Current image fusion methods struggle with real-world composite degradations and lack the flexibility to accommodate user-specific needs. To address this, we propose ControlFusion, a controllable fusion network guided by language-vision prompts that adaptively mitigates composite degradations. On the one hand, we construct a degraded imaging model based on physical mechanisms, such as the Retinex theory and atmospheric scattering principle, to simulate composite degradations and provide a data foundation for addressing realistic degradations. On the other hand, we devise a prompt-modulated restoration and fusion network that dynamically enhances features according to degradation prompts, enabling adaptability to varying degradation levels. To support user-specific preferences in visual quality, a text encoder is incorporated to embed user-defined degradation types and levels as degradation prompts. Moreover, a spatial-frequency collaborative visual adapter is designed to autonomously perceive degradations from source images, thereby reducing complete reliance on user instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ControlFusion outperforms SOTA fusion methods in fusion quality and degradation handling, particularly under real-world and compound degradations.

paragraphs: ControlFusion addresses image fusion when the source images suffer from multiple degradations at once. The problem is both restorative and interactive: the system must combine useful visual information while accommodating different degradation levels and user preferences. A fixed fusion procedure offers limited flexibility when these conditions change.

The authors first build a degradation simulator grounded in imaging mechanisms, including Retinex theory and atmospheric scattering. This supplies examples of compound degradation. They then design a restoration and fusion network whose feature enhancement changes according to degradation prompts. A text encoder translates user descriptions of degradation types and severity into inputs that control this processing.

The framework also includes a visual adapter that examines spatial and frequency information to infer degradation directly from the images. This reduces dependence on users describing every problem correctly. Experiments report better fusion quality and degradation handling than state-of-the-art fusion methods, particularly for real-world and combined degradations. The contribution connects user control with automatic image assessment inside a single adaptive fusion process.
summary.tldr: ControlFusion combines text instructions and visual degradation assessment to adapt image restoration and fusion to compound image damage.

title: ControlFusion: A Controllable Image Fusion Network with Language-Vision Degradation Prompts

abstract: Recent cooperative perception datasets have played a crucial role in advancing smart mobility applications by enabling information exchange between intelligent agents, helping to overcome challenges such as occlusions and improving overall scene understanding. While some existing real-world datasets incorporate both vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure interactions, they are typically limited to a single intersection or a single vehicle. A comprehensive perception dataset featuring multiple connected vehicles and infrastructure sensors across several intersections remains unavailable, limiting the benchmarking of algorithms in diverse traffic environments. Consequently, overfitting can occur, and models may demonstrate misleadingly high performance due to similar intersection layouts and traffic participant behavior. To address this gap, we introduce UrbanIng-V2X, the first large-scale, multi-modal dataset supporting cooperative perception involving vehicles and infrastructure sensors deployed across three urban intersections in Ingolstadt, Germany. UrbanIng-V2X consists of 34 temporally aligned and spatially calibrated sensor sequences, each lasting 20 seconds. All sequences contain recordings from one of three intersections, involving two vehicles and up to three infrastructure-mounted sensor poles operating in coordinated scenarios. In total, UrbanIng-V2X provides data from 12 vehicle-mounted RGB cameras, 2 vehicle LiDARs, 17 infrastructure thermal cameras, and 12 infrastructure LiDARs. All sequences are annotated at a frequency of 10 Hz with 3D bounding boxes spanning 13 object classes, resulting in approximately 712k annotated instances across the dataset. We provide comprehensive evaluations using state-of-the-art cooperative perception methods and publicly release the codebase, dataset, HD map, and a digital twin of the complete data collection environment via https://github.com/thi-ad/UrbanIng-V2X.

UrbanIng-V2X broadens the setting by collecting coordinated observations across three urban intersections in Ingolstadt, Germany.

summary.tldr: UrbanIng-V2X provides synchronized vehicle and roadside sensor data across three intersections for broader cooperative perception evaluation.

title: UrbanIng-V2X: A Large-Scale Multi-Vehicle, Multi-Infrastructure Dataset Across Multiple Intersections for Cooperative Perception

abstract: Reinforcement learning, such as PPO and GRPO, has powered recent breakthroughs in LLM reasoning. Scaling rollout to sample more prompts enables models to selectively use higher-quality data for training, which can stabilize RL training and improve model performance, but at the cost of significant computational overhead. In this paper, we first show that a substantial portion of this overhead can be avoided by skipping uninformative prompts before rollout. Our analysis of reward dynamics reveals a strong temporal consistency in prompt value: prompts that are uninformative in one epoch of training are likely to remain uninformative in near future epochs. Based on these insights, we propose GRESO (GRPO with Efficient Selective Rollout), an online, lightweight pre-rollout filtering algorithm that predicts and skips uninformative prompts using reward training dynamics. By evaluating GRESO on a broad range of math reasoning benchmarks and models, like Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B, we show that GRESO achieves up to 2.4x wall-clock time speedup in rollout and up to 2.0x speedup in total training time without accuracy degradation. We make our code publicly available at https://github.com/Infini-AI-Lab/GRESO/.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for reasoning models can spend considerable computation generating answers to prompts that contribute little to training. Sampling more prompts helps identify useful training examples, but generating those samples is itself expensive. This paper asks whether a model can avoid some of that expense by identifying low-value prompts before producing their answers.

The authors find that prompt value has substantial consistency over nearby training epochs: a prompt that is uninformative now is likely to remain so in the near future. GRESO uses this pattern to predict which prompts to skip. It is a lightweight, online filter applied before rollout, the stage where the model generates responses for reinforcement learning.

Across the reported mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model sizes, GRESO achieves up to 2.4 times faster rollouts and up to twice as fast overall training without observed accuracy degradation. These are maximum reported speedups, rather than uniform gains across every setting. The finding shows that recent reward history can help allocate generation effort more efficiently while preserving the training benefits measured in the experiments.
summary.tldr: GRESO uses recent reward patterns to skip uninformative prompts before generation, achieving up to twice as fast training without measured accuracy loss.

title: Act Only When It Pays: Efficient Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning via Selective Rollouts

abstract: In the field of computer vision, the task of stereo image super-resolution (StereoSR) has garnered significant attention due to its potential applications in augmented reality, virtual reality, and autonomous driving. Traditional Transformer-based models, while powerful, often suffer from attention noise, leading to suboptimal reconstruction issues in super-resolved images. This paper introduces DIFFSSR, a novel neural network architecture designed to address these challenges. We introduce the Diff Cross Attention Block (DCAB) and the Sliding Stereo Cross-Attention Module (SSCAM) to enhance feature integration and mitigate the impact of attention noise. The DCAB differentiates between relevant and irrelevant context, amplifying attention to important features and canceling out noise. The SSCAM, with its sliding window mechanism and disparity-based attention, adapts to local variations in stereo images, preserving details, and addressing the performance degradation due to misalignment of horizontal epipolar lines in stereo images. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that DIFFSSR outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including NAFSSR and SwinFIRSSR, in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

paragraphs: Stereo image super-resolution improves the resolution of paired views of a scene. The two images provide related information, but combining it requires identifying useful correspondences. Transformer attention can also assign weight to irrelevant context, introducing noise that harms reconstructed details. DIFFSSR targets both this attention problem and difficulties caused by imperfect alignment between the views.

Its Diff Cross Attention Block separates relevant from irrelevant context, strengthening useful features while canceling attention noise. A second component, the Sliding Stereo Cross-Attention Module, combines sliding windows with attention based on disparity, the positional difference between corresponding content in the images. This allows feature integration to adapt to local variation.

The sliding mechanism also addresses performance degradation when corresponding image content does not align perfectly along horizontal epipolar lines. Experiments on benchmark datasets show better quantitative results and visual quality than comparison methods including NAFSSR and SwinFIRSSR. Together, the results support using selective attention and more adaptable stereo matching to improve reconstruction.
summary.tldr: DIFFSSR improves stereo super-resolution by suppressing attention noise and adapting cross-view matching to local misalignment.

title: DIFFSSR: Stereo Image Super-resolution Using Differential Transformer

abstract: Recent multimodal image generators such as GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Pro excel at following complex instructions, editing images and maintaining concept consistency. However, they are still evaluated by disjoint toolkits: text-to-image (T2I) benchmarks that lacks multi-modal conditioning, and customized image generation benchmarks that overlook compositional semantics and common knowledge. We propose **MMIG-Bench**, a comprehensive **M**ulti-**M**odal **I**mage **G**eneration **Bench**mark that unifies these tasks by pairing 4,850 richly annotated text prompts with 1,750 multi-view reference images across 380 subjects, spanning humans, animals, objects, and artistic styles. **MMIG-Bench** is equipped with a three-level evaluation framework: (1) low-level metrics for visual artifacts and identity preservation of objects; (2) novel Aspect Matching Score (AMS): a VQA-based mid-level metric that delivers fine-grained prompt-image alignment and shows strong correlation with human judgments; and (3) high-level metrics for aesthetics and human preference. Using **MMIG-Bench**, we benchmark 17 state-of-the-art models, including Gemini 2.5 Pro, FLUX, DreamBooth, and IP-Adapter, and validate our metrics with 32k human ratings, yielding in-depth insights into architecture and data design.
