paragraphs: Image generators increasingly accept both text and reference images, follow complex instructions, and preserve concepts across outputs. Existing evaluations split these abilities across separate toolkits. MMIG-Bench brings them together, covering multimodal conditioning alongside compositional meaning and common knowledge so that more of the generation task can be evaluated within one benchmark.

The dataset pairs 4,850 annotated text prompts with 1,750 reference images showing multiple views of 380 subjects. These subjects span people, animals, objects, and artistic styles. Evaluation operates at three levels: visual artifacts and identity preservation; detailed agreement between instructions and images; and aesthetics and human preference.

For the middle level, the authors introduce Aspect Matching Score, which uses visual question answering to assess fine-grained prompt-image alignment. It shows strong correlation with human judgments. The study evaluates 17 models and validates its metrics with 32,000 human ratings. This layered structure helps distinguish different sources of success or failure, making evaluation more informative than treating generated-image quality as a single undifferentiated outcome.
summary.tldr: MMIG-Bench unifies multimodal image-generation evaluation with layered metrics for fidelity, instruction alignment, aesthetics, and human preference.

title: MMIG-Bench: Towards Comprehensive and Explainable Evaluation of Multi-Modal Image Generation Models

abstract: We present HyPINO, a multi-physics neural operator designed for zero-shot generalization across a broad class of parametric PDEs without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Our approach combines a Swin Transformer-based hypernetwork with mixed supervision: (i) labeled data from analytical solutions generated via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and (ii) unlabeled samples optimized using physics-informed objectives. The model maps PDE parameterizations to target Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and can handle linear elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic equations in two dimensions with varying source terms, geometries, and mixed Dirichlet/Neumann boundary conditions, including interior boundaries. HyPINO achieves strong zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmark problems from PINN literature, outperforming U-Nets, Poseidon, and Physics-Informed Neural Operators (PINO). Further, we introduce an iterative refinement procedure that treats the residual of the generated PINN as "delta PDE" and performs another forward pass to generate a corrective PINN. Summing their contributions and repeating this process forms an ensemble whose combined solution progressively reduces the error on six benchmarks and achieves a >100× lower $L_2$ loss in the best case, while retaining forward-only inference. Additionally, we evaluate the fine-tuning behavior of PINNs initialized by HyPINO and show that they converge faster and to lower final error than both randomly initialized and Reptile-meta-learned PINNs on five benchmarks, performing on par on the remaining two. Our results highlight the potential of this scalable approach as a foundation for extending neural operators toward solving increasingly complex, nonlinear, and high-dimensional PDE problems. The code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/rbischof/hypino.

title: HyPINO: Multi-Physics Neural Operators via HyperPINNs and the Method of Manufactured Solutions

abstract: With video games leading in entertainment revenues, optimizing game development workflows is critical to the industry’s long-term success. Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) hold significant potential to automate and enhance various aspects of game development—particularly video game quality assurance (QA), which remains one of the most labor-intensive processes with limited automation. To effectively measure VLM performance in video game QA tasks and evaluate their ability to handle real-world scenarios, there is a clear need for standardized benchmarks, as current ones fall short in addressing this domain. To bridge this gap, we introduce VideoGameQA-Bench - a comprehensive benchmark designed to encompass a wide range of game QA activities, including visual unit testing, visual regression testing, needle-in-a-haystack, glitch detection, and bug report generation for both images and videos.

It includes both images and videos. This scope covers different forms of visual assessment and the production of written reports, allowing evaluation to extend beyond whether a model can simply describe a game scene.

The stated contribution is a standardized benchmark for assessing these capabilities. Its range of tasks provides a way to examine models across multiple parts of the quality-assurance workflow instead of treating game QA as a single visual question-answering problem. Establishing that evaluation infrastructure supports the paper's goal of measuring how well vision-language models can handle this specialized development domain.
summary.tldr: VideoGameQA-Bench evaluates vision-language models across game testing, glitch detection, and bug reporting using images and videos.

title: VideoGameQA-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models for Video Game Quality Assurance

abstract: In this work, we present a novel level-of-detail (LOD) method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables real-time rendering of large-scale scenes on memory-constrained devices. Our approach introduces a hierarchical LOD representation that iteratively selects optimal subsets of Gaussians based on camera distance, thus largely reducing both rendering time and GPU memory usage. We construct each LOD level by applying a depth-aware 3D smoothing filter, followed by importance-based pruning and fine-tuning to maintain visual fidelity. To further reduce memory overhead, we partition the scene into spatial chunks and dynamically load only relevant Gaussians during rendering, employing an opacity-blending mechanism to avoid visual artifacts at chunk boundaries. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both outdoor (Hierarchical 3DGS) and indoor (Zip-NeRF) datasets, delivering high-quality renderings with reduced latency and memory requirements.

paragraphs: Large scenes represented through 3D Gaussian Splatting can demand substantial rendering time and GPU memory. LODGE addresses both costs with a hierarchy of detail levels. The system selects subsets of Gaussians according to camera distance, aiming to preserve useful visual detail while reducing the amount of scene information processed.

Each level is constructed using depth-aware three-dimensional smoothing, followed by importance-based pruning and fine-tuning. The smoothing and pruning reduce the representation, while fine-tuning helps maintain visual fidelity. The scene is also divided into spatial chunks so that rendering loads only relevant Gaussians. Opacity blending is used to prevent visible artifacts where chunks meet.

These mechanisms address complementary resource demands: detail selection reduces rendering work, and selective loading reduces memory overhead. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on outdoor Hierarchical 3DGS and indoor Zip-NeRF datasets, combining high-quality images with lower latency and memory requirements. The results support real-time rendering of large scenes on devices whose available memory would otherwise constrain the representation.
summary.tldr: LODGE combines distance-dependent Gaussian detail with selective scene loading to reduce rendering latency and memory use.

title: LODGE: Level-of-Detail Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting with Efficient Rendering

abstract: Topic models provide a useful method for dimensionality reduction and exploratory data analysis in large text corpora. Most approaches to topic model learning have been based on a maximum likelihood objective. Efficient algorithms exist that attempt to approximate this objective, but they have no provable guarantees. Recently, algorithms have been introduced that provide provable bounds, but these algorithms are not practical because they are inefficient and not robust to violations of model assumptions. In this paper we present an algorithm for learning topic models that is both provable and practical. The algorithm produces results comparable to the best MCMC implementations while running orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Topic models help summarize large text collections by representing documents through a smaller set of underlying topics. This makes them useful for exploring a corpus and reducing its dimensionality. The paper addresses a gap between methods that work well in practice and methods whose behavior comes with mathematical guarantees.

The authors describe two existing approaches with different weaknesses. Methods built around maximum likelihood can be computationally efficient, but their approximations lack provable guarantees. Earlier algorithms with provable bounds face practical obstacles: they are inefficient and are not robust when their modeling assumptions are violated. The proposed algorithm aims to bring theoretical assurance and practical usefulness together.

The stated result is a topic-learning algorithm that is both provable and practical. Its outputs are reported as comparable to those of the best Markov chain Monte Carlo implementations, while computation is orders of magnitude faster. This matters because it suggests that obtaining formal guarantees need not require sacrificing the speed or output quality needed for exploratory text analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper presents a topic-modeling algorithm with provable guarantees and results comparable to strong MCMC implementations at orders-of-magnitude greater speed.

title: A Practical Algorithm for Topic Modeling with Provable Guarantees

abstract: We address the problem of designing a convex nonsmooth regularizer encouraging multiple structural effects simultaneously. Focusing on the inference of sparse and low-rank matrices we suggest a new complexity index and a convex penalty approximating it. The new penalty term can be written as the trace norm of a linear function of the matrix. By analyzing theoretical properties of this family of regularizers we come up with oracle inequalities and compressed sensing results ensuring the quality of our regularized estimator. We also provide algorithms and supporting numerical experiments.

By analyzing theoretical properties of this family of regularizers we come up with oracle inequalities and compressed sensing results ensuring the quality of our regularized estimator. We also provide algorithms and supporting numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Some estimation problems involve matrices with more than one useful kind of structure. This paper focuses on matrices that are both sparse and low rank: many entries are zero, while the matrix also has a compact underlying representation. The challenge is to design a regularizer that encourages these structural properties simultaneously.

The authors propose a new complexity index and a convex penalty that approximates it. The penalty can be expressed as the trace norm of a linear transformation of the matrix. This gives the joint structural preference a specific mathematical form while preserving convexity, making it suitable for a regularized estimation objective.

The theoretical analysis provides oracle inequalities and compressed sensing results supporting the quality of the resulting estimator. These guarantees connect the proposed regularizer to estimation and recovery performance under the analyzed conditions. The paper also supplies algorithms and numerical experiments, linking its regularizer design to computation. Its main contribution is a principled way to encourage multiple matrix structures within one convex penalty.
summary.tldr: A new convex regularizer jointly encourages sparsity and low rank, with theoretical estimation guarantees and supporting algorithms.

title: Intersecting singularities for multi-structured estimation

abstract: Understanding the diffusion of information in social network and social media requires modeling the text diffusion process. In this work, we develop the HawkesTopic model (HTM) for analyzing text-based cascades, such as "retweeting a post" or "publishing a follow-up blog post". HTM combines Hawkes processes and topic modeling to simultaneously reason about the information diffusion pathways and the topics characterizing the observed textual information. We show how to jointly infer them with a mean-field variational inference algorithm and validate our approach on both synthetic and real-world data sets, including a news media dataset for modeling information diffusion, and an ArXiv publication dataset for modeling scientific influence. The results show that HTM is significantly more accurate than several baselines for both tasks.

paragraphs: Text-based cascades connect documents or posts through events such as retweeting or publishing a follow-up. Understanding them involves both the subject matter of the text and the pathways through which information spreads. HawkesTopic brings these two questions into a single model rather than treating topic discovery and diffusion-network inference as separate tasks.

The model combines Hawkes processes with topic modeling. The former component represents the diffusion process, while the latter characterizes the topics in the observed text. A mean-field variational inference algorithm estimates them jointly. The central modeling choice is to reason about textual content and information pathways together within the same inference procedure.

The authors evaluate HawkesTopic on synthetic and real-world data. Their applications include information diffusion among news media and scientific influence in an ArXiv publication dataset. They report significantly greater accuracy than several baselines for both tasks. These results support joint modeling in the tested settings, showing that the combined approach can improve the inference of topics and diffusion pathways.
summary.tldr: HawkesTopic jointly infers topics and information-diffusion pathways from text cascades using Hawkes processes and variational inference.

title: HawkesTopic: A Joint Model for Network Inference and Topic Modeling from Text-Based Cascades

abstract: Multiview representation learning is popular for latent factor analysis. Many existing approaches formulate the multiview representation learning as convex optimization problems, where global optima can be obtained by certain algorithms in polynomial time. However, many evidences have corroborated that heuristic nonconvex approaches also have good empirical computational performance and convergence to the global optima, although there is a lack of theoretical justification. Such a gap between theory and practice motivates us to study a nonconvex formulation for multiview representation learning, which can be efficiently solved by a simple stochastic gradient descent method. By analyzing the dynamics of the algorithm based on diffusion processes, we establish a global rate of convergence to the global optima. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

paragraphs: Multiview representation learning seeks latent factors using multiple views of data. Many approaches formulate the task as convex optimization, where appropriate algorithms can reach global optima in polynomial time. The paper is motivated by a gap between this theoretical preference and evidence that heuristic nonconvex methods can also be computationally effective and reach global optima.

The authors study a nonconvex formulation that can be solved efficiently with a simple stochastic gradient descent method. Their main contribution is an analysis of the algorithm’s dynamics using diffusion processes. This provides a way to study the behavior of the stochastic updates and establish a global rate of convergence to global optima for the formulation considered.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The significance is a concrete justification for using a simple nonconvex method in this multiview learning problem. The result connects computationally attractive practice with convergence theory for the studied formulation, rather than establishing that arbitrary nonconvex objectives can be optimized globally by stochastic gradient descent.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-based analysis establishes a global convergence rate for stochastic gradient descent on a nonconvex multiview representation-learning formulation.

title: Online Partial Least Square Optimization: Dropping Convexity for Better Efficiency and Scalability

abstract: There is intense interest in applying machine learning to problems of causal inference in fields such as healthcare, economics and education. In particular, individual-level causal inference has important applications such as precision medicine. We give a new theoretical analysis and family of algorithms for predicting individual treatment effect (ITE) from observational data, under the assumption known as strong ignorability. The algorithms learn a “balanced” representation such that the induced treated and control distributions look similar, and we give a novel and intuitive generalization-error bound showing the expected ITE estimation error of a representation is bounded by a sum of the standard generalization-error of that representation and the distance between the treated and control distributions induced by the representation. We use Integral Probability Metrics to measure distances between distributions, deriving explicit bounds for the Wasserstein and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) distances. Experiments on real and simulated data show the new algorithms match or outperform the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Individual treatment-effect estimation asks how a treatment changes an outcome for a particular individual. This paper develops theory and algorithms for predicting these effects from observational data. Its analysis operates under the causal assumption called strong ignorability, which is part of the basis for interpreting the learned predictions as treatment effects.

The algorithms learn representations in which treated and control populations have similar distributions. The authors justify this balancing objective with a generalization bound: expected treatment-effect estimation error is bounded by a combination of ordinary prediction generalization error and the distance between the represented treated and control distributions. The bound therefore connects predictive quality with how comparable the two groups look after transformation.

Distributional distance is measured using Integral Probability Metrics, with explicit bounds for Wasserstein distance and Maximum Mean Discrepancy. Experiments on real and simulated data show performance matching or exceeding the compared state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theory and experiments support learning representations that address both prediction and group balance within the paper's stated causal setting.
summary.tldr: Under strong ignorability, balancing treated and control representations yields treatment-effect algorithms supported by generalization bounds.

title: Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms

abstract: Healthcare companies must submit pharmaceutical drugs or medical device to regulatory bodies before marketing new technology. Regulatory bodies frequently require transparent and interpretable computational modelling to justify a new healthcare technology, but researchers may have several competing models for a biological system and too little data to discriminate between the models. In design of experiments for model discrimination, where the goal is to design maximally informative physical experiments in order to discriminate between rival predictive models, research has focused either on analytical approaches, which cannot manage all functions, or on data-driven approaches, which may have computational difficulties or lack interpretable marginal predictive distributions. We develop a methodology for introducing Gaussian process surrogates in lieu of the original mechanistic models. This allows us to extend existing design and model discrimination methods developed for analytical models to cases of non-analytical models.

This matters in healthcare, where interpretable modeling can help justify a technology to regulators. The paper studies how to choose physical experiments specifically for their ability to distinguish competing predictive models.

Existing approaches face a tradeoff. Analytical methods offer a useful foundation for experiment design but cannot accommodate every model function. Data-driven alternatives can encounter computational difficulties or produce predictive distributions that are harder to interpret. The authors propose a hybrid methodology that uses Gaussian process surrogates in place of the original mechanistic models within the design procedure.

These surrogates allow methods developed for analytical models to be extended to cases involving non-analytical models. The contribution is a bridge between a broader range of model types and established tools for deciding which experiment would be informative. Its stated significance is methodological: it expands how competing biological explanations can be compared through deliberately chosen observations.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process surrogates extend analytical experiment-design methods to distinguishing competing models that are non-analytical.

title: Design of Experiments for Model Discrimination Hybridising Analytical and Data-Driven Approaches

abstract: Motivated by the phenomenon that companies introduce new products to keep abreast with customers’ rapidly changing tastes, we consider a novel online learning setting where a profit-maximizing seller needs to learn customers’ preferences through offering recommendations, which may contain existing products and new products that are launched in the middle of a selling period. We propose a sequential multinomial logit (SMNL) model to characterize customers’ behavior when product recommendations are presented in tiers. For the offline version with known customers’ preferences, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm and characterize the properties of the optimal tiered product recommendation. For the online problem, we propose a learning algorithm and quantify its regret bound. Moreover, we extend the setting to incorporate a constraint which ensures every new product is learned to a given accuracy. Our results demonstrate the tier structure can be used to mitigate the risks associated with learning new products.

paragraphs: A seller introducing products during a selling period must learn customer preferences while continuing to earn profit. This paper studies that problem when recommendations can include both established and newly launched products. Its central modeling choice is to present recommendations in tiers and describe customer responses with a sequential multinomial logit model.

The authors first analyze the offline case, where preferences are already known. They give a polynomial-time algorithm and characterize properties of the best tiered recommendation. They then address the online case, where preferences must be learned through recommendations, proposing an algorithm and a regret bound that quantifies the cost of learning while making selling decisions.

An extension requires every new product to be learned to a specified accuracy. This makes product exploration an explicit obligation within the recommendation problem. The results show that tiered presentation can mitigate the risks of learning about new products. The contribution connects the organization of recommendations with the balance between gathering information and pursuing profit as the product set changes.
summary.tldr: A tiered recommendation model and learning algorithms show how sellers can reduce the risks of exploring newly launched products.

title: Dynamic Learning with Frequent New Product Launches: A Sequential Multinomial Logit Bandit Problem

abstract: We explore models for translating abstract musical ideas (scores, rhythms) into expressive performances using seq2seq and recurrent variational information bottleneck (VIB) models. Though seq2seq models usually require painstakingly aligned corpora, we show that it is possible to adapt an approach from the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) literature (e.g. Pix2Pix, Vid2Vid) to sequences, creating large volumes of paired data by performing simple transformations and training generative models to plausibly invert these transformations. Music, and drumming in particular, provides a strong test case for this approach because many common transformations (quantization, removing voices) have clear semantics, and learning to invert them has real-world applications. Focusing on the case of drum set players, we create and release a new dataset for this purpose, containing over 13 hours of recordings by professional drummers aligned with fine-grained timing and dynamics information. We also explore some of the creative potential of these models, demonstrating improvements on state-of-the-art methods for Humanization (instantiating a performance from a musical score).

paragraphs: Turning a musical score or rhythm into an expressive performance requires recovering details that an abstract description leaves out. This paper explores that translation using sequence-to-sequence models and recurrent variational information bottleneck models. A central challenge is obtaining aligned training pairs that connect simplified musical inputs with expressive outputs.

The authors create paired data by applying simple transformations to performances, then train generative models to plausibly reverse those transformations. In drumming, operations such as quantizing timing or removing voices have clear musical meanings. The original performance supplies the paired target, making the transformation itself a way to generate training examples for the inverse task.

To support this work, the authors release a dataset containing more than 13 hours of professional drum performances, aligned with detailed timing and dynamics information. They also explore creative applications and report improvements over state-of-the-art methods for humanization, the task of producing a performance from a score. The contribution links a practical paired-data construction method with expressive musical generation.
summary.tldr: Models learn expressive drumming by reversing simple musical transformations, supported by a new professional-performance dataset.

title: Learning to Groove with Inverse Sequence Transformations

abstract: We study the problem of estimating the distribution of effect sizes (the mean of the test statistic under the alternate hypothesis) in a multiple testing setting. Knowing this distribution allows us to calculate the power (type II error) of any experimental design. We show that it is possible to estimate this distribution using an inexpensive pilot experiment, which takes significantly fewer samples than would be required by an experiment that identified the discoveries. Our estimator can be used to guarantee the number of discoveries that will be made using a given experimental design in a future experiment. We prove that this simple and computationally efficient estimator enjoys a number of favorable theoretical properties, and demonstrate its effectiveness on data from a gene knockout experiment on influenza inhibition in Drosophila.

paragraphs: When an experiment tests many hypotheses, planning requires some understanding of how large the real effects might be. This paper studies estimation of the distribution of those effect sizes, defined here through the mean of a test statistic under an alternative hypothesis. That distribution supports calculations of statistical power and the risk of missing genuine effects.

The authors show that an inexpensive pilot experiment can estimate this distribution using substantially fewer samples than an experiment would need to identify the individual discoveries. This separates two statistical goals: learning the overall pattern of effects and determining which particular hypotheses correspond to real effects. The first can provide useful planning information before the second becomes feasible.

The proposed estimator is simple and computationally efficient, and the authors establish favorable theoretical properties. They also show how it can support guarantees about the number of discoveries in a future experiment with a specified design. An application to a Drosophila gene knockout experiment studying influenza inhibition demonstrates its effectiveness. The practical contribution is a route from limited pilot data to better-informed experimental planning.
summary.tldr: A computationally efficient estimator uses small pilot experiments to estimate effect-size distributions and support guarantees about future discoveries.

title: Estimating the Number and Effect Sizes of Non-null Hypotheses

abstract: What goals should a multi-goal reinforcement learning agent pursue during training in long-horizon tasks? When the desired (test time) goal distribution is too distant to offer a useful learning signal, we argue that the agent should not pursue unobtainable goals. Instead, it should set its own intrinsic goals that maximize the entropy of the historical achieved goal distribution. We propose to optimize this objective by having the agent pursue past achieved goals in sparsely explored areas of the goal space, which focuses exploration on the frontier of the achievable goal set. We show that our strategy achieves an order of magnitude better sample efficiency than the prior state of the art on long-horizon multi-goal tasks including maze navigation and block stacking.
originalAbstract: What goals should a multi-goal reinforcement learning agent pursue during training in long-horizon tasks? When the desired (test time) goal distribution is too distant to offer a useful learning signal, we argue that the agent should not pursue unobtainable goals. Instead, it should set its own intrinsic goals that maximize the entropy of the historical achieved goal distribution. We propose to optimize this objective by having the agent pursue past achieved goals in sparsely explored areas of the goal space, which focuses exploration on the frontier of the achievable goal set. We show that our strategy achieves an order of magnitude better sample efficiency than the prior state of the art on long-horizon multi-goal tasks including maze navigation and block stacking.

paragraphs: In long-horizon reinforcement learning, an agent's eventual goals may be too distant to provide useful feedback early in training. Repeatedly attempting those goals can leave the agent without a productive learning signal. This paper asks which goals the agent should choose for itself while developing the capabilities needed to reach farther.

The proposed objective increases the entropy of the distribution of goals achieved so far, encouraging broader coverage of achieved outcomes. The agent pursues previously achieved goals in sparsely explored parts of goal space. This focuses training near the frontier of what it can already accomplish, using reachable outcomes to direct further exploration.

The authors report an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency over the prior state of the art on evaluated long-horizon multi-goal tasks, including maze navigation and block stacking. The finding supports choosing training goals according to current exploration history when desired test-time goals offer little guidance. It also gives a concrete objective for selecting intermediate goals, connecting their usefulness to expanded coverage of achievable outcomes.
summary.tldr: Choosing previously achieved goals in sparsely explored regions improves sample efficiency on evaluated long-horizon multi-goal tasks.

title: Maximum Entropy Gain Exploration for Long Horizon Multi-goal Reinforcement Learning

abstract: When presented with Out-of-Distribution (OOD) examples, deep neural networks yield confident, incorrect predictions; detecting OOD examples is challenging, and the potential risks are high. In this paper, we propose to detect OOD examples by identifying inconsistencies between activity patterns and predicted class. We find that characterizing activity patterns by Gram matrices and identifying anomalies in Gram matrix values can yield high OOD detection rates. We identify anomalies in the Gram matrices by simply comparing each value with its respective range observed over the training data. Unlike many approaches, this can be used with any pre-trained softmax classifier and neither requires access to OOD data for fine-tuning hyperparameters, nor does it require OOD access for inferring parameters. We empirically demonstrate applicability across a variety of architectures and vision datasets and, for the important and surprisingly hard task of detecting far out-of-distribution examples, it generally performs better than or equal to state-of-the-art OOD detection methods (including those that do assume access to OOD examples).

paragraphs: A classifier can assign high confidence to an incorrect prediction when an input comes from outside its training distribution. This paper detects such inputs by checking whether the network’s internal activity is consistent with its predicted class. The approach uses Gram matrices to characterize activity patterns, giving the detector information beyond the final softmax prediction.

The anomaly check is simple: compare each Gram-matrix value with the corresponding range observed in training data. Values outside their expected ranges signal inconsistencies. The method can be applied to any pretrained softmax classifier and requires no out-of-distribution examples either to infer parameters or to tune hyperparameters. That makes the available training data sufficient for setting up the detector.

Experiments demonstrate applicability across multiple network architectures and vision datasets. For examples far outside the training distribution, the method generally matches or exceeds state-of-the-art detectors, including methods that use out-of-distribution data. The reported evidence supports internal activity patterns as a useful basis for identifying unfamiliar inputs, particularly in that challenging detection setting.
summary.tldr: Gram-matrix activity checks detect unfamiliar inputs using training-data ranges, without requiring out-of-distribution examples for setup or tuning.

title: Detecting Out-of-Distribution Examples with Gram Matrices

abstract: It has long been argued that minibatch stochastic gradient descent can generalize better than large batch gradient descent in deep neural networks. However recent papers have questioned this claim, arguing that this effect is simply a consequence of suboptimal hyperparameter tuning or insufficient compute budgets when the batch size is large. In this paper, we perform carefully designed experiments and rigorous hyperparameter sweeps on a range of popular models, which verify that small or moderately large batch sizes can substantially outperform very large batches on the test set. This occurs even when both models are trained for the same number of iterations and large batches achieve smaller training losses. Our results confirm that the noise in stochastic gradients can enhance generalization. We study how the optimal learning rate schedule changes as the epoch budget grows, and we provide a theoretical account of our observations based on the stochastic differential equation perspective of SGD dynamics.

In this paper, we perform carefully designed experiments and rigorous hyperparameter sweeps on a range of popular models, which verify that small or moderately large batch sizes can substantially outperform very large batches on the test set. This occurs even when both models are trained for the same number of iterations and large batches achieve smaller training losses. Our results confirm that the noise in stochastic gradients can enhance generalization. We study how the optimal learning rate schedule changes as the epoch budget grows, and we provide a theoretical account of our observations based on the stochastic differential equation perspective of SGD dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper revisits whether noise from minibatch stochastic gradient descent can improve performance on unseen data. A competing explanation is that large-batch methods only appear worse because their hyperparameters are poorly tuned or their computation budgets are insufficient. The authors address that dispute through carefully designed experiments and rigorous hyperparameter sweeps across several popular models.

They find that small or moderately large batches can substantially outperform very large batches on the test set. This occurs even when training uses the same number of iterations and the large-batch models achieve lower training losses. The result separates fitting the training data more closely from performing better on held-out data, supporting a beneficial role for stochastic gradient noise.

The paper also examines how the best learning-rate schedule changes as the available epoch budget increases. It provides a theoretical account using a stochastic differential equation view of SGD dynamics, linking the empirical observations to an analysis of noisy optimization. The conclusion is that gradient noise can enhance generalization, rather than that smaller batches are invariably superior for every model or training setup.
summary.tldr: Carefully tuned experiments show that stochastic gradient noise can improve test performance even when very large batches achieve lower training loss.

title: On the Generalization Benefit of Noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Deep learning empirically achieves high performance in many applications, but its training dynamics has not been fully understood theoretically. In this paper, we explore theoretical analysis on training two-layer ReLU neural networks in a teacher-student regression model, in which a student network learns an unknown teacher network through its outputs. We show that with a specific regularization and sufficient over-parameterization, the student network can identify the parameters of the teacher network with high probability via gradient descent with a norm dependent stepsize even though the objective function is highly non-convex. The key theoretical tool is the measure representation of the neural networks and a novel application of a dual certificate argument for sparse estimation on a measure space. We analyze the global minima and global convergence property in the measure space.
originalAbstract: Deep learning empirically achieves high performance in many applications, but its training dynamics has not been fully understood theoretically. In this paper, we explore theoretical analysis on training two-layer ReLU neural networks in a teacher-student regression model, in which a student network learns an unknown teacher network through its outputs. We show that with a specific regularization and sufficient over-parameterization, the student network can identify the parameters of the teacher network with high probability via gradient descent with a norm dependent stepsize even though the objective function is highly non-convex. The key theoretical tool is the measure representation of the neural networks and a novel application of a dual certificate argument for sparse estimation on a measure space. We analyze the global minima and global convergence property in the measure space.

paragraphs: This paper studies why gradient-based training can succeed despite a neural network's nonconvex objective. It uses a teacher-student regression setting: an unknown two-layer ReLU teacher produces outputs, and a student network learns from them. The theoretical goal goes beyond matching predictions to identifying the teacher's parameters.

The recovery result requires a particular regularization scheme, sufficient overparameterization, and gradient descent with a step size that depends on a norm. Under these conditions, the student identifies the teacher parameters with high probability. These requirements are part of the guarantee; the result does not establish parameter recovery for unrestricted neural network training.

The analysis represents networks as measures and applies a dual certificate argument from sparse estimation in that measure space. This mathematical representation supports the study of global minima and global convergence. The contribution is a conditional explanation of successful learning in a specific neural model: it shows how the chosen regularization, network size, and optimization rule can overcome nonconvexity in the analyzed teacher-student setting.
summary.tldr: Under specific regularization, overparameterization, and step-size conditions, gradient descent can recover a two-layer ReLU teacher's parameters with high probability.

title: On Learnability via Gradient Method for Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks in Teacher-Student Setting

abstract: We consider the pure exploration problem in the fixed-budget linear bandit setting. We provide a new algorithm that identifies the best arm with high probability while being robust to unknown levels of observation noise as well as to moderate levels of misspecification in the linear model. Our technique combines prior approaches to pure exploration in the multi-armed bandit problem with optimal experimental design algorithms to obtain both problem dependent and problem independent bounds. Our success probability is never worse than that of an algorithm that ignores the linear structure, but seamlessly takes advantage of such structure when possible. Furthermore, we only need the number of samples to scale with the dimension of the problem rather than the number of arms. We complement our theoretical results with empirical validation.

paragraphs: Pure exploration asks a learner to identify the best available option using a limited sampling budget. In a linear bandit, structure connects the options and can make observations more informative. This paper develops an algorithm that exploits that structure while tolerating unknown observation noise and moderate inaccuracies in the assumed linear model.

The method combines ideas from multi-armed bandit exploration with optimal experimental design. Its analysis provides both problem-dependent and problem-independent bounds. A central guarantee is that its success probability is no worse than that of an algorithm that ignores linear structure, while it can benefit from that structure when it is useful.

The required sample count scales with the dimension of the problem rather than the number of arms, making the structural benefit especially relevant when many options share a lower-dimensional description. Empirical validation complements the theory. The robustness statement explicitly allows moderate model misspecification, rather than arbitrary departures from linearity. Together, the results describe a way to use structure without sacrificing the stated comparison to an approach that disregards it.
summary.tldr: A fixed-budget exploration algorithm exploits linear structure while remaining robust to unknown noise and moderate model misspecification.

title: Robust Pure Exploration in Linear Bandits with Limited Budget

abstract: Learning to reach goal states and learning diverse skills through mutual information maximization have been proposed as principled frameworks for unsupervised reinforcement learning, allowing agents to acquire broadly applicable multi-task policies with minimal reward engineering. In this paper, we discuss how these two approaches {—} goal-conditioned RL (GCRL) and MI-based RL {—} can be generalized into a single family of methods, interpreting mutual information maximization and variational empowerment as representation learning methods that acquire function-ally aware state representations for goal reaching.Starting from a simple observation that the standard GCRL is encapsulated by the optimization objective of variational empowerment, we can derive novel variants of GCRL and variational empowerment under a single, unified optimization objective, such as adaptive-variance GCRL and linear-mapping GCRL, and study the characteristics of representation learning each variant provides. Furthermore, through the lens of GCRL, we show that adapting powerful techniques fromGCRL such as goal relabeling into the variationalMI context as well as proper regularization on the variational posterior provides substantial gains in algorithm performance, and propose a novel evaluation metric named latent goal reaching (LGR)as an objective measure for evaluating empowerment algorithms akin to goal-based RL. Through principled mathematical derivations and careful experimental validations, our work lays a novel foundation from which representation learning can be evaluated and analyzed in goal-based RL

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning teaches an agent to reach specified states, while mutual-information-based learning encourages diverse skills with little reward engineering. This paper places both within a common family of objectives. It interprets mutual-information maximization and variational empowerment as learning state representations that reflect how states can function as goals.

The starting observation is that the usual goal-conditioned objective is included in variational empowerment’s optimization objective. From this connection, the authors derive variants including adaptive-variance and linear-mapping goal-conditioned learning. They examine the representation-learning behavior of these variants, using the shared objective to relate methods that otherwise appear to pursue different forms of unsupervised learning.

The connection also enables transferring goal relabeling into variational mutual-information methods. Together with suitable regularization of the variational posterior, this yields substantial performance gains in the experiments. The authors introduce latent goal reaching as an evaluation measure for empowerment algorithms. Mathematical derivations and experimental validation support a common basis for analyzing representations through their usefulness for reaching goals.
summary.tldr: A shared objective connects goal-conditioned learning and variational empowerment, enabling new variants, improved training, and goal-reaching evaluation.

title: Variational Empowerment as Representation Learning for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of robust mean estimation and introduce a novel Hamming distance-based measure of distribution shift for coordinate-level corruptions. We show that this measure yields adversary models that capture more realistic corruptions than those used in prior works, and present an information-theoretic analysis of robust mean estimation in these settings. We show that for structured distributions, methods that leverage the structure yield information theoretically more accurate mean estimation. We also focus on practical algorithms for robust mean estimation and study when data cleaning-inspired approaches that first fix corruptions in the input data and then perform robust mean estimation can match the information theoretic bounds of our analysis. We finally demonstrate experimentally that this two-step approach outperforms structure-agnostic robust estimation and provides accurate mean estimation even for high-magnitude corruption.

We show that this measure yields adversary models that capture more realistic corruptions than those used in prior works, and present an information-theoretic analysis of robust mean estimation in these settings. We show that for structured distributions, methods that leverage the structure yield information theoretically more accurate mean estimation. We also focus on practical algorithms for robust mean estimation and study when data cleaning-inspired approaches that first fix corruptions in the input data and then perform robust mean estimation can match the information theoretic bounds of our analysis. We finally demonstrate experimentally that this two-step approach outperforms structure-agnostic robust estimation and provides accurate mean estimation even for high-magnitude corruption.

paragraphs: Robust mean estimation seeks an accurate average despite corrupted observations. This paper focuses on corruption affecting individual coordinates and introduces a distribution-shift measure based on Hamming distance. The measure supports adversary models that the authors argue capture more realistic corruption patterns than models used in earlier work.

The information-theoretic analysis asks how accurately the mean can be estimated under these models. For structured distributions, the authors show that using the distribution’s structure permits more accurate estimation. This makes structural information a substantive part of robustness: achievable accuracy depends on whether the estimator takes advantage of it.

The practical component studies a two-stage strategy that first repairs corrupted input data and then applies robust mean estimation. The authors investigate when this cleaning-inspired procedure can match their information-theoretic bounds. Experiments show that the two-stage approach outperforms structure-agnostic robust estimation and remains accurate with high-magnitude corruption. The results connect a coordinate-level corruption model, theoretical accuracy limits, and a practical procedure that uses structure before estimating the mean.
summary.tldr: Using distribution structure and repairing corrupted coordinates can improve robust mean estimation under the paper’s corruption models.

title: On Robust Mean Estimation under Coordinate-level Corruption

abstract: Local graph clustering is an important algorithmic technique for analysing massive graphs, and has been widely applied in many research fields of data science. While the objective of most (local) graph clustering algorithms is to find a vertex set of low conductance, there has been a sequence of recent studies that highlight the importance of the inter-connection between clusters when analysing real-world datasets. Following this line of research, in this work we study local algorithms for finding a pair of vertex sets defined with respect to their inter-connection and their relationship with the rest of the graph. The key to our analysis is a new reduction technique that relates the structure of multiple sets to a single vertex set in the reduced graph. Among many potential applications, we show that our algorithms successfully recover densely connected clusters in the Interstate Disputes Dataset and the US Migration Dataset.

paragraphs: Local graph clustering helps analyze large networks by finding relevant groups of vertices. Many methods seek a single group with relatively few connections leading outside it, an objective described by low conductance. This paper instead focuses on the connections between groups, making the relationship between two sets part of what the algorithm seeks.

The authors study local algorithms that find a pair of vertex sets according to their interconnection and their links to the rest of the graph. Their main analytical tool is a reduction that transforms questions about multiple sets into a question about one set in a modified graph. This connects the paired structure to a simpler form of graph analysis.

The algorithms successfully recover densely connected clusters in the Interstate Disputes Dataset and the US Migration Dataset. These applications illustrate the value of examining groups through their mutual relationships. The contribution expands the clustering target from the isolation of one group to the joint structure of two groups and their surrounding network.
summary.tldr: New local graph algorithms find pairs of densely connected clusters by reducing a multiple-set structure to a single-set problem.

title: Local Algorithms for Finding Densely Connected Clusters

abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting has numerous applications in analyzing wireless, traffic, and financial networks. Many classical statistical models often fall short in handling the complexity and high non-linearity present in time-series data. Recent advances in deep learning allow for better modelling of spatial and temporal dependencies. While most of these models focus on obtaining accurate point forecasts, they do not characterize the prediction uncertainty. In this work, we consider the time-series data as a random realization from a nonlinear state-space model and target Bayesian inference of the hidden states for probabilistic forecasting. We use particle flow as the tool for approximating the posterior distribution of the states, as it is shown to be highly effective in complex, high-dimensional settings. Thorough experimentation on several real world time-series datasets demonstrates that our approach provides better characterization of uncertainty while maintaining comparable accuracy to the state-of-the-art point forecasting methods.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal forecasting involves data whose behavior depends on both time and relationships across locations or entities. Deep models can capture these dependencies, but accurate point predictions do not describe uncertainty. This paper develops a probabilistic forecasting approach that treats the observed time series as a random realization of a nonlinear state-space model.

The method targets Bayesian inference over hidden states: it seeks a distribution of plausible underlying states rather than a single estimate. Particle flow approximates the posterior distribution of those states. The authors use it because of its effectiveness in complex, high-dimensional settings, making uncertainty about hidden dynamics a central part of the forecasting process.

Experiments on several real-world time-series datasets show better characterization of uncertainty while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art point forecasting methods. This pairing matters because a richer account of predictive uncertainty is useful alongside a competitive central forecast. The reported finding is that the approach supplies that additional probabilistic information without sacrificing comparable point-prediction accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Particle-flow inference over nonlinear hidden states improves forecast uncertainty characterization while retaining competitive point-prediction accuracy.

title: RNN with Particle Flow for Probabilistic Spatio-temporal Forecasting

abstract: Consider a prosthetic arm, learning to adapt to its user’s control signals. We propose \emph{Interaction-Grounded Learning} for this novel setting, in which a learner’s goal is to interact with the environment with no grounding or explicit reward to optimize its policies. Such a problem evades common RL solutions which require an explicit reward. The learning agent observes a multidimensional \emph{context vector}, takes an \emph{action}, and then observes a multidimensional \emph{feedback vector}. This multidimensional feedback vector has \emph{no} explicit reward information. In order to succeed, the algorithm must learn how to evaluate the feedback vector to discover a latent reward signal, with which it can ground its policies without supervision. We show that in an Interaction-Grounded Learning setting, with certain natural assumptions, a learner can discover the latent reward and ground its policy for successful interaction. We provide theoretical guarantees and a proof-of-concept empirical evaluation to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Such a problem evades common RL solutions which require an explicit reward. The learning agent observes a multidimensional \emph{context vector}, takes an \emph{action}, and then observes a multidimensional \emph{feedback vector}. This multidimensional feedback vector has \emph{no} explicit reward information. In order to succeed, the algorithm must learn how to evaluate the feedback vector to discover a latent reward signal, with which it can ground its policies without supervision. paragraphs: The paper introduces a learning setting motivated by a prosthetic arm adapting to its user’s control signals. The learner receives a context vector, chooses an action, and observes a feedback vector. Crucially, that feedback does not explicitly identify a reward, so the learner cannot directly use the reward signal assumed by common reinforcement learning methods.

Interaction-Grounded Learning makes discovering how to evaluate feedback part of the task. The agent must uncover a latent reward signal and use it to ground its policy without supervision. This links two learning problems: interpreting what feedback means for successful interaction and choosing actions based on that interpretation.

The authors show that this is possible under certain natural assumptions in their proposed setting. They provide theoretical guarantees and a proof-of-concept empirical evaluation. The result is conditional on those assumptions; it does not claim that arbitrary feedback always reveals a useful reward. Its contribution is to formalize and demonstrate a route to learning successful interactions when rewards are implicit in multidimensional feedback.
summary.tldr: Interaction-Grounded Learning discovers a latent reward from feedback without explicit reward labels, with guarantees under stated assumptions.

title: Interaction-Grounded Learning

abstract: Vision transformers using self-attention or its proposed alternatives have demonstrated promising results in many image related tasks. However, the underpinning inductive bias of attention is not well understood. To address this issue, this paper analyzes attention through the lens of convex duality. For the non-linear dot-product self-attention, and alternative mechanisms such as MLP-mixer and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), we derive equivalent finite-dimensional convex problems that are interpretable and solvable to global optimality. The convex programs lead to block nuclear-norm regularization that promotes low rank in the latent feature and token dimensions. In particular, we show how self-attention networks implicitly clusters the tokens, based on their latent similarity. We conduct experiments for transferring a pre-trained transformer backbone for CIFAR-100 classification by fine-tuning a variety of convex attention heads. The results indicate the merits of the bias induced by attention compared with the existing MLP or linear heads.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms perform well in vision tasks, but the preferences they build into a model are less well understood. This paper uses convex duality to examine those inductive biases. It analyzes nonlinear dot-product self-attention alongside alternative mechanisms, including MLP-mixer and the Fourier Neural Operator.

The authors derive equivalent finite-dimensional convex optimization problems that can be interpreted and solved to global optimality. These formulations reveal block nuclear-norm regularization, which encourages low-rank structure in latent feature and token dimensions. The analysis also shows that self-attention implicitly groups tokens according to their similarity in the latent representation, giving a concrete interpretation of its bias.

To examine the practical value of this perspective, the paper fine-tunes several convex attention heads on a pretrained transformer backbone for CIFAR-100 classification. The results support the advantages of the bias induced by attention compared with existing MLP and linear heads. The contribution connects interpretable optimization structure to a specific transfer-learning evaluation, rather than treating attention's empirical success as an unexplained architectural property.
summary.tldr: Convex formulations reveal how attention encourages low-rank structure and groups similar tokens, with supporting results from transformer-head fine-tuning.

title: Unraveling Attention via Convex Duality: Analysis and Interpretations of Vision Transformers

abstract: Recently, MLP-like vision models have achieved promising performances on mainstream visual recognition tasks. In contrast with vision transformers and CNNs, the success of MLP-like models shows that simple information fusion operations among tokens and channels can yield a good representation power for deep recognition models. However, existing MLP-like models fuse tokens through static fusion operations, lacking adaptability to the contents of the tokens to be mixed. Thus, customary information fusion procedures are not effective enough. To this end, this paper presents an efficient MLP-like network architecture, dubbed DynaMixer, resorting to dynamic information fusion. Critically, we propose a procedure, on which the DynaMixer model relies, to dynamically generate mixing matrices by leveraging the contents of all the tokens to be mixed. To reduce the time complexity and improve the robustness, a dimensionality reduction technique and a multi-segment fusion mechanism are adopted. Our proposed DynaMixer model (97M parameters) achieves 84.3% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet-1K dataset without extra training data, performing favorably against the state-of-the-art vision MLP models. When the number of parameters is reduced to 26M, it still achieves 82.7% top-1 accuracy, surpassing the existing MLP-like models with a similar capacity. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/ziyuwwang/DynaMixer}.

paragraphs: Vision models based on multilayer perceptrons can recognize images by mixing information across tokens and channels. The paper identifies a weakness in existing versions: their token-mixing operations remain fixed regardless of the content being processed. This limits how the fusion operation adapts to the particular visual input.

DynaMixer generates mixing matrices dynamically from the contents of all tokens involved in the operation. Consequently, the way information is combined depends on what the tokens contain. The architecture also uses dimensionality reduction and a multi-segment fusion mechanism to reduce time complexity and improve robustness while retaining this content-sensitive mixing.

A smaller, 26-million-parameter version achieves 82.7%, exceeding the compared MLP-like models of similar capacity. These results support dynamic mixing as an effective architectural choice at both of the reported model sizes.
summary.tldr: DynaMixer improves vision MLPs by adapting token mixing to image content, with strong ImageNet-1K results at two model sizes.

title: DynaMixer: A Vision MLP Architecture with Dynamic Mixing

abstract: The computational study of equilibria involving constraints on players’ strategies has been largely neglected. However, in real-world applications, players are usually subject to constraints ruling out the feasibility of some of their strategies, such as, e.g., safety requirements and budget caps. Computational studies on constrained versions of the Nash equilibrium have lead to some results under very stringent assumptions, while finding constrained versions of the correlated equilibrium (CE) is still unexplored. In this paper, we introduce and computationally characterize constrained Phi-equilibria—a more general notion than constrained CEs—in normal-form games. We show that computing such equilibria is in general computationally intractable, and also that the set of the equilibria may not be convex, providing a sharp divide with unconstrained CEs. Nevertheless, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm for computing a constrained (approximate) Phi-equilibrium maximizing a given linear function, when either the number of constraints or that of players’ actions is fixed. Moreover, in the special case in which a player’s constraints do not depend on other players’ strategies, we show that an exact, function-maximizing equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time, while one (approximate) equilibrium can be found with an efficient decentralized no-regret learning algorithm.

This paper introduces constrained Phi-equilibria for normal-form games, a notion broad enough to include constrained correlated equilibria. It investigates both the mathematical structure of these equilibria and the difficulty of finding them computationally.

These results make the role of constraint structure explicit: the general difficulty coexists with useful algorithmic guarantees under particular restrictions.
summary.tldr: Constrained Phi-equilibria are generally hard to compute, but particular restrictions on constraints or actions allow efficient algorithms.

title: Constrained Phi-Equilibria

abstract: In the privacy-utility tradeoff of a model trained on benchmark language and vision tasks, remarkable improvements have been widely reported when the model is pretrained on public data. Some gain is expected as these models inherit the benefits of transfer learning, which is the standard motivation in non-private settings. However, the stark contrast in the gain of pretraining between non-private and private machine learning suggests that the gain in the latter is rooted in a fundamentally different cause. To explain this phenomenon, we hypothesize that the non-convex loss landscape of a model training necessitates the optimization algorithm to go through two phases. In the first, the algorithm needs to select a good “basin” in the loss landscape. In the second, the algorithm solves an easy optimization within that basin. The former is a harder problem to solve with private data, while the latter is harder to solve with public data due to a distribution shift or data scarcity. Guided by this intuition, we provide theoretical constructions that provably demonstrate the separation between private training with and without public pretraining. Further, systematic experiments on CIFAR10 and Librispeech provide supporting evidence for our hypothesis.

This paper investigates why. It proposes that the unusual benefit comes from different stages of optimization presenting different difficulties for public and private training.

The authors hypothesize a two-phase process in a non-convex loss landscape. First, optimization must identify a good basin, or region in which to train. Second, it performs an easier optimization within that region. Selecting the basin is harder with private data, while completing the second phase using public data can be hindered by distribution shift or limited data availability.

Guided by this picture, the paper provides theoretical constructions proving a separation between private training with and without public pretraining. Experiments on CIFAR10 and Librispeech offer additional support for the hypothesis. The results give a specific explanation for why public pretraining can be especially valuable under privacy constraints, while keeping the broad two-phase account a hypothesis supported by constructions and experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that public pretraining helps private learning by selecting a good optimization basin, supported by theory and experiments.

title: Why Is Public Pretraining Necessary for Private Model Training?

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new task for code completion that focuses on handling long code input and propose a sparse Transformer model, called LongCoder, to address this task. LongCoder employs a sliding window mechanism for self-attention and introduces two types of globally accessible tokens - bridge tokens and memory tokens - to improve performance and efficiency. Bridge tokens are inserted throughout the input sequence to aggregate local information and facilitate global interaction, while memory tokens are included to highlight important statements that may be invoked later and need to be memorized, such as package imports and definitions of classes, functions, or structures. We conduct experiments on a newly constructed dataset that contains longer code context and the publicly available CodeXGLUE benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate that LongCoder achieves superior performance on code completion tasks compared to previous models while maintaining comparable efficiency in terms of computational resources during inference.

paragraphs: LongCoder addresses code completion when the available code context is long. Useful information can occur far from the point being completed, including earlier imports and definitions. The paper introduces a task focused on this setting and proposes a sparse Transformer designed to combine local processing with access to distant information.

Its attention mechanism uses a sliding window alongside two kinds of globally accessible tokens. Bridge tokens are distributed through the input to collect local information and support interaction across the sequence. Memory tokens highlight statements likely to matter later, such as imports and definitions of classes, functions, or structures. The two mechanisms give global communication and explicit retention of important code distinct roles.

The authors evaluate LongCoder on a newly constructed dataset with longer code contexts and on CodeXGLUE. It outperforms previous models on the tested completion tasks while using comparable computational resources during inference. The result supports the usefulness of selective global access for long-context completion without a corresponding increase in reported inference resource demands.
summary.tldr: LongCoder combines local attention with bridge and memory tokens to improve long-context code completion at comparable inference cost.

title: LongCoder: A Long-Range Pre-trained Language Model for Code Completion

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of inference in high-order structured prediction tasks. In the context of Markov random fields, the goal of a high-order inference task is to maximize a score function on the space of labels, and the score function can be decomposed into sum of unary and high-order potentials. We apply a generative model approach to study the problem of high-order inference, and provide a two-stage convex optimization algorithm for exact label recovery. We also provide a new class of hypergraph structural properties related to hyperedge expansion that drives the success in general high-order inference problems. Finally, we connect the performance of our algorithm and the hyperedge expansion property using a novel hypergraph Cheeger-type inequality.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the problem of inference in high-order structured prediction tasks. In the context of Markov random fields, the goal of a high-order inference task is to maximize a score function on the space of labels, and the score function can be decomposed into sum of unary and high-order potentials. We apply a generative model approach to study the problem of high-order inference, and provide a two-stage convex optimization algorithm for exact label recovery. We also provide a new class of hypergraph structural properties related to hyperedge expansion that drives the success in general high-order inference problems. Finally, we connect the performance of our algorithm and the hyperedge expansion property using a novel hypergraph Cheeger-type inequality.

paragraphs: Structured prediction assigns labels that must be considered together. In the Markov random field setting studied here, an assignment receives a score combining contributions from individual labels and interactions involving larger groups of labels. Inference seeks the assignment with the highest total score, so those group interactions are central to the problem.

The authors study high-order inference through a generative model and introduce a two-stage convex optimization algorithm for exact label recovery. They also identify a class of structural properties of hypergraphs, which represent interactions among groups of variables. These properties concern hyperedge expansion and help explain when the inference procedure succeeds.

The paper then connects the algorithm’s performance to expansion through a new hypergraph Cheeger-type inequality. This gives a mathematical relationship between the structure of the interactions and the ability to recover labels exactly. The contribution therefore includes both an inference procedure and an explanation of its success in terms of hypergraph structure, rather than an unconditional claim that every high-order prediction problem can be solved exactly.
summary.tldr: A two-stage convex inference algorithm connects exact label recovery to hypergraph expansion through a new Cheeger-type inequality.

title: Exact Inference in High-order Structured Prediction

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a powerful algorithm to sample latent variables from Bayesian models. The advent of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) frees users from writing inference algorithms and lets users focus on modeling. However, many models are difficult for HMC to solve directly, and often require tricks like model reparameterization. We are motivated by the fact that many of those models could be simplified by marginalization. We propose to use automatic marginalization as part of the sampling process using HMC in a graphical model extracted from a PPL, which substantially improves sampling from real-world hierarchical models.

We propose to use automatic marginalization as part of the sampling process using HMC in a graphical model extracted from a PPL, which substantially improves sampling from real-world hierarchical models.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming lets users describe a Bayesian model while software handles inference. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a powerful sampling method for these models, but some models remain difficult for it to handle directly. Users may consequently need to restructure their models through techniques such as reparameterization, reducing the convenience of automated inference.

This paper explores automatic marginalization as part of the HMC sampling process. Marginalization simplifies an inference problem by integrating out some variables instead of sampling every variable explicitly. The proposed approach works with a graphical model extracted from a probabilistic program, connecting the program's model structure to the simplification used during inference.

The authors report substantial sampling improvements on real-world hierarchical models. The practical significance is that model simplification can become part of the inference machinery rather than depending entirely on manual intervention. The stated result concerns improved sampling in these hierarchical models, supporting automatic marginalization as a useful way to make probabilistic programming more effective on models that challenge direct HMC.
summary.tldr: Automatically marginalizing variables in probabilistic programs substantially improves HMC sampling on real-world hierarchical models.

title: Automatically marginalized MCMC in probabilistic programming

abstract: We introduce a value-based RL agent, which we call BBF, that achieves super-human performance in the Atari 100K benchmark. BBF relies on scaling the neural networks used for value estimation, as well as a number of other design choices that enable this scaling in a sample-efficient manner. We conduct extensive analyses of these design choices and provide insights for future work. We end with a discussion about updating the goalposts for sample-efficient RL research on the ALE. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/bigger_better_faster.
originalAbstract: We introduce a value-based RL agent, which we call BBF, that achieves super-human performance in the Atari 100K benchmark. BBF relies on scaling the neural networks used for value estimation, as well as a number of other design choices that enable this scaling in a sample-efficient manner. We conduct extensive analyses of these design choices and provide insights for future work. We end with a discussion about updating the goalposts for sample-efficient RL research on the ALE. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/bigger_better_faster.

paragraphs: BBF is a reinforcement learning agent designed to learn effectively from a limited amount of interaction. It uses a value-based approach, estimating how rewarding actions will be and using those estimates to guide behavior. The paper reports super-human performance on the Atari 100K benchmark, making sample efficiency central to its contribution.

A key ingredient is scaling up the neural networks used to estimate value. The authors pair this increase in network size with other design choices that make scaling work in a sample-efficient way. The contribution therefore concerns a combination of model capacity and training design, rather than a claim that increasing network size alone produces the reported result.

The paper extensively analyzes these design choices to provide insights for subsequent research. Its findings show that larger value-estimation networks can be part of an effective approach under the benchmark's interaction budget. The authors also discuss how research goals for sample-efficient learning on the Arcade Learning Environment might evolve in light of such performance.
summary.tldr: BBF achieves super-human Atari 100K performance by combining larger value networks with design choices that support sample-efficient learning.

title: Bigger, Better, Faster: Human-level Atari with human-level efficiency

abstract: Although graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved impressive achievements in graph classification, they often need abundant task-specific labels, which could be extensively costly to acquire. A credible solution is to explore additional labeled graphs to enhance unsupervised learning on the target domain. However, how to apply GNNs to domain adaptation remains unsolved owing to the insufficient exploration of graph topology and the significant domain discrepancy. In this paper, we propose Coupled Contrastive Graph Representation Learning (CoCo), which extracts the topological information from coupled learning branches and reduces the domain discrepancy with coupled contrastive learning. CoCo contains a graph convolutional network branch and a hierarchical graph kernel network branch, which explore graph topology in implicit and explicit manners. Besides, we incorporate coupled branches into a holistic multi-view contrastive learning framework, which not only incorporates graph representations learned from complementary views for enhanced understanding, but also encourages the similarity between cross-domain example pairs with the same semantics for domain alignment. Extensive experiments on popular datasets show that our CoCo outperforms these competing baselines in different settings generally.
