paragraphs: Graph classification often requires many task-specific labels, which can be expensive to obtain. This paper considers using labeled graphs from another domain to support learning in an unlabeled target domain. Two central obstacles are capturing enough information about graph structure and handling differences between the source and target domains.

CoCo addresses both through two coupled learning branches. A graph convolutional branch captures topology implicitly, while a hierarchical graph kernel branch captures it explicitly. A multi-view contrastive learning framework brings these complementary representations together, allowing the model to learn from different views of the same structural information.

The framework also encourages cross-domain examples with the same semantics to have similar representations. This connects richer structural understanding with the goal of aligning domains, rather than treating those objectives separately. Across experiments on popular datasets and different settings, CoCo generally outperforms the competing baselines. The findings support the usefulness of combining complementary graph views with semantic alignment for the domain-adaptation problems evaluated.
summary.tldr: CoCo combines complementary graph representations and cross-domain contrastive learning to improve classification in unlabeled target domains.

title: CoCo: A Coupled Contrastive Framework for Unsupervised Domain Adaptive Graph Classification

abstract: As a type of valuable intellectual property (IP), deep neural network (DNN) models have been protected by techniques like watermarking. However, such passive model protection cannot fully prevent model abuse. In this work, we propose an active model IP protection scheme, namely NNSplitter, which actively protects the model by splitting it into two parts: the obfuscated model that performs poorly due to weight obfuscation, and the model secrets consisting of the indexes and original values of the obfuscated weights, which can only be accessed by authorized users with the support of the trusted execution environment. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of NNSplitter, e.g., by only modifying 275 out of over 11 million (i.e., 0.002%) weights, the accuracy of the obfuscated ResNet-18 model on CIFAR-10 can drop to 10%. Moreover, NNSplitter is stealthy and resilient against norm clipping and fine-tuning attacks, making it an appealing solution for DNN model protection. The code is available at: https://github.com/Tongzhou0101/NNSplitter.

The code is available at: https://github.com/Tongzhou0101/NNSplitter.

paragraphs: A watermark can help establish ownership of a neural network, but passive protection cannot fully prevent misuse. NNSplitter takes an active approach by dividing a model into an intentionally impaired version and a small collection of secrets needed to recover its original weights. Access to those secrets is restricted to authorized users through a trusted execution environment.

The impaired model contains obfuscated weights. The separate secrets record which weights were changed and their original values. This makes useful model operation depend on protected information beyond the distributed model itself. The approach therefore relies on controlled access to the secrets supported by the trusted execution environment.

The experiments demonstrate that changing very few weights can severely degrade performance. In the reported ResNet-18 example on CIFAR-10, modifying 275 of more than 11 million weights reduces accuracy to 10%. The abstract also reports stealthiness and resilience against norm clipping and fine-tuning attacks. These findings support the effectiveness of sparse weight obfuscation in the evaluated protection setting.
summary.tldr: NNSplitter protects a neural network by obfuscating a small number of weights and restricting their original values to authorized users.

title: NNSplitter: An Active Defense Solution for DNN Model via Automated Weight Obfuscation

abstract: Most leading implementations of black-box variational inference (BBVI) are based on optimizing a stochastic evidence lower bound (ELBO). But such approaches to BBVI often converge slowly due to the high variance of their gradient estimates and their sensitivity to hyperparameters. In this work, we propose batch and match (BaM), an alternative approach to BBVI based on a score-based divergence. Notably, this score-based divergence can be optimized by a closed-form proximal update for Gaussian variational families with full covariance matrices. We analyze the convergence of BaM when the target distribution is Gaussian, and we prove that in the limit of infinite batch size the variational parameter updates converge exponentially quickly to the target mean and covariance. We also evaluate the performance of BaM on Gaussian and non-Gaussian target distributions that arise from posterior inference in hierarchical and deep generative models. In these experiments, we find that BaM typically converges in fewer (and sometimes significantly fewer) gradient evaluations than leading implementations of BBVI based on ELBO maximization.

Notably, this score-based divergence can be optimized by a closed-form proximal update for Gaussian variational families with full covariance matrices. In these experiments, we find that BaM typically converges in fewer (and sometimes significantly fewer) gradient evaluations than leading implementations of BBVI based on ELBO maximization.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a target probability distribution with a distribution that is easier to work with. Many black-box implementations optimize an evidence lower bound, or ELBO. The paper identifies noisy gradient estimates and sensitivity to hyperparameters as reasons these methods can converge slowly, and proposes batch and match, abbreviated BaM, as an alternative.

BaM optimizes a divergence based on scores, which describe how log probability changes with the variables. For Gaussian approximations with full covariance matrices, the method admits a closed-form proximal update. This gives a direct update rule for a family that can represent correlations, rather than relying on the usual stochastic ELBO optimization procedure.

The theoretical result concerns a Gaussian target and the limit of infinite batch size: under those conditions, the estimated mean and covariance converge exponentially quickly. Experiments also cover non-Gaussian targets from hierarchical and deep generative models. In these tests, BaM typically needs fewer gradient evaluations than leading ELBO-based implementations, sometimes substantially fewer. The experiments therefore extend the evidence beyond the setting of the convergence proof.
summary.tldr: BaM uses score-based matching and closed-form Gaussian updates to reduce gradient evaluations in tested variational inference problems.

title: Batch and match: black-box variational inference with a score-based divergence

abstract: A multimodal large language model (MLLM) agent can receive instructions, capture images, retrieve histories from memory, and decide which tools to use. Nonetheless, red-teaming efforts have revealed that adversarial images/prompts can jailbreak an MLLM and cause unaligned behaviors. In this work, we report an even more severe safety issue in multi-agent environments, referred to as infectious jailbreak. It entails the adversary simply jailbreaking a single agent, and without any further intervention from the adversary, (almost) all agents will become infected exponentially fast and exhibit harmful behaviors. To validate the feasibility of infectious jailbreak, we simulate multi-agent environments containing up to one million LLaVA-1.5 agents, and employ randomized pair-wise chat as a proof-of-concept instantiation for multi-agent interaction. Our results show that feeding an (infectious) adversarial image into the memory of any randomly chosen agent is sufficient to achieve infectious jailbreak. Finally, we derive a simple principle for determining whether a defense mechanism can provably restrain the spread of infectious jailbreak, but how to design a practical defense that meets this principle remains an open question to investigate.

paragraphs: This paper studies a failure mode in which compromising one multimodal agent can spread harmful behavior through an interacting population. The authors call it infectious jailbreak: after the initial compromise, communication between agents carries the attack onward without further intervention by the adversary.

To test feasibility, the authors simulate populations of up to one million LLaVA-1.5 agents. Their proof-of-concept interaction pattern consists of randomized conversations between pairs. In this setting, placing an infectious adversarial image in the memory of a randomly chosen agent is sufficient to initiate spread, with almost all agents becoming affected exponentially fast.

The result identifies a system-level concern beyond an individual model's response to an adversarial input: agent interaction can propagate an initial failure. Its demonstrated scope is the simulated population and interaction setup described in the study. The authors also derive a principle for deciding whether a defense can provably restrain spread, while leaving the construction of a practical defense satisfying that principle as an open problem.
summary.tldr: Simulations show that one adversarial image can trigger rapidly spreading jailbreaks through a large population of interacting multimodal agents.

title: Agent Smith: A Single Image Can Jailbreak One Million Multimodal LLM Agents Exponentially Fast

abstract: Learning a reward function from demonstrations suffers from low sample-efficiency. Even with abundant data, current inverse reinforcement learning methods that focus on learning from a single environment can fail to handle slight changes in the environment dynamics. We tackle these challenges through adaptive environment design. In our framework, the learner repeatedly interacts with the expert, with the former selecting environments to identify the reward function as quickly as possible from the expert’s demonstrations in said environments. This results in improvements in both sample-efficiency and robustness, as we show experimentally, for both exact and approximate inference.
originalAbstract: Learning a reward function from demonstrations suffers from low sample-efficiency. Even with abundant data, current inverse reinforcement learning methods that focus on learning from a single environment can fail to handle slight changes in the environment dynamics. We tackle these challenges through adaptive environment design. In our framework, the learner repeatedly interacts with the expert, with the former selecting environments to identify the reward function as quickly as possible from the expert’s demonstrations in said environments. This results in improvements in both sample-efficiency and robustness, as we show experimentally, for both exact and approximate inference.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer a reward function from an expert’s demonstrations. The paper highlights two difficulties: learning can require many demonstrations, and a reward inferred from behavior in one environment may fail to handle even small changes in the environment’s dynamics. Collecting more data in that same setting does not necessarily resolve the latter problem.

The proposed framework gives the learner an active role in choosing where demonstrations occur. It repeatedly selects an environment and observes the expert acting there. Environment selection is adaptive, with the aim of identifying the reward function as quickly as possible. The information-gathering process therefore includes choosing the conditions under which expert behavior is observed.

Experiments show improvements in both sample efficiency and robustness, using exact as well as approximate inference. These findings support adaptive environment design as a useful part of reward learning. The approach depends on repeated interaction with an expert in learner-selected environments, making that interaction structure a central feature of how it obtains informative demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Adaptively choosing environments for expert demonstrations improves reward-learning sample efficiency and robustness in the reported experiments.

title: Environment Design for Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Dynamic convolution learns a linear mixture of $n$ static kernels weighted with their input-dependent attentions, demonstrating superior performance than normal convolution. However, it increases the number of convolutional parameters by $n$ times, and thus is not parameter efficient. This leads to no research progress that can allow researchers to explore the setting $n > 100$ (an order of magnitude larger than the typical setting $n < 10$) for pushing forward the performance boundary of dynamic convolution while enjoying parameter efficiency. To fill this gap, in this paper, we propose KernelWarehouse, a more general form of dynamic convolution, which redefines the basic concepts of “kernels”, “assembling kernels” and “attention function” through the lens of exploiting convolutional parameter dependencies within the same layer and across neighboring layers of a ConvNet. We testify the effectiveness of KernelWarehouse on ImageNet and MS-COCO datasets using various ConvNet architectures. Intriguingly, KernelWarehouse is also applicable to Vision Transformers, and it can even reduce the model size of a backbone while improving the model accuracy. For instance, KernelWarehouse ($n = 4$) achieves 5.61%|3.90%|4.38% absolute top-1 accuracy gain on the ResNet18|MobileNetV2|DeiT-Tiny backbone, and KernelWarehouse ($n = 1/4$) with 65.10% model size reduction still achieves 2.29% gain on the ResNet18 backbone. The code and models are available at https://github.com/OSVAI/KernelWarehouse.

To fill this gap, in this paper, we propose KernelWarehouse, a more general form of dynamic convolution, which redefines the basic concepts of “kernels”, “assembling kernels” and “attention function” through the lens of exploiting convolutional parameter dependencies within the same layer and across neighboring layers of a ConvNet. We testify the effectiveness of KernelWarehouse on ImageNet and MS-COCO datasets using various ConvNet architectures. Intriguingly, KernelWarehouse is also applicable to Vision Transformers, and it can even reduce the model size of a backbone while improving the model accuracy. For instance, KernelWarehouse ($n = 4$) achieves 5.61%|3.90%|4.38% absolute top-1 accuracy gain on the ResNet18|MobileNetV2|DeiT-Tiny backbone, and KernelWarehouse ($n = 1/4$) with 65.10% model size reduction still achieves 2.29% gain on the ResNet18 backbone. The code and models are available at https://github.com/OSVAI/KernelWarehouse.

paragraphs: Dynamic convolution adapts to an input by mixing static kernels with input-dependent attention weights. Its flexibility comes with a parameter cost: using n kernels multiplies convolutional parameters by n. KernelWarehouse addresses this obstacle by reconsidering what counts as a kernel, how kernels are assembled, and how the attention function operates.

The method exploits dependencies among convolutional parameters within a layer and across neighboring layers. This broader formulation is intended to make large kernel mixtures compatible with parameter efficiency, including settings beyond 100 where conventional approaches typically use fewer than 10. The paper evaluates the method across multiple convolutional architectures and also demonstrates applicability to Vision Transformers.

Experiments use ImageNet and MS-COCO. With n = 4, reported absolute top-1 accuracy gains are 5.61%, 3.90%, and 4.38% for ResNet18, MobileNetV2, and DeiT-Tiny, respectively. A ResNet18 configuration with n = 1/4 reduces model size by 65.10% while gaining 2.29% accuracy. These examples show that the formulation can improve accuracy even in a configuration that substantially reduces model size.
summary.tldr: KernelWarehouse redesigns dynamic convolution around parameter dependencies, enabling accuracy improvements and configurations with substantially smaller models.

title: KernelWarehouse: Rethinking the Design of Dynamic Convolution

abstract: Gaussian process factor analysis (GPFA) is a latent variable modeling technique commonly used to identify smooth, low-dimensional latent trajectories underlying high-dimensional neural recordings. Specifically, researchers model spiking rates as Gaussian observations, resulting in tractable inference. Recently, GPFA has been extended to model spike count data. However, due to the non-conjugacy of the likelihood, the inference becomes intractable. Prior works rely on either black-box inference techniques, numerical integration or polynomial approximations of the likelihood to handle intractability. To overcome this challenge, we propose a conditionally-conjugate Gaussian process factor analysis (ccGPFA) resulting in both analytically and computationally tractable inference for modeling neural activity from spike count data. In particular, we develop a novel data augmentation based method that renders the model conditionally conjugate. Consequently, our model enjoys the advantage of simple closed-form updates using a variational EM algorithm. Furthermore, due to its conditional conjugacy, we show our model can be readily scaled using sparse Gaussian Processes and accelerated inference via natural gradients. To validate our method, we empirically demonstrate its efficacy through experiments.

paragraphs: Gaussian process factor analysis seeks smooth, low-dimensional patterns underlying recordings from many neurons. Treating neural firing rates as Gaussian observations makes inference tractable, but directly modeling spike counts creates a harder mathematical problem. The likelihood no longer combines conveniently with the rest of the model, prompting earlier approaches to use numerical integration, approximations, or black-box inference.

The proposed ccGPFA method changes this computational situation through data augmentation. It introduces auxiliary quantities that make the model conditionally conjugate: once those quantities are included, the relevant inference updates take an analytically convenient form. This enables closed-form updates within a variational expectation-maximization algorithm while retaining a model for spike count observations.

The same structure supports further computational improvements. The authors show how to use sparse Gaussian processes for scaling and natural gradients to accelerate inference. They also report experiments demonstrating the method's efficacy. The contribution is a count-data formulation whose mathematical structure directly supports simpler inference, scalable computation, and recovery of latent neural activity trajectories.
summary.tldr: ccGPFA uses data augmentation to make latent trajectory inference from neural spike counts analytically and computationally tractable.

title: Conditionally-Conjugate Gaussian Process Factor Analysis for Spike Count Data via Data Augmentation

abstract: Static sparse training aims to train sparse models from scratch, achieving remarkable results in recent years. A key design choice is given by the sparse initialization, which determines the trainable sub-network through a binary mask. Existing methods mainly select such mask based on a predefined dense initialization. Such an approach may not efficiently leverage the mask’s potential impact on the optimization. An alternative direction, inspired by research into dynamical isometry, is to introduce orthogonality in the sparse subnetwork, which helps in stabilizing the gradient signal. In this work, we propose Exact Orthogonal Initialization (EOI), a novel sparse orthogonal initialization scheme based on composing random Givens rotations. Contrary to other existing approaches, our method provides exact (not approximated) orthogonality and enables the creation of layers with arbitrary densities. We demonstrate the superior effectiveness and efficiency of EOI through experiments, consistently outperforming common sparse initialization techniques. Our method enables training highly sparse 1000-layer MLP and CNN networks without residual connections or normalization techniques, emphasizing the crucial role of weight initialization in static sparse training alongside sparse mask selection.

paragraphs: Static sparse training starts with a network in which only selected connections are trainable. A binary mask defines this subnetwork, and many initialization methods choose that mask around an already initialized dense model. This paper argues that the weights within the sparse subnetwork also deserve direct attention because their initialization affects optimization.

The proposed Exact Orthogonal Initialization, or EOI, composes random Givens rotations to produce sparse orthogonal weights. Orthogonality is motivated by its ability to help stabilize gradient signals. The method provides exact rather than approximate orthogonality and allows layers to be created at arbitrary densities, connecting a mathematical property of the weights with control over sparsity.

Experiments show improvements in effectiveness and efficiency over common sparse initialization techniques. Particularly striking demonstrations train highly sparse, 1,000-layer multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks without residual connections or normalization. These results emphasize that successful static sparse training depends on how the retained connections are initialized as well as on which connections the mask selects.
summary.tldr: Exact Orthogonal Initialization improves static sparse training and enables highly sparse 1,000-layer networks without residual connections or normalization.

title: Sparser, Better, Deeper, Stronger: Improving Static Sparse Training with Exact Orthogonal Initialization

abstract: Cancer, a leading cause of death globally, occurs due to genomic changes and manifests heterogeneously across patients. To advance research on personalized treatment strategies, the effectiveness of various drugs on cells derived from cancers (’cell lines’) is experimentally determined in laboratory settings. Nevertheless, variations in the distribution of genomic data and drug responses between cell lines and humans arise due to biological and environmental differences. Moreover, while genomic profiles of many cancer patients are readily available, the scarcity of corresponding drug response data limits the ability to train machine learning models that can predict drug response in patients effectively. Recent cancer drug response prediction methods have largely followed the paradigm of unsupervised domain-invariant representation learning followed by a downstream drug response classification step. Introducing supervision in both stages is challenging due to heterogeneous patient response to drugs and limited drug response data. This paper addresses these challenges through a novel representation learning method in the first phase and weak supervision in the second. Experimental results on real patient data demonstrate the efficacy of our method WISER (Weak supervISion and supErvised Representation learning) over state-of-the-art alternatives on predicting personalized drug response. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/kyrs/WISER

paragraphs: Drug responses measured in laboratory cancer cell lines do not directly match responses in patients. Biological and environmental differences affect both genomic data and drug response, while patient datasets often lack the response labels needed for supervised learning. WISER addresses this combination of distribution differences and limited patient supervision.

Many existing approaches first learn representations without supervision that aim to remove differences between domains, then classify drug response. WISER instead introduces a supervised representation-learning method in the first phase and weak supervision in the second. This brings supervision into both stages despite the difficulty created by heterogeneous patient responses and scarce response data.

Experiments on real patient data show that WISER improves personalized drug-response prediction over state-of-the-art alternatives. The result supports the proposed combination of representation learning and weak supervision for the evaluated prediction task. Its significance lies in making use of limited response information while addressing the mismatch between laboratory and patient data, a central obstacle to transferring drug-response models into patient-focused research.
summary.tldr: WISER combines supervised representation learning with weak supervision to improve reported cancer drug-response prediction on real patient data.

title: WISER: Weak Supervision and Supervised Representation Learning to Improve Drug Response Prediction in Cancer

abstract: Privacy, data quality, and data sharing concerns pose a key limitation for tabular data applications. While generating synthetic data resembling the original distribution addresses some of these issues, most applications would benefit from additional customization on the generated data. However, existing synthetic data approaches are limited to particular constraints, e.g., differential privacy (DP) or fairness. In this work, we introduce CuTS, the first customizable synthetic tabular data generation framework. Customization in CuTS is achieved via declarative statistical and logical expressions, supporting a wide range of requirements (e.g., DP or fairness, among others). To ensure high synthetic data quality in the presence of custom specifications, CuTS is pre-trained on the original dataset and fine-tuned on a differentiable loss automatically derived from the provided specifications using novel relaxations. We evaluate CuTS over four datasets and on numerous custom specifications, outperforming state-of-the-art specialized approaches on several tasks while being more general. In particular, at the same fairness level, we achieve 2.3% higher downstream accuracy than the state-of-the-art in fair synthetic data generation on the Adult dataset.

paragraphs: Synthetic tables are often intended to resemble an original dataset while addressing concerns about sharing, privacy, or data quality. Applications may also require specific statistical or logical properties. CuTS offers a framework for expressing such requirements declaratively, including requirements involving differential privacy or fairness, instead of restricting customization to one specialized objective.

The generator first trains on the original data. It is then fine-tuned using a differentiable loss automatically constructed from the user’s specifications. New relaxations make those specifications usable in gradient-based training. This two-stage approach connects learning the original distribution with adapting the generated data to additional requirements.

The authors evaluate CuTS on four datasets and numerous specifications, reporting better results than specialized state-of-the-art approaches on several tasks. On the Adult dataset, they report 2.3% higher downstream accuracy at the same fairness level than the compared leading fair-data generator. The findings support the possibility of broader customization while retaining useful synthetic data quality, with improvements demonstrated in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: CuTS translates statistical and logical specifications into training losses for customizable synthetic tabular data.

title: CuTS: Customizable Tabular Synthetic Data Generation

abstract: Neural network compression has been an increasingly important subject, not only due to its practical relevance, but also due to its theoretical implications, as there is an explicit connection between compressibility and generalization error. Recent studies have shown that the choice of the hyperparameters of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can have an effect on the compressibility of the learned parameter vector. These results, however, rely on unverifiable assumptions and the resulting theory does not provide a practical guideline due to its implicitness. In this study, we propose a simple modification for SGD, such that the outputs of the algorithm will be provably compressible without making any nontrivial assumptions. We consider a one-hidden-layer neural network trained with SGD, and show that if we inject additive heavy-tailed noise to the iterates at each iteration, for any compression rate, there exists a level of overparametrization such that the output of the algorithm will be compressible with high probability. To achieve this result, we make two main technical contributions: (i) we prove a "propagation of chaos" result for a class of heavy-tailed stochastic differential equations, and (ii) we derive error estimates for their Euler discretization. Our experiments suggest that the proposed approach not only achieves increased compressibility with various models and datasets, but also leads to robust test performance under pruning, even in more realistic architectures that lie beyond our theoretical setting.

title: Implicit Compressibility of Overparametrized Neural Networks Trained with Heavy-Tailed SGD

abstract: Conditional Stochastic Optimization (CSO) is a powerful modelling paradigm for optimization under uncertainty. The existing literature on CSO is mainly based on the independence assumption of data, which shows that the solution of CSO is asymptotically consistent and enjoys a finite sample guarantee. The independence assumption, however, does not typically hold in many important applications with dependence patterns, such as time series analysis, operational control, and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap and consider a Sample Average Approximation (SAA) for CSO with dependent data. Leveraging covariance inequalities and independent block sampling technique, we provide theoretical guarantees of SAA for CSO with dependent data. In particular, we show that SAA for CSO retains asymptotic consistency and a finite sample guarantee under mild conditions. In addition, we establish the sample complexity $O(d / \varepsilon^4)$ of SAA for CSO, which is shown to be of the same order as independent cases. Through experiments on several applications, we verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that dependence does not degrade the performance of the SAA approach in real data applications.

Much of its existing theory assumes independent data, even though dependence appears in applications such as time series, operational control, and reinforcement learning. This paper studies sample average approximation for that dependent-data setting, asking whether its established statistical guarantees can be retained.

The analysis combines covariance inequalities with an independent-block sampling technique. Under conditions described as mild, the authors prove asymptotic consistency and a finite-sample guarantee. Consistency concerns the behavior as data accumulates, while the finite-sample result addresses accuracy with a limited amount of data; both extend the theoretical basis for using the approximation with dependence.

The paper also establishes sample complexity O(d/ε⁴), matching the order reported for independent-data cases. Experiments across several applications support the theory and show no performance degradation from dependence in the tested real-data settings. The implication is conditional: the analyzed dependence need not worsen the sample-complexity order, and the empirical results support practical use in the applications examined.
summary.tldr: Under mild conditions, sample average approximation retains consistency and independent-case sample-complexity order for conditional optimization with dependent data.

title: Sample Average Approximation for Conditional Stochastic Optimization with Dependent Data

abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) is a foundational framework for the estimation of solutions to statistical and machine learning problems. Characterizing the distributional properties of the minimum empirical risk (MER) provides valuable tools for conducting inference and assessing the goodness of model fit. We provide a comprehensive account of the asymptotic distribution for the order-$\sqrt{n}$ blowup of the MER under generic and abstract assumptions, and present practical conditions under which our theorems hold. Our results improve upon and relax the assumptions made in previous works. Specifically, we provide asymptotic distributions for MERs for non-independent and identically distributed data, and when the loss functions may be discontinuous or indexed by non-Euclidean spaces. We further present results that enable the application of these asymptotics for statistical inference. Specifically, the construction of consistent confidence sets using the bootstrap and consistent hypothesis tests using penalized model selection. We illustrate the utility of our approach by applying our results to neural network problems.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization selects a model by minimizing its observed loss. This paper studies the statistical behavior of the minimum loss value itself. Understanding how that value varies across data samples can support inference and judgments about model fit, adding a statistical interpretation to the output of optimization.

The authors characterize its asymptotic distribution at square-root-of-sample-size scaling under generic assumptions and provide practical conditions for applying the results. Their theory relaxes earlier requirements and covers settings beyond independent, identically distributed observations. It also accommodates potentially discontinuous losses and losses indexed by non-Euclidean spaces, broadening the range of estimation problems addressed.

The paper then connects these asymptotic results to statistical procedures. summary.tldr: The paper broadens asymptotic theory for minimum empirical risk and derives tools for confidence sets and hypothesis testing.

title: On the Asymptotic Distribution of the Minimum Empirical Risk

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the empirical counterpart of Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GDRO), which aims to minimize the maximal empirical risk across $m$ distinct groups. We formulate empirical GDRO as a two-level finite-sum convex-concave minimax optimization problem and develop an algorithm called ALEG to benefit from its special structure. ALEG is a double-looped stochastic primal-dual algorithm that incorporates variance reduction techniques into a modified mirror prox routine. To exploit the two-level finite-sum structure, we propose a simple group sampling strategy to construct the stochastic gradient with a smaller Lipschitz constant and then perform variance reduction for all groups. Theoretical analysis shows that ALEG achieves $\varepsilon$-accuracy within a computation complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{m\sqrt{\bar{n}\ln{m}}}{\varepsilon}\right)$, where $\bar n$ is the average number of samples among $m$ groups. Notably, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art method by a factor of $\sqrt{m}$. Based on ALEG, we further develop a two-stage optimization algorithm called ALEM to deal with the empirical Minimax Excess Risk Optimization (MERO) problem. The computation complexity of ALEM nearly matches that of ALEG, surpassing the rates of existing methods.

paragraphs: Group distributionally robust optimization aims to reduce the largest risk across several groups. This paper studies its empirical version, where each group’s risk is computed from available samples. The objective therefore has two levels of structure: samples within groups and competition between groups over which has the highest risk.

The authors formulate this as a convex-concave minimax problem and develop ALEG, a stochastic primal-dual algorithm with two nested loops. It combines a modified mirror-prox routine with variance reduction. A group-sampling strategy produces a stochastic gradient with a smaller Lipschitz constant, while variance reduction is applied across every group to exploit the full two-level structure.

The analysis gives ALEG a computation bound of O(m√(n̄ ln m)/ε), where m is the group count, n̄ is average group size, and ε is the target accuracy. This improves the stated best prior method by a factor of √m. A second, two-stage algorithm called ALEM extends the approach to empirical minimax excess risk optimization, nearly matching ALEG’s complexity and improving on existing rates.
summary.tldr: ALEG exploits the nested group-and-sample structure of empirical robust optimization to improve theoretical computation bounds.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Empirical Group Distributionally Robust Optimization and Beyond

abstract: Pre-trained Transformers inherently possess the characteristic of sparse activation, where only a small fraction of the neurons are activated for each token. While sparse activation has been explored through post-training methods, its potential in pre-training remains untapped. In this work, we first study how activation properties change during pre-training. Our examination reveals that Transformers exhibit sparse activation throughout the majority of the pre-training process while the activation correlation keeps evolving as training progresses. Leveraging this observation, we propose Switchable Sparse-Dense Learning (SSD). SSD adaptively switches between the Mixtures-of-Experts (MoE) based sparse training and the conventional dense training during the pre-training process, leveraging the efficiency of sparse training and avoiding the static activation correlation of sparse training. Compared to dense training, SSD achieves comparable performance with identical model size and reduces pre-training costs. Moreover, the models trained with SSD can be directly used as MoE models for sparse inference and achieve the same performance as dense models with up to $2\times$ faster inference speed. Codes are available at https://github.com/thunlp/moefication.

paragraphs: Transformers often activate only a small fraction of their neurons for a given token. This paper investigates whether that property can reduce computation during pretraining. The authors find sparse activation through most of training, but also observe that correlations among activations continue to change as learning progresses.

That combination motivates Switchable Sparse-Dense Learning, or SSD. It adaptively alternates between sparse training based on mixtures of experts and conventional dense training. Sparse phases provide computational efficiency, while dense phases address the static activation correlations associated with sparse training. The method therefore uses the observed evolution of activations to inform how computation is allocated during pretraining.

Compared with dense training at the same model size, SSD achieves comparable performance while reducing pretraining costs. Its trained models can also be used directly as mixture-of-experts models for sparse inference. The authors report the same performance as dense models with inference speedups of up to two times. The findings connect training efficiency and inference efficiency within a single pretraining approach.
summary.tldr: SSD alternates sparse and dense pretraining to reduce training costs and enable sparse inference with reported speedups of up to two times.

title: Exploring the Benefit of Activation Sparsity in Pre-training

abstract: Current challenges in developing foundational models for volumetric imaging data, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), stem from the computational complexity of state-of-the-art architectures in high dimensions and curating sufficiently large datasets of volumes. To address these challenges, we introduce Raptor (Random Planar Tensor Reduction), a train-free method for generating semantically rich embeddings for volumetric data. Raptor leverages a frozen 2D foundation model, pretrained on natural images, to extract visual tokens from individual cross-sections of medical volumes. These tokens are then spatially compressed using random projections, significantly reducing computational complexity while retaining rich semantic information. Extensive experiments on 10 diverse medical volume tasks verify the superior performance of Raptor over state-of-the-art methods, including those pretrained exclusively on medical volumes (+3% SuPreM, +6% MISFM, +10% Merlin, +13% VoCo, and +14% SLIViT), while entirely bypassing the need for costly training. Our results highlight Raptor’s effectiveness and versatility as a foundation for advancing deep learning-based methods for medical volumes (code: github.com/sriramlab/raptor).

Raptor leverages a frozen 2D foundation model, pretrained on natural images, to extract visual tokens from individual cross-sections of medical volumes. Extensive experiments on 10 diverse medical volume tasks verify the superior performance of Raptor over state-of-the-art methods, including those pretrained exclusively on medical volumes (+3% SuPreM, +6% MISFM, +10% Merlin, +13% VoCo, and +14% SLIViT), while entirely bypassing the need for costly training. Our results highlight Raptor’s effectiveness and versatility as a foundation for advancing deep learning-based methods for medical volumes (code: github.com/sriramlab/raptor).

paragraphs: Learning representations for three-dimensional medical scans is challenging because volumetric models are computationally expensive and large training collections are difficult to assemble. Raptor addresses this by generating volume embeddings without additional training. It reuses a frozen two-dimensional foundation model that was pretrained on natural images.

The method processes individual cross-sections of a medical volume to extract visual tokens. It then compresses these tokens spatially using random projections. This combination lets it draw on an existing image representation while reducing the computation needed to represent a full volume. The aim is to preserve useful semantic information through a compact representation of the cross-sectional features.

Across ten medical-volume tasks, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art methods, including models pretrained specifically on medical volumes. The abstract lists improvements ranging from 3% to 14% against the named alternatives. These findings support the usefulness of frozen natural-image features combined with random spatial compression for volumetric tasks, while avoiding the costly training otherwise needed to produce the proposed embeddings.
summary.tldr: Raptor creates medical-volume embeddings without additional training by combining frozen 2D image features with random spatial projections.

title: Raptor: Scalable Train-Free Embeddings for 3D Medical Volumes Leveraging Pretrained 2D Foundation Models

abstract: The learnware paradigm aims to establish a learnware dock system that contains numerous leanwares, each consisting of a well-trained model and a specification, enabling users to reuse high-performing models for their tasks instead of training from scratch. The specification, as a unique characterization of the model’s specialties, dominates the effectiveness of model reuse. Existing specification methods mainly employ distribution alignment to generate specifications. However, this approach overlooks the model’s discriminative performance, hindering an adequate specialty characterization. In this paper, we claim that it is beneficial to incorporate such discriminative performance for high-quality specification generation. Accordingly, a novel specification approach named Dali, i.e., Learnware Specification via Dual ALIgnment, is proposed. In Dali, the characterization of the model’s discriminative performance is modeled as discriminative alignment, which is considered along with distribution alignment in the specification generation process. Theoretical and empirical analyses clearly demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of facilitating model reuse in the learnware paradigm with high-quality specification generation.

paragraphs: A repository of trained models is useful only if users can identify which model suits their task. In the learnware paradigm, each model carries a specification describing its specialties. This paper argues that matching data distributions alone overlooks how well a model actually distinguishes the outcomes relevant to a task.

Dali generates specifications through dual alignment. Alongside distribution alignment, it includes discriminative alignment to characterize the model’s predictive behavior. The specification is therefore intended to describe both the data a model relates to and the distinctions it is capable of making, giving model reuse a richer basis than distribution similarity alone.

Theoretical and empirical analyses show that the resulting specifications improve model reuse in the learnware setting. The contribution concerns model description and selection rather than training every user’s model from scratch. The abstract does not provide numerical reuse gains or detail the access needed to measure discriminative performance, which are important implementation considerations.
summary.tldr: Dali combines distribution and discriminative alignment to describe model specialties more effectively for reuse.

title: Learnware Specification via Dual Alignment

abstract: This paper studies the long-tailed semi-supervised learning (LTSSL) with distribution mismatch, where the class distribution of the labeled training data follows a long-tailed distribution and mismatches with that of the unlabeled training data. Most existing methods introduce auxiliary classifiers (experts) to model various unlabeled data distributions and produce pseudo-labels, but the expertises of various experts are not fully utilized. We observe that different experts are good at predicting different intervals of samples, e.g., long-tailed expert is skilled in samples located in the head interval and uniform expert excels in samples located in the medium interval. Therefore, we propose a dynamic expert assignment module that can estimate the class membership (i.e., head, medium, or tail class) of samples, and dynamically assigns suitable expert to each sample based on the estimated membership to produce high-quality pseudo-label in the training phase and produce prediction in the testing phase. We also theoretically reveal that integrating different experts’ strengths will lead to a smaller generalization error bound. Moreover, we find that the deeper features are more biased toward the head class but with more discriminative ability, while the shallower features are less biased but also with less discriminative ability. We, therefore, propose a multi-depth feature fusion module to utilize different depth features to mitigate the model bias. Our method demonstrates its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments on the CIFAR-10-LT, STL-10-LT, and SVHN-LT datasets across various settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning from a small labeled collection and a larger unlabeled collection when their class frequencies differ. The labeled data has a long tail: some classes appear frequently, while others have few examples. Classifiers trained for different distributions can help label the unlabeled data, but their strengths vary across samples.

The proposed method estimates whether each sample belongs to a frequent, moderately represented, or rare class, then assigns a suitable expert. That expert supplies a pseudo-label during training and a prediction during testing. The authors also show theoretically that combining experts' strengths yields a smaller bound on generalization error, supporting the use of selective assignments.

A second component combines features from multiple network depths. Deeper features distinguish classes more effectively but favor frequent classes more strongly; shallower features show the opposite trade-off. Fusing them aims to reduce this bias while retaining useful discrimination. Experiments across different settings on CIFAR-10-LT, STL-10-LT, and SVHN-LT demonstrate the method's effectiveness under the distribution mismatch it was designed to address.
summary.tldr: Dynamic expert assignment and features from multiple depths improve learning when labeled and unlabeled class distributions differ.

title: A Square Peg in a Square Hole: Meta-Expert for Long-Tailed Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL) focuses on continual learning in non-stationary environments, requiring models to adjust to evolving domains while preserving historical knowledge. DIL faces two critical challenges in the context of imbalanced data: intra-domain class imbalance and cross-domain class distribution shifts. These challenges significantly hinder model performance, as intra-domain imbalance leads to underfitting of few-shot classes, while cross-domain shifts require maintaining well-learned many-shot classes and transferring knowledge to improve few-shot class performance in old domains. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Dual-Balance Collaborative Experts (DCE) framework. DCE employs a frequency-aware expert group, where each expert is guided by specialized loss functions to learn features for specific frequency groups, effectively addressing intra-domain class imbalance. Subsequently, a dynamic expert selector is learned by synthesizing pseudo-features through balanced Gaussian sampling from historical class statistics. This mechanism navigates the trade-off between preserving many-shot knowledge of previous domains and leveraging new data to improve few-shot class performance in earlier tasks. Extensive experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate DCE’s state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Learning across changing domains becomes harder when classes appear at very different frequencies. Within a domain, scarce classes can remain poorly learned. Across domains, the frequency pattern can change, creating a second problem: a model must retain knowledge of previously common classes while using new observations to improve classes that were previously rare.

Dual-Balance Collaborative Experts addresses these two problems through different parts of its design. A group of experts specializes in classes with particular frequency levels, using tailored training losses. A dynamic selector then determines how to use these experts. The selector learns from synthetic features produced through balanced Gaussian sampling based on historical class statistics.

These synthetic features let the selection mechanism account for earlier class distributions when learning how to combine expertise. The intended balance is between preserving strong existing knowledge and improving weak historical knowledge with newly available data. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance, supporting this combined treatment of imbalance within domains and distribution changes across them.
summary.tldr: DCE combines frequency-specialized experts with a learned selector to handle class imbalance as domains change.

title: Addressing Imbalanced Domain-Incremental Learning through Dual-Balance Collaborative Experts

abstract: Electronic health records (EHR) aggregate extensive data critical for advancing patient care and refining intervention strategies. EHR data is essential for epidemiological study, more commonly referred to as cohort study, where patients with shared characteristics or similar diseases are analyzed over time. Unfortunately, existing studies on cohort modeling are limited, struggling to derive fine-grained cohorts or effectively utilize cohort information, which hinders their ability to uncover intrinsic relationships between cohorts. To this end, we propose NeuralCohort, a cohort-aware neural representation learning method that precisely segments patients into finer-grained cohorts via an innovative cohort contextualization mechanism and captures both intra- and inter-cohort information using a Biscale Cohort Learning Module. Designed as a plug-in, NeuralCohort integrates seamlessly with existing backbone models, enhancing their cohort analysis capabilities by infusing deep cohort insights into the representation learning processes. The effectiveness and generalizability of NeuralCohort are validated across extensive real-world EHR datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that NeuralCohort consistently improves the performance of various backbone models, achieving up to an 8.1% increase in AUROC.

paragraphs: Electronic health records support cohort studies, where patients sharing characteristics or diseases are examined over time. This paper argues that existing approaches struggle to form sufficiently detailed cohorts and to make effective use of the cohort information they contain.

NeuralCohort introduces a contextualization mechanism that divides patients into finer-grained cohorts. Its Biscale Cohort Learning Module then captures information at two levels: relationships among patients within a cohort and relationships across cohorts. These signals become part of the learned patient representations. The method is designed as a plug-in, allowing existing backbone models to incorporate cohort structure into their learning process.

Evaluations on real-world health-record datasets show consistent improvements across various backbone models, with a reported AUROC increase of up to 8.1%. That upper-end result describes predictive performance in the experiments. The broader finding is that explicitly modeling cohort context can improve existing representations rather than requiring a completely new backbone.
summary.tldr: NeuralCohort adds fine-grained patient grouping and within- and across-cohort learning to existing health-record models, improving their reported predictive performance.

title: NeuralCohort: Cohort-aware Neural Representation Learning for Healthcare Analytics

abstract: For the fundamental linear programming (LP) problems, the simplex method remains popular, which usually requires an appropriate initial basis as a warm start to accelerate the solving process. Predicting an initial basis close to an optimal one can often accelerate the solver, but a closer initial basis does not always result in greater acceleration. To achieve better acceleration, we propose a GNN model based on a tripartite graph representation inspired by LP duality. This approach enables more effective feature extraction for general LP problems and enhances the expressiveness of GNNs. Additionally, we introduce novel loss functions targeting basic variable selection and basis feasibility, along with data preprocessing schemes, to further improve learning capability. In addition to achieving high prediction accuracy, we enhance the quality of the initial basis for practical use. Experimental results show that our approach greatly surpasses the state-of-the-art method in predicting initial basis with greater accuracy and in reducing the number of iterations and solving time of the LP solver.

paragraphs: The simplex method solves linear programs by working from an initial basis, so choosing a useful starting basis can accelerate the solver. This paper emphasizes that resemblance to an optimal basis is not enough: a more accurate prediction does not always produce a larger speedup. The learning task therefore needs to address the practical quality of the starting point.

The authors propose a graph neural network using a three-part graph representation inspired by linear-programming duality. This representation is designed to improve feature extraction for general linear programs and make the network more expressive. They also introduce loss functions for selecting basic variables and encouraging basis feasibility, together with data preprocessing schemes.

These components aim to make predicted bases useful to the solver as well as accurate as predictions. Experiments report substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art method in basis-prediction accuracy, simplex iteration count, and solving time. The findings support evaluating learned warm starts through their downstream optimization benefits, with supervision that explicitly accounts for feasibility.
summary.tldr: A duality-inspired graph network learns feasible, useful simplex starting bases, improving prediction accuracy and reducing solver iterations and runtime.

title: Learning Initial Basis Selection for Linear Programming via Duality-Inspired Tripartite Graph Representation and Comprehensive Supervision

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) and transformers dominate the language modeling landscape. However, they are constrained to a lower computational complexity than classical recurrent neural networks (RNNs), limiting their expressivity. In contrast, RNNs lack parallelization during training, raising fundamental questions about the trade off between parallelization and expressivity. We propose implicit SSMs, which iterate a transformation until convergence to a fixed point. Theoretically, we show that implicit SSMs implement the non-linear state-transitions of RNNs. Empirically, we find that only approximate fixed-point convergence suffices, enabling the design of a scalable training curriculum that largely retains parallelization, with full convergence required only for a small subset of tokens. Our approach demonstrates superior state-tracking capabilities on regular languages, surpassing transformers and SSMs. We further scale implicit SSMs to natural language reasoning tasks and pretraining of large-scale language models up to 1.3B parameters on 207B tokens - representing, to our knowledge, the largest implicit model trained to date. Notably, our implicit models outperform their explicit counterparts on standard benchmarks. Our code is publicly available at github.com/microsoft/implicit_languagemodels

paragraphs: Language modeling faces a tradeoff between training parallelism and computational expressivity. Classical recurrent neural networks support nonlinear state updates but are difficult to train in parallel. This paper proposes implicit state-space models that repeatedly apply a transformation until it reaches a fixed point, connecting a more parallelizable architecture to recurrent computation.

The theoretical analysis shows that these implicit models implement the nonlinear state transitions of recurrent networks. Empirically, approximate convergence is sufficient for much of the computation. This observation supports a scalable training curriculum that largely preserves parallelization, with full convergence needed only for a small subset of tokens in the reported approach.

The models outperform transformers and conventional state-space models on regular-language state tracking. The authors also extend them to natural-language reasoning and pretraining, reaching 1.3 billion parameters trained on 207 billion tokens. Implicit models outperform their explicit counterparts on standard benchmarks. These results suggest that iterative computation can recover useful recurrent capabilities while retaining substantial training parallelism.
summary.tldr: Implicit state-space models recover nonlinear recurrent computation while largely retaining parallel training and improving reported benchmark performance.

title: Implicit Language Models are RNNs: Balancing Parallelization and Expressivity

abstract: Compositional understanding is crucial for human intelligence, yet it remains unclear whether contemporary vision models exhibit it. The dominant machine learning paradigm is built on the premise that scaling data and model sizes will improve out-of-distribution performance, including compositional generalization. We test this premise through controlled experiments that systematically vary data scale, concept diversity, and combination coverage. We find that compositional generalization is driven by data diversity, not mere data scale. Increased combinatorial coverage forces models to discover a linearly factored representational structure, where concepts decompose into additive components. We prove this structure is key to efficiency, enabling perfect generalization from few observed combinations. Evaluating pretrained models (DINO, CLIP), we find above-random yet imperfect performance, suggesting partial presence of this structure. Our work motivates stronger emphasis on constructing diverse datasets for compositional generalization, and considering the importance of representational structure that enables efficient compositional learning.

paragraphs: The paper asks what helps vision models understand combinations of concepts beyond those seen during training. It tests the premise that simply increasing data and model scale improves this compositional generalization. Controlled experiments vary the amount of data, the diversity of concepts, and the coverage of combinations, separating factors that can otherwise change together.

The findings identify diversity as the driver of compositional generalization in these experiments. Greater coverage of combinations pushes models toward representations in which concepts have separate additive components. The authors prove that this linearly factored structure enables efficient learning, allowing perfect generalization from only a few observed combinations within their theoretical account.

Tests of pretrained DINO and CLIP models show performance above chance but short of perfect. The authors interpret this as suggesting that the useful representational structure is only partially present. The work therefore motivates attention to which concepts and combinations a dataset contains, and to whether models organize those concepts in a form that supports recombination.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments link visual compositional generalization to diverse concept combinations and additive representations, rather than data volume alone.

title: Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization?

abstract: Recent advances in geometric deep learning and generative modeling have enabled the design of novel proteins with a wide range of desired properties. However, current state-of-the-art approaches are typically restricted to generating proteins with only static target properties, such as motifs and symmetries. In this work, we take a step towards overcoming this limitation by proposing a framework to condition structure generation on flexibility, which is crucial for key functionalities such as catalysis or molecular recognition. We first introduce BackFlip, an equivariant neural network for predicting per-residue flexibility from an input backbone structure. Relying on BackFlip, we propose FliPS, an SE(3)-equivariant conditional flow matching model that solves the inverse problem, that is, generating backbones that display a target flexibility profile. In our experiments, we show that FliPS is able to generate novel and diverse protein backbones with the desired flexibility, verified by Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations. FliPS and BackFlip are available at https://github.com/graeter-group/flips.

paragraphs: Protein design often specifies static structural properties, such as a motif or symmetry. This paper instead targets flexibility: how different parts of a protein can move. Because flexibility matters for activities including catalysis and molecular recognition, conditioning on it adds a dynamic property to the design objective.

The framework has two connected models. BackFlip predicts flexibility at each residue from a protein backbone. FliPS then uses BackFlip to tackle the inverse task, generating a backbone for a requested flexibility profile. FliPS is a conditional flow-matching model with SE(3) equivariance, preserving the appropriate behavior under rotations and translations.

In the reported experiments, FliPS generates novel and diverse backbones with the desired flexibility, which the authors verify using molecular dynamics simulations. This supports the feasibility of directing structure generation through a movement-related target. The demonstrated result concerns backbone flexibility; the motivation from protein function explains why that control is useful without equating a matching flexibility profile with demonstrated catalytic or recognition performance.
summary.tldr: BackFlip and FliPS connect flexibility prediction with protein-backbone generation, producing target flexibility profiles verified through molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Flexibility-conditioned protein structure design with flow matching

abstract: Since the introduction of Vision Transformer (ViT), patchification has long been regarded as a common image pre-processing approach for plain visual architectures. By compressing the spatial size of images, this approach can effectively shorten the token sequence and reduce the computational cost of ViT-like plain architectures. In this work, we aim to thoroughly examine the information loss caused by this patchification-based compressive encoding paradigm and how it affects visual understanding. We conduct extensive patch size scaling experiments and excitedly observe an intriguing scaling law in patchification: the models can consistently benefit from decreased patch sizes and attain improved predictive performance, until it reaches the minimum patch size of 1*1, i.e., pixel tokenization. This conclusion is broadly applicable across different vision tasks, various input scales, and diverse architectures such as ViT and the recent Mamba models. Moreover, as a by-product, we discover that with smaller patches, task-specific decoder heads become less critical for dense prediction. In the experiments, we successfully scale up the visual sequence to an exceptional length of 50,176 tokens, achieving a competitive test accuracy of 84.6% with a base-sized model on the ImageNet-1k benchmark. We hope this study can provide insights and theoretical foundations for future works of building non-compressive vision models.

paragraphs: Vision models often divide images into patches to shorten the sequence they must process. This reduces computation, but the paper investigates the information lost through that compression. The researchers systematically decrease patch size to examine whether preserving finer spatial detail improves visual understanding, continuing down to treating each individual pixel as a token.

Across their experiments, smaller patches consistently improve predictive performance, including at the smallest possible patch size. The observed pattern spans different vision tasks, image scales, and architectures, including Vision Transformers and Mamba models. Its main implication is that patch size deserves attention as a consequential modeling choice: the computational savings of compression can come with lost predictive information. The reported scaling behavior provides empirical motivation for developing vision models that preserve more of the image.
summary.tldr: Smaller image patches consistently improve performance in the reported experiments, with benefits extending to one token per pixel.

title: Scaling Laws in Patchification: An Image Is Worth 50,176 Tokens And More

abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model’s activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

paragraphs: Understanding why language models refuse requests requires examining how refusal is represented internally. Earlier work suggested that a single direction in activation space determines this behavior. This paper develops a gradient-based representation-engineering approach and uses it to investigate whether refusal instead involves a richer collection of internal structures.

The authors identify multiple independent refusal directions as well as multidimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. They also show that orthogonality, meaning directions are geometrically perpendicular, does not establish independence when those directions are manipulated. This distinction matters because a geometric relationship between representations does not fully describe how interventions affect the model’s behavior.

To address that gap, the paper introduces representational independence, accounting for both linear and nonlinear effects. Using this framework, it identifies mechanistically independent refusal directions and concludes that multiple distinct mechanisms contribute to refusal in the studied models. The contribution is therefore both a more complex account of refusal geometry and a method for examining functional independence, with potential use in further research on language-model internals.
summary.tldr: Refusal involves multiple independent directions and concept cones, and geometric orthogonality alone does not establish independence under intervention.

title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence

abstract: Conditional mean independence (CMI) testing is crucial for statistical tasks including model determination and variable importance evaluation. In this work, we introduce a novel population CMI measure and a bootstrap-based testing procedure that utilizes deep generative neural networks to estimate the conditional mean functions involved in the population measure. The test statistic is thoughtfully constructed to ensure that even slowly decaying nonparametric estimation errors do not affect the asymptotic accuracy of the test. Our approach demonstrates strong empirical performance in scenarios with high-dimensional covariates and response variable, can handle multivariate responses, and maintains nontrivial power against local alternatives outside an $n^{-1/2}$ neighborhood of the null hypothesis. We also use numerical simulations and real-world imaging data applications to highlight the efficacy and versatility of our testing procedure.

paragraphs: Conditional mean independence testing asks whether a variable adds information about a response’s mean after accounting for other variables. This question matters for choosing models and evaluating variable importance. The paper introduces a population-level measure of conditional mean independence and a corresponding statistical testing procedure built around that measure.

Deep generative neural networks estimate the conditional mean functions needed by the measure, and a bootstrap procedure supports the test. A central design choice is the test statistic: it is constructed so that even slowly decreasing nonparametric estimation errors do not undermine asymptotic accuracy. This addresses the interaction between learning the necessary functions and making a valid statistical decision.

The method handles multivariate responses and shows strong empirical performance with high-dimensional covariates and responses. It also retains nontrivial power against local alternatives outside an n^(-1/2) neighborhood of the null hypothesis. Simulations and real-world imaging applications demonstrate its effectiveness, complementing the theoretical treatment of estimation error and sensitivity to departures from the null.
summary.tldr: This conditional mean independence test uses generative networks and a statistic designed to preserve asymptotic accuracy despite slowly decaying estimation errors.

title: Testing Conditional Mean Independence Using Generative Neural Networks

abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a popular weakly-supervised method for various applications, with a particular interest in histological whole slide image (WSI) classification. Due to the gigapixel resolution of WSI, applications of MIL in WSI typically necessitate a two-stage training scheme: first, extract features from the pre-trained backbone and then perform MIL aggregation. However, it is well-known that this suboptimal training scheme suffers from "noisy" feature embeddings from the backbone and inherent weak supervision, hindering MIL from learning rich and generalizable features. However, the most commonly used technique (i.e., dropout) for mitigating this issue has yet to be explored in MIL. In this paper, we empirically explore how effective the dropout can be in MIL. Interestingly, we observe that dropping the top-k most important instances within a bag leads to better performance and generalization even under noise attack. Based on this key observation, we propose a novel MIL-specific dropout method, termed MIL-Dropout, which systematically determines which instances to drop. Experiments on five MIL benchmark datasets and two WSI datasets demonstrate that MIL-Dropout boosts the performance of current MIL methods with a negligible computational cost. The code is available at https://github.com/ChongQingNoSubway/MILDropout.

The paper identifies noisy backbone features and weak supervision as obstacles to learning representations that generalize well.

The authors empirically investigate dropout in this setting. Their central observation is that removing the top-k most important instances from a bag can improve performance and generalization, including under a noise attack. This motivates MIL-Dropout, a method designed specifically for multiple instance learning that systematically chooses which instances to discard.

The findings indicate that the selection of dropped instances matters: deliberately removing highly influential instances can be useful during training. The paper turns that empirical observation into a targeted dropout procedure for the aggregation stage.
summary.tldr: MIL-Dropout improves multiple instance learning by systematically dropping influential instances, with negligible computational cost.

title: How Effective Can Dropout Be in Multiple Instance Learning ?

abstract: It has become increasingly challenging to understand and evaluate LLM capabilities as these models exhibit a broader range of behaviors. In this position paper, we argue that LLM researchers should draw on the lessons from another field which has developed a rich set of experimental paradigms and design practices for probing the behavior of complex intelligent systems: animal cognition. We present five core principles of evaluation drawn from animal cognition research, and explain how they provide invaluable guidance for understanding LLM capabilities and behavior. We ground these principles in an empirical case study, and show how they can already provide a richer picture of one particular reasoning capability: transitive inference.

This position paper argues that researchers can learn from animal cognition, a field with extensive experience designing experiments to investigate complex intelligent behavior. The proposed connection is methodological: borrow useful experimental principles for studying systems whose capabilities must be inferred from behavior.

The authors present five evaluation principles drawn from animal cognition research and explain how they can guide language model studies. They ground the proposal in an empirical case study of transitive inference, a particular reasoning capability. This gives the argument a concrete application rather than leaving it solely as a recommendation to consult another discipline.

The case study shows that these principles can yield a richer picture of transitive inference in language models. The stated finding concerns that capability, while the paper’s broader position advocates using the principles more widely. Its contribution is an approach to experimental design that aims to make capability claims more informative by learning from an established science of intelligent behavior.
summary.tldr: Five principles from animal cognition research offer guidance for LLM evaluation, illustrated through an empirical study of transitive inference.

title: Position: Principles of Animal Cognition to Improve LLM Evaluations

abstract: Offline decision-making via diffusion models often produces trajectories that are misaligned with system dynamics, limiting their reliability for control. We propose Model Predictive Diffuser (MPDiffuser), a compositional diffusion framework that combines a diffusion planner with a dynamics diffusion model to generate task-aligned and dynamically plausible trajectories. MPDiffuser interleaves planner and dynamics updates during sampling, progressively correcting feasibility while preserving task intent. A lightweight ranking module then selects trajectories that best satisfy task objectives. The compositional design improves sample efficiency and adaptability by enabling the dynamics model to leverage diverse and previously unseen data independently of the planner. Empirically, we demonstrate consistent improvements over prior diffusion-based methods on unconstrained (D4RL) and constrained (DSRL) benchmarks, and validate practicality through deployment on a real quadrupedal robot.
