paragraphs: A generated action trajectory can look useful for a task yet conflict with how the controlled system actually moves. This mismatch limits diffusion-based planning from offline data. Model Predictive Diffuser, or MPDiffuser, addresses it by combining a diffusion planner with a separate diffusion model of system dynamics during trajectory generation.

Sampling alternates between planner updates and dynamics updates. The planner contributes task intent, while the dynamics model progressively corrects feasibility. A lightweight ranking module then selects trajectories that best meet task objectives. The architecture also lets the dynamics component learn from diverse and previously unseen data independently of the planner, which the authors identify as a source of improved sample efficiency and adaptability.

Experiments report consistent improvements over earlier diffusion-based methods on both unconstrained D4RL tasks and constrained DSRL tasks. Deployment on a real quadrupedal robot provides an additional practical demonstration. The central contribution is to incorporate dynamics correction throughout sampling, producing trajectories that better combine task alignment with dynamic plausibility in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MPDiffuser interleaves task planning with learned dynamics corrections to improve diffusion-generated control trajectories on benchmarks and a quadrupedal robot.

title: Model-Based Diffusion Sampling for Predictive Control in Offline Decision Making

abstract: The evaluation of large language models relies heavily on standardized benchmarks. These benchmarks provide useful aggregated metrics, but can obscure (i) particular sub-areas where the models are weak ("model gaps") and (ii) imbalanced coverage in the benchmarks themselves ("benchmark gaps"). To automatically uncover both types of gaps, we propose a simple new method using concept activations from sparse autoencoders, to identify fine-grained gaps on a per-concept basis. The method also benefits from grounding evaluation in the model’s internal representations, as well as easy comparison across benchmarks. We applied the method to five popular open-source models and more than a dozen benchmarks, as illustrative examples. As validation of the approach, we found that our automatic, unsupervised method was able to recover model gaps that have been previously documented in the literature (e.g. relating to sycophancy), in addition to identifying novel model gaps. We were also able to automatically uncover benchmark gaps: core concepts that should fall within the scope of a given benchmark. Our "competency gaps" method can be used to complement existing benchmarks, by providing a concept-level decomposition of model behavior, and by helping benchmark developers iterate upon benchmark design. Code is available at https://competency-gaps.github.io.

This paper develops an automatic method to expose both kinds of gap. It uses concept activations from sparse autoencoders to break evaluation into finer-grained, concept-level assessments.

It additionally uncovers missing coverage of concepts that belong within benchmark scope. The contribution is a complement to established evaluations: concept-level decomposition helps explain what aggregate scores conceal and gives benchmark developers information they can use when revising coverage.
summary.tldr: Sparse-autoencoder concept activations reveal model weaknesses and benchmark coverage gaps hidden by aggregate evaluation scores.

title: Uncovering Competency Gaps in Large Language Models and Their Benchmarks

abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) demonstrate impressive in-context learning abilities from few multimodal demonstrations, yet the internal mechanisms supporting such task learning remain opaque. Building on prior work of Large Language Models, we show that a small subset of attention heads in Large Multimodal Models is responsible for transmitting representations of visual relations. The activations of these attention heads, termed $\textit{function vectors}$, can be extracted and manipulated to alter an LMM’s performance on relational tasks. First, using synthetic and real image datasets, we apply causal mediation analysis to identify attention heads that strongly influence relational predictions, and extract multimodal function vectors that improve zero-shot accuracy at inference time. We further demonstrate that these multimodal function vectors can be fine-tuned with a modest amount of training data, while keeping LMM parameters frozen, to significantly outperform in-context learning baselines. Finally, we show that relation-specific function vectors can be linearly combined to solve analogy problems involving novel and untrained visual relations, highlighting the strong generalization ability of this approach. Through experiments on two LMMs, including OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL, our results show that these models encode visual relational knowledge within localized internal structures, which can be systematically extracted and optimized, thereby advancing our understanding of model modularity and enhancing control over relational reasoning in LMMs.

title: Multimodal Function Vectors for Visual Relations

abstract: Multiview subspace clustering (MvSC) has shown remarkable potential in exploring underlying structures of high-dimensional data. However, existing MvSC methods still suffer from two shortcomings: (1) the commonly use of convex low-rank approximations inadequately capture high-order correlations across views, while sensitivity to noise and outliers degrades clustering performance, and (2) they lack the ability to preserve global correlations and local geometric patterns simultaneously. To address these issues, we propose a novel nonconvex regularized MvSC model with deep prior, which not only accurately characterizes the intrinsic low-rank structure and suppresses the effect of outliers, but also preserves local structural properties through deep networks. By mathematically analyzing the optimal solution of the optimization problem in our proposed model, we develop an efficient ADMM-based algorithm with provable convergence guarantees to solve it. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model. MATLAB code is available at https://github.com/wangzhi-swu/NRDN-MvSC.

paragraphs: Multiview subspace clustering seeks underlying groups in high-dimensional data described through multiple views. The paper identifies two difficulties in existing approaches: conventional convex low-rank approximations can miss higher-order relationships across views, and methods struggle to retain global correlations together with local geometric patterns. Noise and outliers further weaken clustering.

The proposed model combines nonconvex low-rank regularization with a deep prior. The low-rank component is designed to characterize shared underlying structure and suppress outlier effects, while deep networks preserve local structural properties. Combining them gives the model separate mechanisms for capturing broad cross-view relationships and finer patterns within the data.

The authors analyze the optimization problem’s optimal solution and derive an efficient algorithm based on ADMM, with provable convergence guarantees. Experiments across multiple datasets report superior clustering performance. The contribution therefore includes both a richer representation objective and a supported procedure for solving it. The empirical results back the proposed combination of global low-rank structure, outlier handling, and learned local information.
summary.tldr: The method combines nonconvex low-rank modeling and deep priors to improve multiview clustering while preserving global and local structure.

title: Nonconvex Low-Rank Tensor Representation with Deep Priors for Multiview Subspace Clustering

abstract: Machine learning–based surrogate models have emerged as more efficient alternatives to numerical solvers for physical simulations over complex geometries, such as car bodies. Many existing models incorporate the simulation mesh as an additional input, thereby reducing prediction errors. However, generating a simulation mesh for new geometries is computationally costly. In contrast, mesh-free methods, which do not rely on the simulation mesh, typically incur higher errors. Motivated by these considerations, we introduce SMART, a neural surrogate model that predicts physical quantities at arbitrary query locations using only a point-cloud representation of the geometry, without requiring access to the simulation mesh. The geometry and simulation parameters are encoded into a shared latent space that captures both structural and parametric characteristics of the physical field. A physics decoder then attends to the encoder’s intermediate latent representations to map spatial queries to physical quantities. Through this cross-layer interaction, the model jointly updates latent geometric features and the evolving physical field. Extensive experiments show that SMART is competitive with and often outperforms existing methods that rely on the simulation mesh as input, demonstrating its capabilities for industry-level simulations.

paragraphs: Learning-based physical simulation often benefits from a simulation mesh, but constructing that mesh for a new geometry is costly. Methods that avoid meshes typically pay for the convenience with higher prediction errors. SMART addresses this tradeoff by predicting physical quantities at arbitrary query locations from a point-cloud representation of the geometry and simulation parameters.

Its physics decoder attends to intermediate representations from the encoder to answer spatial queries. This cross-layer interaction jointly updates the geometric features and the evolving representation of the physical field.

Experiments show that SMART is competitive with, and often better than, existing methods that receive the simulation mesh as input. The results demonstrate that avoiding a mesh need not entail the accuracy penalty seen in earlier mesh-free approaches in the evaluated settings. Its contribution is a way to combine raw geometric input with query-based physical prediction for industry-level simulations.
summary.tldr: SMART predicts physical fields from point-cloud geometry without a simulation mesh, often outperforming mesh-dependent methods in experiments.

title: SMART: Scalable Mesh-free Aerodynamic Simulations from Raw Geometries using a Transformer-based Surrogate Model

abstract: For many real-world systems, causal ground truth is difficult to obtain, making claims about causal effects hard to assess. We develop methods for evaluating collections of bivariate causal statements, one for each pair of variables in a fixed system. In the setting of acyclic linear statements, any such collection can be extended to a unique multivariate causal model, but we argue that this induced model is implausible if it imposes substantial additional confounding to explain observed correlations. We introduce a compatibility score that quantifies this notion of plausibility, notably without relying on the faithfulness assumption. Additionally, we define an incompatibility score for purely graphical bivariate causal statements, based on global consistency constraints that are derived from acyclicity and faithfulness assumptions. We give theoretical and empirical evidence that both scores can successfully distinguish correct from incorrect causal statements in generic settings. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our methods by analyzing causal claims made by large language models. Our work aims to provide a foundation for assessing the reliability of causal information derived from human experts or artificial intelligence in settings where alternative forms of validation are unavailable.

paragraphs: Causal claims are difficult to validate when the true causal system is unknown. This paper examines whether a collection of claims about pairs of variables makes sense when considered together. The central idea is to assess mutual compatibility across a fixed system, using constraints that individual pairwise statements may conceal.

For acyclic linear statements, the authors show that a collection extends to a unique multivariate causal model. They assess that model’s plausibility by asking how much additional confounding it must introduce to explain observed correlations. Their compatibility score measures this issue without requiring the faithfulness assumption. A separate score handles purely graphical statements using global consistency constraints that do depend on acyclicity and faithfulness.

Theoretical and empirical evidence indicates that both scores can distinguish correct from incorrect statements in generic settings. The authors also apply the methods to causal claims produced by language models. These scores provide a way to assess reliability when other validation is unavailable, with different assumptions supporting the linear and graphical versions rather than one assumption-free test of causal truth.
summary.tldr: Compatibility scores assess collections of pairwise causal claims by checking their joint plausibility and global consistency.

title: Evaluating Bivariate Causal Statements Based on Mutual Compatibility

abstract: Graph-based attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) detection methods have been extensively studied, but comparatively less attention has been paid to short-term brain functional reorganization. In this paper, we propose an ADHD disease detection model based on short- and long-term brain function encoding and memory graph network. We first exploit a novel brain map sequence construction method based on short-term windows to extract short-term brain function features. Then, we design a short-term state and temporal dependency encoder to characterize short-term sequence patterns of brain function. Furthermore, a brain function memory is introduced to capture the association of brain activity patterns and historical sequence patterns. Concurrently, GNN-based long-term brain function feature extraction network is used to extract brain structure features, which are fused with short-term features for ADHD detection. Experimental validation on the publicly available neuroimaging datasets ADHD-200 and OpenNeuro-ds002424 demonstrates the superior performance of our model in brain disorder detection.

paragraphs: This paper develops an ADHD detection model that combines brief changes in brain function with longer-term brain features. Its motivation is that existing graph-based approaches have given comparatively little attention to short-term functional reorganization. The proposed model therefore treats the sequence of changing brain activity patterns as useful information alongside the broader structure captured by a graph network.

The method first constructs a sequence of brain maps from short time windows. An encoder then represents both the state within those windows and the dependencies between them. A memory component connects current brain activity patterns with historical sequence patterns, giving the model a way to incorporate recurring temporal information. Separately, a graph neural network extracts longer-term features, which are combined with the short-term representation for detection.

Experiments on ADHD-200 and OpenNeuro-ds002424 report superior detection performance. These findings support the usefulness of combining information across timescales in the evaluated neuroimaging datasets, with memory providing an additional connection between present activity and earlier patterns.
summary.tldr: The model combines short-term brain activity sequences, historical memory, and longer-term graph features to improve ADHD detection on two neuroimaging datasets.

title: ADHD Disease Detection Based on Short- and Long-Term Brain Function Encoding and Memory Graph Network

abstract: The ability to adapt to physical actions and constraints in an environment is crucial for embodied agents (e.g., robots) to effectively collaborate with humans. Such physically grounded human-AI collaboration must account for the increased complexity of the continuous state-action space and constrained dynamics caused by physical constraints. However, most existing collaboration benchmarks are discrete or do not consider physical attributes and constraints. To address this, we introduce Moving Out, a human-AI collaboration benchmark that resembles a wide range of collaboration modes affected by physical attributes and constraints, such as moving heavy items together and coordinating actions to move an item around a corner. Moving Out consists of two challenges and human-human interaction data to comprehensively evaluate models’ abilities to adapt to diverse human behaviors and unseen physical attributes. To give embodied agents the capability to collaborate with humans under physical attributes and constraints, we propose a novel method, BASS (Behavior Augmentation, Simulation, and Selection), to enhance the diversity of agents and their understanding of the outcome of actions. We systematically compare BASS and state-of-the-art models in AI-AI and human-AI experiments, showing that BASS can effectively collaborate with both unseen AI and humans.

paragraphs: Collaborating on a physical task requires adapting to both a partner’s behavior and the environment’s constraints. Moving a heavy object together or guiding it around a corner involves continuous actions and physically restricted motion. Moving Out introduces a benchmark designed to test this kind of human–AI coordination.

The benchmark contains two challenges and human–human interaction data. Its evaluation targets adaptation to diverse human behaviors and previously unseen physical attributes. This addresses a gap in collaboration benchmarks that use discrete interactions or omit physical properties, where successful coordination may not require the same sensitivity to motion and constraints.

The authors also introduce BASS, short for Behavior Augmentation, Simulation, and Selection. The method aims to increase agent diversity and improve understanding of action outcomes, both of which matter when a partner’s behavior is unfamiliar. The reported results show that BASS can collaborate effectively with unseen AI partners and humans, supporting evaluation and method development that explicitly account for the physical setting.
summary.tldr: Moving Out benchmarks collaboration under physical constraints, and BASS demonstrates effective coordination with unfamiliar AI and human partners.

title: Moving Out: Physically-grounded Human-AI Collaboration

abstract: We investigate which architectural and input-pipeline choices make vision models more robust to additive Gaussian noise and convert these empirical insights into simple, actionable design rules. Specifically, we performed extensive evaluations on 1,174 pretrained vision models, empirically identifying four consistent factors for improved robustness against Gaussian noise: larger stem kernels, resolution-dependent downsampling under a pre-resize sensor-noise protocol, average pooling, and supervised vision transformers (ViTs) rather than CLIP ViTs, which yield up to 506 rank improvements and 21.6%p accuracy gains. First, we prove that low-pass stem kernels attenuate noise with a gain that decreases quadratically with kernel size and that anti-aliased downsampling reduces noise energy roughly in proportion to the square of the downsampling factor. Second, we demonstrate that average pooling is unbiased and suppresses noise in proportion to the pooling window area, whereas max pooling incurs a positive bias that grows slowly with window size and yields a relatively higher mean-squared error and greater worst-case sensitivity. Third, we reveal and explain the vulnerability of CLIP ViTs via a pixel-space Lipschitz bound: The smaller normalization standard deviations used in CLIP preprocessing amplify worst-case sensitivity by up to 1.91 times relative to the Inception-style preprocessing common in supervised ViTs. Our results collectively disentangle robustness into interpretable modules, provide a theory that explains the observed trends, and build practical, plug-and-play guidelines for designing vision models more robust against Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: This paper examines which vision-model design choices improve resistance to additive Gaussian noise. Evaluating 1,174 pretrained models, the authors identify four recurring factors: larger initial convolution kernels, resolution-dependent downsampling under a protocol that adds sensor noise before resizing, average pooling, and supervised vision transformers compared with CLIP vision transformers.

The theoretical analysis explains several of these trends. Low-pass initial kernels attenuate noise, with noise gain decreasing quadratically with kernel size. Anti-aliased downsampling reduces noise energy roughly according to the square of its factor. Average pooling is unbiased and suppresses noise with pooling area, whereas max pooling introduces a positive bias and has greater error and worst-case sensitivity in the analysis.

The authors also connect CLIP preprocessing to increased sensitivity: smaller normalization standard deviations amplify a pixel-space worst-case bound by up to 1.91 times relative to the compared preprocessing. Reported empirical gains reach 506 ranking positions and 21.6 percentage points of accuracy. The findings yield concrete guidance for Gaussian-noise robustness while preserving the relevance of the specific noise and resizing protocol.
summary.tldr: A large empirical study and theoretical analysis identify architecture and preprocessing choices that improve vision-model robustness to Gaussian noise.

title: Unlocking Noise-Resistant Vision: Key Architectural Secrets for Robust Models Against Gaussian Noise

abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is widely adopted to quantize language models by training full-precision weights using gradients from the quantized model. The main bottleneck is its slow convergence and early performance plateau, particularly below 4-bit-widths. While this problem has been observed in prior work, its precise cause remains unclear. In this paper, we analyze the convergence of QAT by estimating the spectrum of the loss-surface Hessians. We find that the weights converge to flat regions around saddle points, where a large fraction of the Hessian eigenvalues are both positive and negative. During training, an increasing fraction of Hessian eigenvalues concentrates around zero, whose magnitude decreases. At lower bit-widths, the magnitude of eigenvalues in the Hessian spectrum is significantly smaller. To mitigate these issues, we propose an algorithm called WinQ to accelerate QAT, which involves: (1) periodically resetting weights to the linear interpolation of full-precision and quantized weights, reducing the distance to the quantization grid and increasing eigenvalue magnitude, and (2) computing gradients of noise-injected weights to regularize the Hessian. Extensive experiments show that WinQ accelerates QAT by up to 4$\times$ across various quantization methods and models. Under the same training cost, WinQ improves state-of-the-art sub-4-bit quantization by up to 8.8%. These results are consistent across 16 settings with different language models, quantization methods, and bit widths.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training updates full-precision weights using gradients from a quantized model, but convergence can be slow, especially below four bits. This paper investigates the loss surface through Hessian spectra. It finds training settles into flat regions around saddle points, with increasingly many eigenvalues near zero and smaller eigenvalue magnitudes at lower bit widths.

WinQ responds with two modifications. It periodically moves weights to a linear interpolation between their full-precision and quantized values, reducing their distance from the quantization grid and increasing eigenvalue magnitudes. It also computes gradients using noise-injected weights to regularize the Hessian. Both changes target the geometry associated with slow progress.

Across different models and quantization methods, WinQ accelerates training by up to four times. At the same training cost, it improves state-of-the-art sub-four-bit quantization performance by up to 8.8%. Results are consistent across 16 settings. These findings support intervening in the local loss geometry as a way to improve both convergence speed and the performance attainable within a fixed training budget.
summary.tldr: WinQ accelerates quantization-aware training by periodically interpolating weights toward quantized values and computing gradients with injected noise.

title: WinQ: Accelerating Quantization-Aware Training of Language Models Around Saddle Points

abstract: Relational Deep Learning aims to learn directly on multi-table databases, yet current methods face a fundamental tension: Transformers’ quadratic complexity prohibits the large contexts relational data demands, while GNNs sacrifice global context for efficiency. We introduce Ramba, the first selective state-space model for relational databases. Our approach features two innovations: (1) Topology-Aware Linearization, which processes cells via global columnar serialization in O(L) complexity while recovering relational structure through sparse entity and foreign-key attention masks; and (2) Schema Dynamic Gating, which modulates SSM state transitions based on semantic alignment between the currently scanned attribute and the prediction target, enabling cross-table relevance filtering without relying on value distributions. Together, these enable Ramba to ingest vast relational contexts while selectively retaining semantically relevant information, a combination existing architectures cannot achieve. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance with linear scalability across diverse relational benchmarks.

paragraphs: Ramba is a selective state-space model designed to learn directly from databases containing multiple related tables. The paper targets a tension between large-context access and efficiency: Transformer costs grow quadratically, while graph neural networks give up global context to remain efficient. Ramba aims to process broad relational context while retaining relevant information selectively.

Topology-Aware Linearization arranges cells into a global column-based sequence with linear processing complexity. Sparse attention masks for entities and foreign keys recover relational structure within that sequence. Schema Dynamic Gating then adjusts state transitions according to the semantic relationship between the attribute currently being read and the prediction target. This filters relevance across tables using schema meaning rather than relying on value distributions.

Experiments across relational benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with linear scalability. The architectural contribution joins an efficient sequential representation with mechanisms that preserve database relationships and prediction-specific relevance. The findings suggest that large relational contexts can be useful without requiring every cell to interact densely with every other cell during processing.
summary.tldr: Ramba combines selective state-space processing with relational structure and schema-aware gating to learn efficiently across database tables.

title: Ramba: Selective State-Space Models for Relational Deep Learning

abstract: State-space language models such as Mamba and gated linear attention (GLA) offer linear-complexity, parallelisable alternatives to transformers, but often lack the expressivity and robust state-tracking needed for complex reasoning. We address this by reframing sequence modeling through a probabilistic lens, with Bayesian filters as the core primitive. Classical Kalman filters provide principled state and uncertainty estimation but are typically viewed as inherently sequential. We show that reparameterising the Kalman filter in information form casts its updates as an associative scan, enabling efficient parallel training. The resulting Kalman Linear Attention (KLA) layer performs time-parallel probabilistic inference while maintaining explicit belief-state uncertainty, offering strictly more expressive nonlinear updates and gating than GLA variants while retaining their computational advantages. On language modeling tasks, KLA matches or outperforms modern SSMs and GLAs on discrete token-manipulation, state-tracking, and zero-shot commonsense-reasoning benchmarks, and is among the first stacked Bayesian-filtering primitives pretrained at the billion-token scale.

paragraphs: Efficient sequence models can process long inputs with linear computational complexity, but they may struggle to maintain the expressive state representations needed for reasoning. This paper approaches sequence modeling through Bayesian filtering: maintaining a belief about the current state together with explicit uncertainty about that belief as observations arrive.

Classical Kalman filtering is usually treated as a sequential computation. The authors show that expressing it in information form turns its updates into an associative scan, a structure that permits parallel computation across time during training. Their Kalman Linear Attention layer therefore combines probabilistic state tracking with efficient parallel execution, while providing more expressive nonlinear updates and gating than the GLA variants considered.

Experiments report that KLA matches or exceeds modern state-space models and gated linear attention on discrete token manipulation, state tracking, and zero-shot commonsense reasoning benchmarks. The work also pretrains stacked Bayesian-filtering components at billion-token scale. Its central contribution is making explicit uncertainty tracking compatible with the computational advantages that motivate efficient alternatives to Transformers.
summary.tldr: Kalman Linear Attention reformulates Bayesian filtering for parallel training, combining explicit uncertainty tracking with efficient, expressive sequence modeling.

title: Kalman Linear Attention: Parallel Bayesian Filtering For Efficient Language Modeling and State Tracking

abstract: Link prediction is a core challenge in graph machine learning, demanding models that capture rich and complex topological dependencies. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are the standard solution, state-of-the-art pipelines often rely on explicit structural heuristics or memory-intensive node embeddings—approaches that struggle to generalize or scale to massive graphs. Emerging Graph Transformers (GTs) offer a potential alternative but often incur significant overhead due to complex structural encodings, hindering their applications to large-scale link prediction. We challenge these sophisticated paradigms with PENCIL, an encoder-only plain Transformer that replaces hand-crafted priors with attention over sampled local subgraphs, retaining the scalability and hardware efficiency of standard Transformers. Through experimental and theoretical analysis, we show that PENCIL extracts richer structural signals than GNNs, implicitly generalizing a broad class of heuristics and subgraph-based expressivity. Empirically, PENCIL outperforms heuristic-informed GNNs and is far more parameter-efficient than ID-embedding–based alternatives, while remaining competitive across diverse benchmarks—even without node features. Our results challenge the prevailing reliance on complex engineering techniques, demonstrating that simple design choices are potentially sufficient to achieve the same capabilities. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/quang-truong/pencil.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections should exist in a graph. Strong systems often combine graph neural networks with hand-designed structural signals or large tables of node embeddings. Graph Transformers offer another route, but elaborate structural encodings can add substantial overhead. PENCIL investigates how much a plain Transformer can accomplish with a simpler input design.

The model is an encoder-only Transformer that attends over sampled local subgraphs. This allows attention to extract structural relationships from the sampled neighborhood while retaining standard Transformer hardware efficiency and scalability. The paper’s theoretical and experimental analyses show that PENCIL captures richer structural signals than GNNs and implicitly generalizes a broad class of graph heuristics and subgraph-based expressivity.

Across the reported benchmarks, PENCIL outperforms heuristic-informed GNNs, uses far fewer parameters than alternatives based on node identities, and remains competitive even without node features. The findings suggest that some capabilities associated with elaborate graph-specific engineering can emerge from attention over suitable local inputs. The claim is that simple choices may suffice, rather than that every link-prediction setting benefits equally.
summary.tldr: PENCIL shows that a plain Transformer attending to sampled local subgraphs can deliver strong, parameter-efficient link prediction.

title: Plain Transformers are Surprisingly Powerful Link Predictors

abstract: State-space language models such as Mamba match Transformer quality while permitting linear complexity inference, yet still comprise billions of parameters that hinder deployment. While existing one-shot pruning methods are effective for generic linear and attention blocks, they are not designed with the overall Mamba architecture in mind and fail to account for the time-shared and discretized state-transition matrix at the heart of the selective state-space module (SSM). In this paper, we introduce SparseSSM, the first training-free pruning framework that extends the classic optimal brain surgeon (OBS) framework to state space architectures. Our layer-wise algorithm (i) derives an approximate second-order saliency score that aggregates Hessian-trace information across time steps, (ii) incorporates a component sensitivity analysis to guide feed-forward network (FFN) pruning, which also sheds light on where redundancy resides in mamba architecture, (iii) can be easily extended to semi-structured and structured sparsity, and generalized to other SSM-based architectures. Empirically, we prune 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning and observe only limited performance degradation, achieving the current state-of-the-art one-shot pruning algorithm for Mamba-based LLMs.

paragraphs: State-space language models such as Mamba make inference efficient, but their large parameter counts still complicate deployment. Generic pruning methods overlook an important architectural detail: the state-transition matrix is discretized and shared across time. SparseSSM adapts pruning to that structure so that weight importance reflects how the state-space module actually operates.

The framework extends optimal brain surgeon pruning through a layer-wise, approximate second-order importance score. It aggregates Hessian-trace information across time steps, incorporating curvature information from the repeated use of parameters. A separate component-sensitivity analysis guides pruning of feed-forward networks and helps identify where redundancy lies within Mamba.

The authors report removing 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning while observing limited performance degradation, and describe the method as state of the art for one-shot pruning of Mamba-based language models. The framework can also extend to semi-structured and structured sparsity and other state-space architectures. Its main contribution is architecture-aware, training-free compression: repeated temporal use of state-space parameters becomes part of the pruning decision rather than being ignored.
summary.tldr: SparseSSM accounts for state-space dynamics to prune 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning and with limited reported degradation.

title: SparseSSM: Efficient Selective Structured State Space Models Can Be Pruned in One-Shot

abstract: We introduce UCS-Bench, a dataset spanning 170+ hours of egocentric visual observations with 8.1K+ timestamped questions for diagnosing User-Centric Continual Spatial intelligence in egocentric video streams. UCS-Bench targets a new problem that emphasizes dynamic spatial reasoning, long-term memory, and their alignment with users’ real-time locations. We propose DirectMe, a framework that incrementally constructs and maintains a structured spatial memory from streaming egocentric observations. DirectMe enables robust tracking and recall of object locations, all relative to the user’s movement over time. By tightly coupling visual perception with memory updates and spatial reasoning, our approach supports long-horizon queries that require recalling interactions, resolving viewpoint-induced ambiguities, and adapting to dynamic scenes. Our experiments show that DirectMe significantly improves the spatial reasoning of leading multimodal LLMs; it also surpasses many spatially aware and long-form streaming video models. We hope our benchmark and solution will advance spatial intelligence research for egocentric AI assistants. Data and code are available at https://github.com/cocowy1/UCS-Bench.

paragraphs: An assistant watching first-person video needs to remember where objects were and interpret those locations as its user moves. This paper introduces UCS-Bench to evaluate that combination of spatial reasoning, long-term memory, and alignment with the user's current position. The dataset contains more than 170 hours of observations and over 8,100 timestamped questions.

The proposed DirectMe framework incrementally builds and maintains structured spatial memory from incoming video. It connects visual perception to memory updates and spatial reasoning, supporting object tracking and later recall relative to the user's movement. This is designed for questions that span long periods, revisit earlier interactions, or involve ambiguity caused by changes in viewpoint.

Experiments report significant improvements in the spatial reasoning of leading multimodal language models. DirectMe also outperforms many spatially aware models and models for long streaming videos. These results support explicitly maintained spatial memory as a useful component for assistants that must reason about changing scenes and past observations from a moving user's perspective.
summary.tldr: UCS-Bench evaluates continual spatial reasoning from first-person video, and DirectMe improves performance using incrementally updated spatial memory.

title: Keep It in Mind: User Centric Continual Spatial Intelligence Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams

abstract: The additive noise mechanism is a foundational tool for differential privacy (DP) of $T$-dimensional real-valued vector queries. The Gaussian mechanism, utilizing Gaussian noise, is the mostly widely used such mechanism, due to its simplicity and strong privacy guarantees. In this work, we provide justification for this choice, showing that as the dimension $T\to\infty$, no additive-noise mechanism can asymptotically improve on the Gaussian mechanism’s privacy–utility tradeoff for the strong privacy settings typically used. We also develop a new family of Spherical Generalized Gamma DP mechanisms, which contains both the Gaussian mechanism and the recently studied $\ell_2$ mechanism (Joseph et al., ICML 2025). We identify members of this family that outperform both the Gaussian and $\ell_2$ mechanisms in certain low-dimensional settings, and show tight composition of all mechanisms in this family, answering an open question of Joseph et al. regarding the $\ell_2$ mechanism.

paragraphs: Differential privacy can protect a numerical query by adding random noise to its answer. The central tradeoff is how much accuracy must be sacrificed for a given privacy guarantee. This paper examines whether the widely used Gaussian noise distribution is the best choice when the answer contains many coordinates.

The authors show that, as the number of dimensions grows without bound, no additive noise mechanism can asymptotically improve on the Gaussian mechanism’s privacy–utility tradeoff in the strong privacy settings they study. The result gives a theoretical justification for Gaussian noise, with its scope tied to both the high-dimensional limit and those privacy settings.

For certain low-dimensional settings, however, the authors identify better alternatives within a family called Spherical Generalized Gamma mechanisms. This family includes Gaussian noise and the existing l2 mechanism. They also establish tight composition results across the family, describing privacy behavior when mechanisms are combined. Together, the findings distinguish where Gaussian noise has an optimality justification from where other distributions can improve utility.
summary.tldr: Gaussian noise is asymptotically optimal among additive noise mechanisms in the studied strong-privacy regime, while new mechanisms improve certain low-dimensional cases.

title: Asymptotic Optimality of the High-Dimensional Gaussian Mechanism and Improved Low-Dimensional Mechanisms for Differential Privacy

abstract: The performance of autonomous Web GUI agents heavily relies on the quality and quantity of their training data. However, a fundamental bottleneck persists: collecting interaction trajectories from real-world websites is expensive and difficult to verify. The underlying state transitions are hidden, leading to reliance on inconsistent and costly external verifiers (e.g., human or LLM judges) to evaluate step-level correctness. To address this, we propose AutoWebWorld, a novel framework for synthesizing controllable and verifiable web environments by modeling them as Finite State Machines (FSMs) and use coding agents to translate FSMs into interactive websites. Unlike real websites, where state transitions are implicit, AutoWebWorld explicitly defines all states, actions, and transition rules. This enables programmatic verification: action correctness is checked against predefined rules, and task success is confirmed by reaching a goal state in the FSM graph. AutoWebWorld enables a fully automated search-and-verify pipeline, generating over 11,663 verified trajectories from 29 diverse web environments at only $0.04 per trajectory. Training on this synthetic data significantly boosts real-world performance. Our 7B Web GUI agent achieves state-of-the-art on WebVoyager, outperforming all baselines within 15 steps. Furthermore, we observe a clear scaling law: as the synthetic data volume increases, performance on WebVoyager and Online-Mind2Web consistently improves.

paragraphs: Training web agents requires examples of actions that successfully complete tasks, but collecting and checking those examples on real websites is expensive. AutoWebWorld addresses this by generating websites from explicit finite state machines. Each machine specifies the available states, permitted actions, and rules governing how actions move the environment between states.

Coding agents turn these specifications into interactive websites. Because the underlying rules are known, correctness can be checked programmatically: individual actions are compared with transition rules, and completion is verified by reaching a designated goal state. This supports an automated search-and-verification pipeline that produced more than 11,663 verified trajectories across 29 environments at a reported cost of $0.04 per trajectory.

The authors report that training on these synthetic interactions improves performance on real-world web benchmarks. Their 7B agent achieves state-of-the-art results on WebVoyager within a 15-step budget. Increasing synthetic data also consistently improves results on WebVoyager and Online-Mind2Web in their experiments. The contribution connects controllable training environments with verifiable supervision and demonstrated transfer to real website tasks.
summary.tldr: AutoWebWorld generates websites with explicit transition rules, enabling inexpensive verified training trajectories that improve real-world web-agent performance.

title: AutoWebWorld: Synthesizing Infinite Verifiable Web Environments via Finite State Machines

abstract: Traditional robot co-design approaches typically converge to one configuration, which do not explore the flexibility from reconfiguration on heterogeneous environments. On the other hand, existing designs for reconfigurable robots require human-designed configurations. We present Learning to Reconfigure, a holistic pipeline for configuration-control co-optimization of reconfigurable robots in heterogeneous locomotion tasks consisting of several sub-tasks. Our pipeline proposes low-level specialized primitives with a high-level scheduler. To jointly optimize configuration design and control, our primitives employ a multi-tail architecture that disentangles these distinct objectives. Building on this, the scheduler learns to dynamically switch configurations based on global task progress. We evaluate our pipeline on locomotion tasks across walking, flying, and swimming, and compare with the state-of-the-art baselines, including single-robot control and multi-morphology co-optimization algorithms. Quantitative results based on traversal progress show that our pipeline outperforms single-robot baselines by 5.95x average progress. Compared with the reconfiguration-free design given by the co-design algorithms, our robots also exhibit 9.81x progress on average. These results highlight the critical role of configuration adaptation in achieving versatile robotic autonomy in complex worlds.

Learning to Reconfigure jointly learns robot configurations and their control for tasks containing heterogeneous subtasks.

The pipeline separates specialized low-level primitives from a high-level scheduler. Each primitive uses a multi-tail architecture to disentangle configuration design and control while optimizing them together. The scheduler then learns when to switch configurations based on progress through the overall task, connecting local capabilities to the demands of the full route.

Evaluations cover walking, flying, and swimming locomotion tasks. The reported average traversal progress is 5.95 times that of single-robot baselines and 9.81 times that of reconfiguration-free designs produced by co-design algorithms. These are task-progress comparisons in the evaluated settings. They support the value of learning both how to move and when to change configuration for heterogeneous locomotion.
summary.tldr: Learning to Reconfigure jointly learns robot configurations, specialized controllers, and when to switch between them.

title: Learning to Reconfigure: Configuration-Control Co-optimization of Reconfigurable Robots for Heterogeneous Locomotion

abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly capable of tackling complex real-world tasks, yet their reliance on inter-agent coordination, tool use, and long-horizon reasoning makes error recognition particularly challenging. Minor errors can propagate across agents, escalating into task failures while producing long, intertwined execution trajectories that impose significant costs for both human developers and automated systems to debug and analyze. Our key insight is that, despite surface differences in failure trajectories (e.g., logs), MAS errors often recur with similar structural patterns. This paper presents CORRECT, the first lightweight, training-free framework that leverages an online cache of distilled error schemata to recognize and transfer knowledge of failure structures across new requests. This cache-based reuse allows LLMs to perform targeted error localization at inference time, avoiding the need for expensive retraining while adapting to dynamic MAS deployments in subseconds. To support rigorous study in this domain, we also introduce CORRECT-Error, a large-scale dataset of over 2,000 annotated trajectories collected through a novel error-injection pipeline guided by real-world distributions, and further validated through human evaluation to ensure alignment with natural failure patterns. Experiments across seven diverse MAS applications show that CORRECT improves step-level error localization up to 19.8% over existing advances while at near-zero overhead, substantially narrowing the gap between automated and human-level error recognition.

This makes identifying the responsible step difficult, even when a failure began with a small mistake. CORRECT builds on the observation that different-looking execution logs often contain recurring structural patterns of failure.

The framework stores condensed descriptions of those patterns in an online cache. When a new request produces a trajectory to inspect, an LLM can reuse relevant cached knowledge to target its search for the error. This transfers experience without retraining, with the abstract reporting adaptation to changing deployments in subseconds.

summary.tldr: CORRECT reuses cached failure patterns to locate errors in multi-agent systems without retraining, improving localization by up to 19.8%.

title: CORRECT: COndensed eRror RECognition via knowledge Transfer in multi-agent systems

abstract: Recent reinforcement learning (RL) techniques have yielded impressive reasoning improvements in language models, yet it remains unclear whether RL truly extends a model’s reasoning ability beyond pre-training. A central challenge is the lack of control in modern training pipelines, where opaque pre-training data, underexplored mid-training, and complex RL interactions obscure causal effects. To resolve this ambiguity, we develop a controlled experimental framework that isolates the causal contributions of pre-training, mid-training, and RL-based post-training. Our approach employs synthetic reasoning tasks with explicit atomic operations, parseable step-by-step reasoning traces, and systematic manipulation of training distributions. We evaluate along: extrapolative generalization to more complex compositions and contextual generalization across surface contexts. Using this framework, we reconcile competing views on RL’s effectiveness: 1) RL produces true capability gains (pass@128) only when pre-training leaves sufficient headroom and RL data target the model’s edge of competence, tasks that are difficult but not yet out of reach. 2) Contextual generalization requires minimal yet sufficient pre-training exposure, after which RL reliably transfers. 3) Mid-training significantly enhances performance under fixed compute compared with RL alone, demonstrating its central but underexplored role. 4) Process-level rewards reduce reward hacking and improve reasoning fidelity. Together, these results clarify the interplay between pre-training, mid-training, and RL, offering a foundation for improving reasoning language models training strategies. Codes and data are avaialble at Github and HuggingFace

paragraphs: Whether reinforcement learning expands reasoning ability is hard to determine when earlier training data and stages are poorly controlled. This paper builds a controlled framework using synthetic tasks with explicit atomic operations and readable reasoning traces. By manipulating training distributions, it separates contributions from pre-training, mid-training, and reinforcement-learning post-training.

The evaluation distinguishes handling more complex compositions from transferring across surface contexts. In this framework, gains in capability measured by pass@128 appear only when pre-training leaves sufficient room for improvement and reinforcement-learning data targets tasks near the model’s current competence boundary. Transfer across contexts requires a minimal but sufficient amount of pre-training exposure, after which reinforcement learning transfers reliably.

The authors also find that mid-training improves performance under fixed compute compared with reinforcement learning alone. Rewards for intermediate reasoning steps reduce reward hacking and improve the fidelity of reasoning traces. Together, these controlled results explain why reinforcement learning can produce different outcomes depending on prior training and task selection, and identify mid-training and reward design as consequential parts of the pipeline.
summary.tldr: Controlled synthetic experiments show how reasoning gains from reinforcement learning depend on prior training, task difficulty, mid-training, and reward design.

title: On the Interplay of Pre-Training, Mid-Training, and RL on Reasoning Language Models

abstract: Deeper modern architectures are costly to tune, and the base learning rate is often one of the most sensitive hyperparameters. Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) helps explain why many hyperparameters transfer across width. Yet depthwise learning-rate scaling is less understood for modern architectures with convolution, residual aggregation, and attention. To unify various non-recurrent multi-path neural networks such as CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers, we introduce an architecture-dependent notion of effective depth. Under stabilizing initializations and a maximal-update criterion, we derive a shared leading-order -3/2 law for the base learning-rate scale as effective depth grows. Here, the budget controls typical one-step representation-update energy at initialization, and effective depth counts sequential update-bearing units while absorbing fixed local structure into constants. Experiments across diverse architectures confirm the predicted slope and enable reliable zero-shot transfer of learning rates across depths and widths, turning depth scaling into a predictable hyperparameter-transfer problem.

paragraphs: Learning rates are sensitive tuning choices, and selecting them repeatedly becomes expensive as networks grow deeper. Existing maximal-update parametrization helps explain transfer across network width. This paper extends the analysis of learning-rate scaling across depth for non-recurrent architectures with multiple computational paths, including CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers.

The authors define effective depth in a way that depends on architecture. It counts sequential units that contribute updates while absorbing fixed local structure into constants. Under stabilizing initializations and a maximal-update criterion, they derive a shared leading-order rule: the base learning-rate scale decreases with effective depth to the power of minus three-halves. The update budget concerns typical representation changes from one step at initialization.

Experiments across different architectures confirm the predicted slope and support learning-rate transfer across both depth and width without retuning the destination model. The significance is a common scaling rule expressed through architecture-aware depth. Its theoretical scope remains tied to the stated initialization and update conditions, and to leading-order behavior as effective depth grows.
summary.tldr: Under stated initialization and update conditions, a shared effective-depth scaling law enables learning-rate transfer across several network architectures.

title: Hyperparameter Transfer Laws for Non-Recurrent Multi-Path Neural Networks

abstract: Large Language Models have significantly advanced autonomous agents through their sophisticated perception and execution capabilities. Despite effective, agents still struggle with robust decision-making due to passive learning from similar experiences that often confound correlation with causality. Inspired by the Scientific Method, we propose a Cycle-of-Science framework that autonomously explores potential causal pathways through an iterative loop of Hypothesis, Experiment, and Validation, enabling agents to identify truly effective causal dependencies. To be specific, we first leverage causal knowledge to guide the initial hypotheses generation. These hypotheses are then analyzed through experiments using counterfactual samples. Afterward, we perform causal analysis to quantify effects of interventions, deriving well-validated hypotheses for next agent steps. To train our policy, we further introduce a two-stage pipeline that integrates supervised fine-tuning with Counterfactual Preference Optimization, which constructs preference signals from intervention outcomes to reinforce validated reasoning chains. Experiments on benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art approaches.

To be specific, we first leverage causal knowledge to guide the initial hypotheses generation. These hypotheses are then analyzed through experiments using counterfactual samples. To train our policy, we further introduce a two-stage pipeline that integrates supervised fine-tuning with Counterfactual Preference Optimization, which constructs preference signals from intervention outcomes to reinforce validated reasoning chains. paragraphs: An agent can repeat actions associated with successful experiences without understanding which actions caused that success. Cycle-of-Science addresses this weakness by organizing decision making around hypothesis generation, experimentation, and validation. The aim is to give the agent evidence about interventions before it selects its next steps, rather than relying only on resemblance to previous situations.

The framework begins with hypotheses guided by causal knowledge. It then examines them using counterfactual samples, which represent alternatives relevant to testing those hypotheses. Causal analysis measures intervention effects, producing validated hypotheses to guide subsequent actions. This repeated cycle makes experimentation part of the reasoning process and gives proposed decisions a basis in analyzed outcomes.

Training combines supervised fine-tuning with Counterfactual Preference Optimization. The latter turns intervention outcomes into preference signals that favor reasoning chains supported by the validation process. Benchmark experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution therefore connects an agent’s decision procedure with its training objective: both emphasize reasoning that survives counterfactual evaluation.
summary.tldr: Cycle-of-Science trains agents to improve decisions through repeated hypothesis testing, counterfactual experiments, and causal validation.

title: Cycle-of-Science: Reliable Reasoning through Counterfactual Verification for Agent Decision Making

abstract: Attribute interactions are the irreducible dependencies between attributes.Interactions underlie feature relevance and selection, the structure of jointprobability and classification models: if and only if the attributes interact,they should be connected. While the issue of 2-way interactions, especially ofthose between an attribute and the label, has already been addressed, weintroduce an operational definition of a generalized n-way interaction byhighlighting two models: the reductionistic part-to-whole approximation, wherethe model of the whole is reconstructed from models of the parts, and theholistic reference model, where the whole is modelled directly. An interactionis deemed significant if these two models are significantly different. In thispaper, we propose the Kirkwood superposition approximation for constructingpart-to-whole approximations. To model data, we do not assume a particularstructure of interactions, but instead construct the model by testing for thepresence of interactions. The resulting map of significant interactions is agraphical model learned from the data. We confirm that the P-values computedwith the assumption of the asymptotic chi-squared distribution closely matchthose obtained with the bootstrap.

paragraphs: This paper defines attribute interactions through dependencies that cannot be reduced to relationships among smaller parts. It extends the discussion beyond pairwise interactions to general groups of attributes. The operational question is whether a model reconstructed from the parts differs significantly from a model fitted directly to the whole group.

The authors use the Kirkwood superposition approximation to build the part-to-whole model. Comparing it with the direct model supplies a test for interaction. They then construct a model by testing which interactions are present, producing a graphical map of significant relationships learned from the data rather than assuming an interaction structure in advance.

The paper also compares significance calculations based on an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with those obtained by bootstrap. The resulting P-values closely match. This finding supports the reported significance calculations, while the broader contribution is a test-based route from an operational definition of higher-order interaction to the structure of a graphical model.
summary.tldr: The paper tests higher-order attribute interactions by comparing whole-group models with reconstructions from their parts, then builds graphical models from significant interactions.

title: Testing the significance of attribute interactions

abstract: We extend the PAC-Bayes theorem to the sample-compression setting where each classifier is represented by two independent sources of information: a compression set which consists of a small subset of the training data, and a message string of the additional information needed to obtain a classifier. The new bound is obtained by using a prior over a data-independent set of objects where each object gives a classifier only when the training data is provided. The new PAC-Bayes theorem states that a Gibbs classifier defined on a posterior over samplecompressed classifiers can have a smaller risk bound than any such (deterministic) samplecompressed classifier.
originalAbstract: We extend the PAC-Bayes theorem to the sample-compression setting where each classifier is represented by two independent sources of information: a compression set which consists of a small subset of the training data, and a message string of the additional information needed to obtain a classifier. The new bound is obtained by using a prior over a data-independent set of objects where each object gives a classifier only when the training data is provided. The new PAC-Bayes theorem states that a Gibbs classifier defined on a posterior over samplecompressed classifiers can have a smaller risk bound than any such (deterministic) samplecompressed classifier.

paragraphs: This paper extends PAC-Bayes theory to classifiers represented through sample compression. Each classifier is specified by two independent information sources: a small subset of the training examples and a message containing the extra information needed to reconstruct the classifier. The theoretical problem is to bound risk for classifiers described in this way.

The authors construct a prior over a set of objects that does not depend on the observed data. Each object produces a classifier only once the training data is supplied. This distinction between a data-independent object and the classifier it later defines provides the basis for the new bound in the sample-compression setting.

The resulting theorem applies to a Gibbs classifier defined through a posterior distribution over compressed classifiers. It shows that this randomized classifier can receive a smaller risk bound than any individual deterministic compressed classifier under consideration. The statement concerns a possible improvement in the bound, rather than a guarantee of lower actual error in every case. It gives a theoretical reason to consider distributions over compressed classifiers alongside single compressed solutions.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayes extension shows that a Gibbs distribution over sample-compressed classifiers can have a tighter risk bound than individual deterministic classifiers.

title: PAC-Bayes risk bounds for sample-compressed Gibbs classifiers

abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a commonly used step in many algorithms for visualization, classification, clustering and modeling. Most dimensionality reduction algorithms find a low dimensional embedding that preserves the structure of high-dimensional data points. This paper proposes Local Minima Embedding (LME), a technique to find a low-dimensional embedding that preserves the local minima structure of a given objective function. LME provides an embedding that is useful for visualizing and understanding the relation between the original variables that create local minima. Additionally, the embedding can potentially be used to sample the original function to discover new local minima. The function in the embedded space takes an analytic form and hence the gradients can be computed analytically. We illustrate the benefits of LME in both synthetic data and real problems in the context of image alignment. To the best of our knowledge this is the first paper that addresses the problem of finding an embedding that preserves local minima properties of an objective function.

paragraphs: Local Minima Embedding approaches dimensionality reduction through the structure of an objective function. The goal is to construct a lower-dimensional representation that preserves its local minima. This focuses the embedding on how the objective behaves, especially on relationships among the original variables that give rise to those minima.

The resulting representation is intended to help visualize and understand that structure. The function in the embedded space has an analytic form, so its gradients can also be computed analytically. The authors additionally suggest that sampling through the embedding could help discover new local minima of the original function; this is presented as a potential use.

The paper illustrates the method with synthetic data and real image-alignment problems. The authors describe preserving an objective's local-minimum properties through embedding as a previously unaddressed problem, to their knowledge. Its contribution is a different target for dimensionality reduction: a compact view of optimization structure that supports interpretation and may also assist further exploration of the objective.
summary.tldr: Local Minima Embedding creates a low-dimensional view that preserves an objective's local-minimum structure for visualization and potential exploration.

title: Local Minima Embedding

abstract: This paper introduces Learn Structure and Exploit RMax (LSE-RMax), a novel model based structure learning algorithm for ergodic factored-state MDPs. Given a planning horizon that satisfies a condition, LSE-RMax provably guarantees a return very close to the optimal return, with a high certainty, without requiring any prior knowledge of the in-degree of the transition function as input. LSE-RMax is fully implemented with a thorough analysis of its sample complexity. We also present empirical results demonstrating its effectiveness compared to prior approaches to the problem.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces Learn Structure and Exploit RMax (LSE-RMax), a novel model based structure learning algorithm for ergodic factored-state MDPs. Given a planning horizon that satisfies a condition, LSE-RMax provably guarantees a return very close to the optimal return, with a high certainty, without requiring any prior knowledge of the in-degree of the transition function as input. LSE-RMax is fully implemented with a thorough analysis of its sample complexity. We also present empirical results demonstrating its effectiveness compared to prior approaches to the problem.

paragraphs: The paper introduces LSE-RMax, a model-based algorithm for learning structure in ergodic factored-state Markov decision processes. Factored states describe the environment through multiple components, making the dependencies governing transitions part of the learning problem. The algorithm addresses this setting without requiring the transition function’s in-degree to be supplied beforehand.

The in-degree concerns how many inputs participate in a transition dependency. Removing the need for prior knowledge of it reduces the structural information that must be given to the learner. The main guarantee is conditional: when the planning horizon satisfies a stated condition, LSE-RMax achieves a return very close to optimal with high certainty.

The authors fully implement the algorithm and provide a detailed sample-complexity analysis, examining the data demands of learning. They also report empirical effectiveness compared with prior approaches. The contribution combines structure learning, a conditional near-optimality guarantee, and an implemented method, with the guarantee explicitly situated in ergodic factored environments and the required planning-horizon condition.
summary.tldr: LSE-RMax learns factored MDP structure without a supplied transition in-degree and guarantees near-optimal return under a planning-horizon condition.

title: Structure Learning in Ergodic Factored MDPs without Knowledge of the Transition Function's In-Degree

abstract: We study the problem of identifying botnets and the IP addresses which they comprise, based on the observation of a fraction of the global email spam traffic. Observed mailing campaigns constitute evidence for joint botnet membership, they are represented by cliques in the graph of all messages. No evidence against an association of nodes is ever available. We reduce the problem of identifying botnets to a problem of finding a minimal clustering of the graph of messages. We directly model the distribution of clusterings given the input graph; this avoids potential errors caused by distributional assumptions of a generative model. We report on a case study in which we evaluate the model by its ability to predict the spam campaign that a given IP address is going to participate in.

Observed mailing campaigns constitute evidence for joint botnet membership, they are represented by cliques in the graph of all messages. No evidence against an association of nodes is ever available. We reduce the problem of identifying botnets to a problem of finding a minimal clustering of the graph of messages. We directly model the distribution of clusterings given the input graph; this avoids potential errors caused by distributional assumptions of a generative model. We report on a case study in which we evaluate the model by its ability to predict the spam campaign that a given IP address is going to participate in.

paragraphs: The paper investigates identifying botnets and their member IP addresses from a partial view of global spam traffic. Shared participation in an observed mailing campaign provides evidence that addresses belong together. A crucial feature of the setting is that there is no evidence against an association: failing to observe a connection does not establish that two addresses are unrelated.

The authors represent observed campaigns as cliques in a message graph and reduce botnet identification to finding a minimal clustering of that graph. They model the distribution of clusterings directly, conditioned on the observed graph. This avoids potential errors arising from assumptions in a generative model of how the observations were produced.

The evaluation is a case study that asks whether the model can predict which spam campaign a given IP address will participate in. This tests whether the inferred organization captures relationships useful for predicting campaign participation. The abstract describes this evaluation without claiming a particular numerical accuracy or a general guarantee of complete botnet recovery.
summary.tldr: The paper infers botnet groupings from partial spam observations by directly modeling minimal graph clusterings using positive association evidence.

title: Finding Botnets Using Minimal Graph Clusterings
